en: In the preface to the *Zengji xù chuándēng lù*, I happened to read the "Biographies of Confucius" (*Kǒngzǐ shìjiā*) by Sīmà Qiàn. The eulogy states: "Reading the books of Confucius, one can imagine his character.

When visiting Lǔ, I beheld the ancestral temple, the carriages, robes, and ritual vessels of Zhòngní; the students were practicing the rites at their appointed times, and his family [lineage] remained reverent."

It is said that although one may wish to remain, one cannot stay; and that among the kings, lords, and sages of the world, though they were honored in their own time, they have long since passed away.
Yet Confucius was but a commoner whose teachings have been transmitted for over ten generations, and scholars revere him as their master.
In the year Jihai (1409), I resided at Lingyan Mountain in Wu, which during the Yongle era served as the monastic center for the Venerable Nanshi. There, I read the Venerable’s recorded sayings.
I longed to meet these men. On the day of Gengzi, the Imperial Preceptor Qian of Mount Yu bestowed upon me two books:

one titled *Zengji xù chuándēng lù* (Supplementary Collection of the Continued Record of the Lamp), by Master Nanshi; the other titled *Shān'ān zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Mountain Hermitage), by Master Shuzhong.
Reading these two books, I again longed to meet the ancients of old. Formerly, Shuzhong resided at Ruiyan, and Nanshi formerly resided at Lingyan.
I served as the abbot of both Yan’ge and Yueyan, serving the two masters in succession.
When I contemplate those two elders, I see them as the ancients of old; when I contemplate later generations, I see them as the people of today—their sentiments of resonance are much the same.

The records extend only to four generations; though the literary and historical documentation is incomplete, the fundamental principles can still be verified. Thus, later students take them as their model.
This has eradicated the habit of superficial and diffuse proliferation. May those who are like "Zen-shell" practitioners of the present age find some cure!
Three years later, I compiled the *Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* and presented it first to the printers, providing this preface.
Preface to the Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp, Compiled and Augmented by Lingyan Hongzhu, a junior scholar who formerly resided at Ruiyan Baolin Jingtu Monastery on Mount Tiantai.
During my youth, I once read the *Xiu Zizhi Rentian Baojian* (The Precious Mirror of Humans and Devas by Xiu Zizhi). Its preface states: "The former masters..."
That there are virtuous deeds that cannot shine brightly upon the world is the fault of later students.
Upon examining the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps), I observed that such venerable masters as Miaofeng, Beijian, Songyuan, and Pō’ān had all passed away before this book was compiled;
yet they possessed the resolve to compose such works. Consequently, whenever I encountered Chan lineage texts, stupa inscriptions, or biographies, from the end of the Song dynasty onwards...

I have thus committed to writing the words and deeds of those eminent masters of the Yuan dynasty and thereafter whose conduct was exceptionally outstanding. It has now been more than thirty years since then;
however, as I have been unable to travel extensively throughout the rivers and lakes to seek them out, my heart remains unsatisfied.
Therefore, in the year Yiwu of the Yongle era, I sent letters to various great masters and venerable elders, fortunately including the Venerable Huangu of Linggu and [the Venerable] Tiantong.
Master An then searched for them through various channels. Subsequently, he also obtained the assistance of the local man Wu Daoxuan to extensively seek out the lost records.

Having achieved a modest degree of success, he proceeded to arrange them in order. Upon examining the *Xu chuandeng lu* (Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp) following the *Wudeng huiyuan* (Compendium of the Five Lamps), it appears that from the eighteenth to the twentieth generations after Dajian, three generations were included; however, as for their inclusion...
As these [records] were not yet exhaustive, even those already collected were said to be too brief. Now, I have added further entries beyond what was previously gathered;
therefore, this work is titled the *Supplementary Collection of the Continuation of the Lamp Record*. Alas! Generally, those who compose writings must value literary elegance.

I am ashamed of my own lack of literary skill; however, regarding the Way of our school—the direct pointing and single transmission—it is most precious that one writes straightforwardly to manifest its essential meaning.
[End of] Preface. Furthermore, what need is there for elaborate writing? Let those within my school who have attained the essence of the lineage examine this.
Written by the former abbot of Jingshan Chan Monastery, the bhikṣu Wénxiù, in the third month of the fifteenth year of the Yongle era (Dīngyǒu).
This concludes the General Rules for the Expanded Collection of the Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp.
The *Jingde Chuandeng Lu*, compiled by the śramaṇa Daoyuan during the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, is appropriately titled;

moreover, it is based upon authoritative sources. Although the collections compiled by later masters—whether titled *Xudeng* (Continued Lamp), *Lian deng* (Linked Lamp), *Pudeng* (Universal Lamp), or *Guangdeng* (Extensive Lamp)—each possess their own intended significance, they ultimately lack a singular consistency.

The newly acquired *Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp* (Xu chuandeng lu), recently published as part of the Tripitaka by Dabaoen Temple, is a title that is both highly appropriate and well-established.
However, this work was compiled in haste, and its contents are far too meager;
it contains only the recorded sayings and karmic encounters of forty-one individuals, spanning from the eighteenth to the twentieth generations after the Great Mirror (Da Jian).
All others are merely empty names; moreover, there are many errors among the forty-one individuals [previously recorded].

Now, having collected and added to those included in the *Xu chuandeng lu*, it is therefore titled the *Zengji xu chuandeng lu* (Supplementary Collection of the Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
The collection of biographical rules follows the precedent of the *Chuan deng lu*, taking the essential tenets of the school as its primary focus.

Regarding those whose conduct was exceptionally outstanding and worthy of serving as a model for the world, as well as the ancestral masters who transmitted the lineage, their origins and backgrounds are briefly recorded to serve as a standard of emulation for future generations;
others are not recorded in full detail.
The reason why the lineages of transmission have been based solely on Dajian [Huiming] without mentioning Nanyue or Qingyuan is that there was a specific intention behind it.
For our school originates from a single patriarch; why should it be divided into five branches?
Such fragmentation serves no purpose and lacks any underlying meaning. Therefore, what has been compiled here does not differentiate them.
The compilation began from the eighteenth generation of Dajian (Daoyuan).
That it could not be completed within a single generation and had to cease was because the duration of the lineages of transmission—descending from the two masters Dahui and Huqiu—varied in length.
Among the twenty-one individuals within the eighteen generations of the Great Mirror (Dajian), their names have already appeared in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*.
They are now listed again in this succession of biographies for the sake of ease of consultation; beneath each entry in the table of contents, it is noted as "Old Tradition" (*jiuzhuan*).
Regarding those whose biographies appear in the *Xu chuandeng lu* (Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), the note beneath their names in the catalog states "Continued Record.
As for errors within these Continued Records, I have now examined and corrected them; the note beneath their names in the catalog has been changed to "Augmented and Corrected."
Those entries in the *Xu zhuan* (Continued Biographies) that were excessively brief have now been supplemented. Under the titles in the catalog, it is noted as "added for completeness.

Based on various ancestral charts and clarifications from my predecessors, where only the names could be obtained but no records of the occasions of teaching, dialogues, funerary inscriptions, or biographies were found, I have now merely listed those names within the catalog. This is so that they may still be seen in the transmission.
The *Liúyǒuzì* (Origins of the Streams) has its own sources; it would be fortunate if future enthusiasts could search out and supplement it.

Although the seventeenth generation of the Great Mirror (*Dàjiàn*) is already fully contained within the *Wǔdēnghuìyuán* (Compendium of the Five Lamps), there are still some instances therein that were not fully collected.
I have now compiled them separately into a single volume titled *Huìyuánbùyí* (Supplement to the Compendium of the Five Lamps), to await future generations.
In this reprinted edition of the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, these [records] have been added so that they may not perish.
For those whose dharma heirs are not clearly detailed, I have followed the precedent of the *Chuandeng Lu* by attaching them separately at the end of the volume.

Compiled by the former abbot of Jingshan Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Monastery, the bhikṣu Wénxiù of Wújùn,

Chan Master Miaoyun Xianjie of Siming was the son of the Zheng family of Fuzhou. His mother dreamed that an old monk from Mount Lu entered her residence before she gave birth to him.
From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and awakened; he left home to become a monk and did not shy away from traveling about to visit various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*).

The verse on the monk’s return to Fengshan Mountain says: A phoenix chick beneath Fenghuang Mountain— Its plumage just revealed, its wings now complete.
Though iron nets cover the heavens, they cannot restrain it; Its heart to return already rests upon the green wutong branches.
Master Chan Shuan-an Fancong of Yunju in Jiangzhou ascended the hall and, citing the story of Baizhang and the wild fox, offered this verse:
*Baizhang’s wild fox,* *A stone maiden without a husband.* *Once a tear falls,* *The vast ocean dries up.* He then offered a verse on the Buddha’s descent into the world:
*How joyful it is that today the Sole Honored One has descended;* *Shuan-an has nothing to celebrate his birthday.* *I shall simply take this fleeting moment...*
Rosewater: Washing away the pure Dharma-body of lake and mountains.
Chan Master Kong-sou Zongyin of Yuyang at Siming’s Yuyang Monastery was a native of Western Sichuan. Initially, he resided at Chongguang Baoshou on Lake Mountain.
A monk asked, "What is the original body? The Master said, "Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun. The monk asked, "What is the underlying meaning?"
"How is it? The Master said, "Nailed down and glued shut. A monk asked, "What is the matter beyond the Buddha?
The Master said, "Not a Buddha. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "Two slow, three fast. The monk asked, "Since it cannot be named or described, why do you say 'not'?
Furthermore, how is it so? The Master said, "Be careful not to misapprehend it. A monk asked, "What is the Nurturing [Monastery]?"

The King is the ultimate ground for all beings. The Master said, "Under the staff, there is no room for deliberation. A monk said, "The doors and windows have been flung wide open; the subtle mysteries have been swept away.
The Master said, "Do not slander him. He ascended the hall and said: "Seizing the tiger’s head and gathering in its tail—this is to clarify the fundamental principle beneath the first phrase.
Even if you were to clarify the fundamental principle beneath that phrase, what you have grasped would still fall short by a hundred thousand miles. Why?
Therefore, the Great Wisdom Patriarch hung up a goat’s head here while selling dog meat; the Elder Fozhao falsely assumed another’s name here to farm the government fields.
Now that this humble monk has come to succeed their fragrant dust, how ultimately shall he provide for them?
He raises his staff and says: "In my whole life I have possessed nothing; I have only this single cane. He ascends the hall and says: "The Great Way is level and expansive, transcending all names."
To negate appearances is to lose the essential meaning; to establish them is to deviate from the fundamental principle.

From the time of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old until the present day, whenever good spiritual friends manifest great capacity and display great function, they have all been like locking the void or dreaming within a dream—transgressions as vast as the heavens.
Did Sealer (Yinzhuo) manage to avoid having his face flayed when he smashed it open? After a long silence, he struck the meditation seat and said: "It does not enter the realm of the startling."

Waves. It is difficult to encounter a fish that suits one's taste. [The Master] ascends the hall: "Two arise from the existence of one; do not cling even to the one. Upon the level ground, there are countless dead people.
When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. In the pit of excrement, heads emerge and submerge. Solitary and towering, lofty and majestic:
the flowers must bloom throughout the night; do not wait for the morning breeze. [The Master] ascends the hall: "The Iron K'un-lun Child."
He takes a tumble. The Persian from the South Sea cannot finish his dance; at midnight he loses his waist-cloth.
Old Uncle Wang of the East Village falls over laughing. He strikes the meditation seat once and descends.
Chan Master Tienniu Yin of Lingyin Temple in Hangzhou ascended the hall and said: He cited Nanquan’s address to the assembly:
"Since I was young, I have raised a water buffalo. If I intend to let it loose to the east of the stream, it will inevitably eat the king’s grass and water;
if I let it loose to the west of the stream, it will likewise inevitably eat the king’s grass and water. Now, I cannot help but follow..."
To offer a mere trifle is not to see it all. The verse says: It is better to offer a mere trifle according to one's means;
To call this an ordinary matter is already a mistake. When the horns and head are revealed by the green grass at the stream’s edge, To whom does that single raincoat belong amidst the mist and rain?
Chan Master Shigan Zhenghao’s Verse on Returning to the Lakeside: Birds do not startle in flight, the waters do not flow;
The azure clarity is vast and empty, a cool and secluded autumn. Upon the tip of the single strand there is no fragrant bait; The wind rolls the reed blossoms down onto the fishing boat.
○ Regarding Zen Master Hai-men Shi Qi of the Tian-tong Monastery in Ming-chao:

Having been summoned from Rui-yan in Tai-zhou by imperial decree to ascend to Tian-tong, there was a novice (tong-xing) named Ri who followed the Master as he offered incense at each of the various halls. When the ceremony was concluded, they returned to the abbot’s quarters (fang-wang).

Before the Buddha, the Master addressed the Buddha, saying: "In the early morning, I recite one fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and dedicate the merit toward True Suchness (*tathatā*), and so forth.
It was when the Master was leaving the door of the abbot’s quarters that he began reciting from the "Chapter on the Exquisite Adornments of the World-Ruling Lord" (*Lokēśvararāja-vyūha*).
By the time he had returned to the abbot’s quarters, his recitation was finished. A novice monk reported these events to the assembly of monks, but none of them believed him. The Master—
He said, "Each of you eighty-one people take up one scroll of scripture. I, an old monk, shall recite it from the Dharma seat.

The assembly of monks followed his command. When the Master finished reciting one scroll, each of the eighty-one people heard themselves reciting the scroll they held in their own hands until it was finished.
Only then were the doubts of the assembly resolved, and they knew that the Master was an incarnation of a Great Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Yan of Donglin Wan’an:
○ Chan Master Zuzhu of Dun’an, Gong’an County, Jingnan Prefecture, a native of Nanping. Entering the hall, he said: "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
All the drool of the wild foxes has been squeezed out; the mountain-demon’s cave has been overturned. On the level fields and shallow grass..."
Inside, the scorched-tailed tiger is revealed. Amidst the vast expanse of the great void, the magnificent falcon soars through the high heavens.
A-he-he! Its wind-bone is exposed. Carelessly drawn forth before the multitude, what exactly is this thing? Clearly manifest! *Du-du!* (A cry of realization).
Ascending the hall, he said: "Jade dew hangs from the green grass; the golden wind stirs the white pondweed. A single cry from a cold wild goose awakens those who have not yet awakened.
Tingzhou Baoen Chan Master Fayuan was a native of Guozhou. Ascending the hall, he cited the story of the cause concerning Juzhi’s raising of his finger.
[The Master said: "A beautiful woman rises from sleep too lazy to comb her hair; she takes up a golden hairpin and, having inserted it, leaves it as it is.
For the most part, it is because her natural form and bones are so excellent that she is elegant even without applying rouge or powder."
Chan Master Kengtang Yanchong of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou Prefecture was the son of the Sheng family from Yuqian.
In his youth, he relied upon Master Yikan of Mingkong Monastery as his teacher. He first studied under Dayu Hongzhi and Zhengtang Dayuan. Later, he heard Donglin say to the assembly:
"In this place of mine, there is nothing else mysterious or subtle; there is only soup made of wood shavings and rice made of iron nails. It is up to you..."

As he chewed [the food], his spirit felt a secret joy. He went directly to pay his respects and set forth his insights and understanding. Lin said, "According to your point of view, you are sitting squarely within the realm of perception.
The Master remained in doubt and could not cease his inquiry; he cast aside everything he had previously attained all at once.
One day, hearing a monk cite Nanquan’s saying, "People of this age see this single stalk of flower as if it were a dream," he was suddenly silent with realization.
Suojue said, "Striking the grass is only intended to startle the snake. The next day, when entering the room, Lin asked, "Where was it that Yantou secretly revealed his meaning?
The Master said, "Today I have caught this old thief. Lin said, "The life of the Great Master Bodhidharma rests in your hands.
As the Master was about to open his mouth, he was suddenly struck a fist to the chest. He attained great enlightenment immediately. Directly—
Sweat broke out and soaked his back. Nodding his head, he said to himself, "Linji’s claim that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma was not much was no empty talk.
He then presented this verse: "To act for others, one must act to the end; To kill a man, one must see blood.

Deshan and Yantou— Ten thousand miles, a single bar of iron. Linyan approved of him. Later, after taking up residence, he ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One preached what is not preaching."
“Kāśyapa heard what was not heard. [The Master] planted his staff upright and said: “Where do the flowing waters and yellow leaves come from?
An ox, trailing crows of winter, passes through a distant village. He ascended the hall and cited Xuefeng’s instruction to the assembly: “The entire earth is this gate of liberation.
For what reason, when one takes it by the hand, can one not pull oneself in? The Master said: “Xuefeng of great stature has split his statement into two pieces. Since the entire earth...”
"This is a gate of liberation. What is the use of dragging it about? He ascended the hall and said: "If you go on exclusively like this, the grass before the Dharma Hall will be ten feet deep.
If you come back exclusively like this, the mud underfoot will be three feet deep. Tell me, what then is the way?"

A leap month occurs once every three years; the rooster cries toward the fifth watch. Entering the hall, the Master raised the example of his late teacher, Wan’an: “Sitting upon the Buddha’s throne, he hacked at the Buddha’s feet; he did not respect Confucius of the Eastern House, but instead sought ritual and music in a foreign land. The Master said: [The Master then continued: “If you wish to see the true face of the Buddha, you must first see the true face of yourself. If you can see your own true face, then you will naturally understand the meaning of ‘hacking at the Buddha’s feet. But tell me, where is the true face of the Buddha? And where is the true face of yourself? He struck the meditation seat once and descended. [Later, the Master added: “Three years pass and a leap month arrives; the rooster cries toward the fifth watch. This is the time when the old fellow Wan’an appeared in the world. He sat upon the Buddha’s throne and hacked at the Buddha’s feet—not out of disrespect for Confucius of the Eastern House, but because he was seeking the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

If you can understand this, you will know that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not something to be found in books or in the words of others. It is something you must realize within yourself. Do not seek it elsewhere; look back at your own mind. If you can see your own mind, you will see the Buddha. If you can see the Buddha, you will see the Way. If you can see the Way, you will see the self. When these three are seen as one, then you have attained the Great Matter. He struck the meditation seat once more and descended.
Entering the mud and entering the water is not non-existent. As for the former masters, how can one help them? A cicada clings to a withered tree;
its weeping is exhausted, yet it does not turn its head back. [Hitting the meditation staff] he said: "Truly, there is one who does not turn his head back.

I, Jingci, shall pay you three prostrations within this broken vessel. He ascended the hall and said: "The Buddhas of the three periods speak of existence within non-existence. *Lai* (pronounced lǎng; a poisonous drug) and *dàng* (pronounced dàng; a medicinal herb). *Shí* (to gather).
Flower-needles. The six ancestral masters sought within and found nothing. A monkey reaching for the moon in the water—how can one speak of this beyond these two paths?
I care not for matters of rise or fall; all day long I dwell amidst the clouds over Lake Dongting.
Yuan’an, having accepted the invitation from Zhizhe, led the assembly, saying: "On South Mountain there is an old demon king; his piercing eyes flash with lightning."
With a mouth like a blood-basin, he reviled the Buddhas and Patriarchs; with teeth like sword-trees, he scolded all quarters. Though the winds of karma blew many times, they could not move him.
When the winds did finally move him, at the side of Mount Yun Huang, together with Śaṇavāsa and the Great Being Fu, he shattered his dwelling in a single fire.
He remains, as ever, Old Man Meng; he deceives countless foolish men and women, opening their eyes wide as they enter the cauldron of boiling oil.
Suddenly, if a monk were to come forth and ask, "Since you are a *kalyāṇamitra*, why do you deceive people into entering the cauldron?
one should simply tell him, "This is not your realm. Later, he passed away and was interred in a south-facing hermitage within the monastery.

Chan Master Zhizhe Yu’ān Zhēncí of Wǔzhōu was a native of Tóngchuān. His secular surname was Lǐ. Initially, he relied upon Chengdū Zhèngfǎ Monastery to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
Later, he traveled among the lecture halls and listened to the *Niyuanjue Jing* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra). Upon reaching the passage: “The four elements are each separate;
where, then, does this illusory body now reside? Ultimately it has no substance and is truly identical to a phantom,” he attained a profound realization.
He composed a verse, saying: "A single bright pearl is here with me; touched or moved, it emits light that shakes the earth.
He presented this to various lecturers, but none were able to understand it. Upon returning, he presented it to his own teacher, who then tested him with the koan of "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature.
The teacher said, "Even hundreds of thousands of millions of koans do not go beyond this verse. His teacher—
Considering this to be insolent, he rebuked him and expelled him. The Master then traveled south to Mount Lu, where he registered as a resident at Yuan Tong.

At that time, Wan’an was serving as the West Hall Preceptor; when he entered the room for the assembly, he raised the following koan: "A monk asked Yunmen, 'When one brushes away the dust and sees the Buddha, what then?'"

The Gatekeeper said, "Even the Buddha is but a defilement. As soon as he heard these words, the Master gave a shout and pointed his finger at his own chest, saying, "Even the Buddha is but a defilement.
The Master then offered this verse: "Seeking the Buddha by brushing away defilements— The Buddha, too, is but a defilement. Question finished, answer finished; In an instant, one turns over."
"I urge you to drink one more cup of wine; once you have gone west past the Yang Pass, there will be no old friends. Furthermore, he offered this verse on the Samādhi of Dust-to-Dust:
"Rice in the bowl, water in the bucket; The Treasure-King Kunlun sits at the bottom of the abyss.
Upon every speck of dust, Mount Sumeru walks; A clear-eyed Persian laughs and snaps his fingers. From the branches of coral, a pure breeze arises. Wan’an deeply approved of this.
Chan Master Shaoyuan of Zhaojue in Chengdu Prefecture ascended the hall and said: A monk asked Yunmen, "What is it like when the trees wither and the leaves fall?
Yunmen replied, "The body is exposed to the golden wind. The Master said: "To understand the mechanism of falling into the tiger's trap, one must be a patch-robed monk of true substance.
Great Master Yunmen possessed a samādhi that transcends the common herd; he struck the joints and knocked at the gates within a flash of insight."
"From amidst a flash of lightning, a hand emerges to untangle the glue, remove the bonds, pull out the wedges, and extract the nails.
Not bad at all—a truly skilled hand! But examine it closely, and it is much like lending a ladder to a thief. I, Zhaojue, am not like this. Suppose a monk were to ask:
'What is it like when the tree withers and the leaves fall? I would simply answer him: 'The setting clouds and the solitary wild goose fly together.'"
"The autumn waters share the same color as the vast sky. Now tell me, is this the same as Yunmen’s [teaching], or is it different?
He spoke again: "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and inconceivable. Ascending the hall, he said: "Melting the jars, plates, hairpins, and bracelets into a single gold;

churning the cream, curd, and clarified butter into a single flavor. Thus, when guest and host are in accord and inner and outer are harmonious, this is the Way of the Five Ranks of Lord and臣 (Minister)."
A simultaneous penetration. These four kinds of critical examination are strung together as one. If you let go, there is fine rain misting and the autumn wind whistling;
if you hold fast, it is utterly empty—dare anyone look directly at it? Now tell me, is it better to help people by letting go, or is it better to help people by holding fast?
He spoke again: "Casually, it is like the arrival of the autumn wind; without intent, it cools others, yet they cool themselves."
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: When Zhaozhou first met Nanquan, he asked, "What is the Way? Nanquan said, "The ordinary mind is the Way.
Zhaozhou asked, "Is it still necessary to direct one's intention toward it? Nanquan said, "To intend to direct oneself toward it is already to deviate.
Zhaozhou said, "If one does not intend to direct oneself, how can one know it is the Way? Nanquan said, "The Way belongs neither to knowing nor to not-knowing. Knowing is deluded awareness; not..."
"Know this to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). If one truly penetrates the Way of non-doubt, it is vast and open like the great void, without any obstruction.
The Master said, "How extraordinary, you venerable practitioners of Zen! Although this is a novice śrāmaṇera who has only just entered the Path, he turned [the situation] around with a single stroke;
is he not a person of spiritual acuity? Nanquan was like a skilled archer releasing an arrow; the arrow released struck the red heart. If it were not...
This is Zhaozhou; it is truly difficult to take up. He immediately strikes the pivot at the very point where "the ordinary is the Way.
He discards the objects within the breast and loses the mechanism before one's eyes. Thus, he is clear in every instance and manifest in every thing.

Being able to walk with his feet guided by faith and speak with his mouth guided by faith, he casually brings forth [the teaching], and in every step there is a path for emerging. By what means does he do this?
Consider this: Did you not see when a monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? and the reply was, "The cypress tree in the courtyard"?
When he asked, "All phenomena return to One; where does the One return? the reply was, "I am making a cotton robe in Qingzhou that weighs seven catties.
And when he asked, "What is Zhaozhou? the reply was, "The east gate, the west gate, the south gate, and the north gate."
To untangle the adhesions and remove the bonds for others, to pull out the nails and extract the wedges;

to cut off the tongues of all people under heaven and pierce through the nostrils of all people under heaven—is this not precisely the pivotal mechanism of the teaching that "ordinary mind is the Way"?
It is certainly not mere decorative rhetoric or stacked-up verses intended to push people into stagnant water. This very thing is the sand.
"Midi, you must learn how to take this up. How so? It is said: 'If one wishes to travel a thousand li, the first step is the beginning.
Under the bright sun and clear sky, exert yourself with all your vigor."
When the Senior Monk Jian of Huizhou was serving as the Head Seat under Wan’an at Mount Jing, Wan’an asked him:
“One, two, three, four, five, six, seven—no clear-eyed monk can count them out. Try counting them for me. Jian gave a shout.
Wan’an then said, “Seven, six, five, four, three, two, one—what do you make of that? As Jian prepared to respond, Wan’an struck him.
Chushi said, "For now, do not speak so recklessly. Jian was suddenly enlightened by these words and immediately spoke a verse:
"For now, do not speak so recklessly; my hair stands on end with cold. I knew only that the plum had ripened, unaware that my nose had gone numb.

He also once composed a verse on the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature: "The old fellow Zhaozhou has no face at all. To speak thus is to deviate from the essence beneath the words. He was truly divine.
It was known as "The Wailing of Ghosts. He passed away at the age of only thirty, and among his friends and associates, there was none who did not mourn him deeply.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Lan’an Xū of Xīchán.
Chan Master Mùān Ānyǒng of Gǔshān, Fúzhōu, was the son of the Rǔ clan of Mínciàn. He entered the monastic order at the age of twenty.
Before long, he visited Lǎn’ān at Yúnmén. One day, while entering the inner room for instruction, Lǎn’ān said, "I do not ask about words, nor do I ask about wordlessness;
when the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time, you must not seek understanding in that place where the World-Honored One remained silent. He then let out a shout.
The Master suddenly attained awakening and prostrated, saying, "Had it not been for today’s inquiry, how could I have lost this opportunity before my very eyes? Lǎn’ān granted him approval.
Ascending the hall after residing [at the monastery]: To clarify this matter, one must possess the skillful means of the "flashing lightning and striking sparks.
Only then can one cast off the whole body at the precipitous head of the cliff and attain great settled dwelling in the depths of the white clouds.
If you instead peer upon the ground searching for a golden needle, your skull will surely burst right now. Reaching this point, even if you were to perceive the opportune moment—
Transformation. Without meeting a sharp edge, one’s entire body is uniquely liberated; it is like wading through flowing water.

But as for this one phrase of the fundamental portion being fully raised—how would you speak of it? He struck the whisk and said: "The seven-star light is drawn forth, brilliant and radiant; releasing attachments, one may roam freely throughout the world.
Ascending the hall, he cited Master Muzhou’s address to the assembly, saying: "If you people have not yet attained a point of entry, you must..."
"Once you have attained an entry point, you must not forget this old monk. The Master said, "Speaking in such a manner, how thick is your face?
Muduan said, "It is not so. As long as you have not attained an entry point, you must attain one.
Once you have attained an entry point, you must cast that very entry point away before you can succeed. He then took up his staff while ascending the hall.
The staff said, "Linji’s little page has never hit the mark. Today he is acting entirely foolish, yet he wants everyone to know that there is something here.
He threw down his staff and descended from the seat. A monk asked, "What is it like when one turns over and stands upside down atop Mount Sumeru?
The Master said, "I have never seen the Morning Star appear. The monk said, "In that case, the oceans overflow and the mountains collapse."
[The monk] departs. The Master says, "Do not act recklessly. The monk then shouts. The Master says, "The sound of thunder is vast, yet there is not a single drop of rain.
Zen Master Nanya of Longxiang Baitang in Wenzhou ascends the hall and says: "Upon the summit of Rui Peak, by the Phoenix Pavilion, we rely on each other with a bowl of plain congee;
with our heads shrouded in a patchwork robe, we sit in meditation. The Second Patriarch prostrated three times and remained in his place."
To stand [in such a position] is already to be fully exposed as a mere "old barbarian" (lao zāohú) of the Dharma; it is a scene of total ruin from marrow to skin.
As for the rest of such a lot, what is there to say? When Baitang speaks thus, does he avoid being censured by those in all quarters? Or not?

[He] struck the meditation seat and said: "It would have been better to let the prisoner go free and allow his wisdom to grow. Ascending the hall, he said: "The great capacity values directness; the great function values sudden manifestation.
Even if there were a 'biting the bullet' capacity, it must be killed with a single blow of the hammer.

Why? Because within the treasury of our King, there is no such blade. Ascending the hall, [he said]: "Purple ferns stretch out their fists as bamboo shoots break through the tips; the willow flowers have flown away, and the green shadows interlace. It is clear."
The single-line transmission of the Western Patriarch: the yellow oriole sings its song while nesting.

If you can see this clearly here and have deep conviction in it, then according to the standards of other quarters, you would certainly be settled beneath a bright window. But under the gate of Longxiang, we simply strike them dead with a single blow.
Why? It is not that I find it difficult to dwell together with others; it is mostly because the monastic and the lay must be clearly distinguished.
Chan Master Tianwang Zhiqing of Fuzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his whisk, he said:
"This very thing cannot be covered by heaven nor carried by earth; it pervades the world and pervades space, forming a whole and forming a mass.
Reaching this point, where can the Buddhas of the three periods find it to grasp? Where can the Patriarchs of the six generations find it to uphold? Throughout the world..."
Where can one describe or delineate a patch-robed monk? Unless one has attained it for oneself and realized it for oneself, one will merely practice the dual movement of "knocking" and "singing.
Even so, this is not yet the place where a patch-robed monk walks. What, then, is the place where a patch-robed monk walks?
This is not leaping across the sea; it is walking freely through a thicket of jackals and tigers.
The Master of the Anfen Hermitage at Jianmen in Nanjian Prefecture had, in his youth, studied under Mukan at Anguo Temple.
Later, he relied upon Lan’an, yet did not attain profound realization. He took his leave to visit Daie at Jing Mountain. As he was traveling along the riverbank, he gazed up toward the palace.

[The text is] missing. Upon hearing the yamen officials announce that the Minister was coming, he was suddenly and greatly enlightened. He composed a verse, saying: "For many years this matter has hung upon my breast;
I have questioned all quarters, yet my eyes remained unopened. Now, at this moment, liver and gall are both rent asunder— A single cry:
'The Minister comes upon the river! He then went directly back to Xichan. Lan’an welcomed him and bestowed upon him the *kāṣāya*. From then on, he did not observe formal regulations.
He later lived in a hermitage at Jianmen, where his transformative influence spread throughout the regions south of the Ling Mountains. Scholars followed him;
the gāthās and verses he composed flowed from his hand, totaling over a thousand pieces that circulated widely in the world. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"Regarding this very field of land, you all—tell me, before heaven and earth were yet divided, where did it abide? Penetrate this directly."

"Life and nature are entirely in the hands of this mountain monk. When one examines them closely, there are immeasurable transgressions.

Before the fifth day, all the stars in the heavens arch toward the north; after the fifteenth day, there is no water in the human world that does not flow toward the east.
Having set aside both what precedes and what follows, the local dialects differ in every place. Then, counting on his fingers, he said:

The Dharma Successor of Chan Master Jiaozhongguang:
Chan Master Zhong’an Huikong of Fashi Monastery in Quanzhou, a native of the Cai family of Ganzhou. On a spring day, he ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
He held up his staff and struck once, saying, "First, strike the head of the spring ox. He struck again, saying, "Afterward, strike the tail of the spring ox.
Startled, the void enters into the space within a lotus fiber; Śākyamuni has no way to hide his tracks, and Maitreya flees for a thousand miles.
Mañjuśrī, however, knows where it lands; he claps his hands and laughs with joy. But tell me, what is it that he rejoices in?
"Ma! Last night the spring breeze entered the gate; immediately one sees a thousand flowers blooming upon the pestle's tip. [He ascends the hall.
"In the pavilions and towers of a thousand homes, a sudden autumn wind blows; one only notices the coolness arising in one’s sleeves, unaware that the leaves are falling from the groves.

The Sūtra says: The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
Why is this? The Tathāgata says that all these minds are 'not-minds'; it is for this reason they are called 'minds'."
"Do you understand? When one’s ambitions are fulfilled by the spring breeze, the horse’s hooves gallop swiftly; in a single day, one beholds all the flowers of Chang’an.

Chan Master Hunyuan Tanmi of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Lu family of Tiantai. He left home life under Dao-rong of Zifu Temple.

At the age of sixteen, he received full ordination and studied the teachings of the Tiantai school. Later, he abandoned that path to visit Dahui at Mount Jing, where he met Xuechao Yi and Ciyuan Yuan.
Upon entering Min, he stayed at both Dong and Xi Chan monasteries but did not experience awakening. He then went to Jiaozhong in Quannan, where he was made to delight [the master].

Having resigned from his official duties and returned to his former status as a retired monk, he happened to encounter the karmic conditions of Xiangyan’s striking of the bamboo. Suddenly, he attained a profound realization.

He composed a verse and presented it to Zhong, who tested him with the words, "Xuansha did not yet fully penetrate," and [Xuanjue] responded without any obstruction. Zhong said, "Only then may you go see Miaoxi.
He then took his leave and went to Mei Yang, where he served diligently for four years. Later, when he ascended the hall to teach, he said: "The Buddhas appearing in the world—strike them down!"

[The Master] ascends the hall. Deshan’s informal teaching (xiaocan) was "no answering of questions," yet for a thousand ages it has become a subject of talk within the monastic community.

Before even stepping onto the ship's railing, he deserves thirty blows. As before, they continue to deceive one another. Hunyuan today makes such a judgment;

Later, he manifested parinirvāṇa; his stupa was erected at his home mountain.
Chan Master Weiyin of Xin’an, Qingyuan in Jizhou, was the son of the Li family of Changle in Fu.
At the age of eleven, he left Min and relied upon Master Guang of Ganjiang Chan-yue Lan-’e as a novice. He shaved his head and received the five white precepts.
Daoguang obtained monastic robes and subsequently bestowed upon the various *maṇavas* the "Verses on the Fifty-three Spiritual Friends of the Buddha-land.

without affairs, contemplate the single mind," he immediately grasped the essential point. Daoguang was amazed by his spiritual capacity and sent him back to Min to visit Mount Gu.
Foceng Cairen of Dongchan, Yue’an Gaofeng of Xichan, and Lan’an Xu of Xichan were all honored with official degrees;

At that time, Huiahan was residing at Guishan; he had been there for barely a month when, while groping for his bedding in the night, he found the *Jingde Record*.

he simply said, "Rest, and you are *bodhi*. The nature-pure, luminous mind is not obtained from others. If it cannot be obtained from others, one must find its gate.
They have been running headlong from south to north and back and forth from east to west, reaching the end of years and the exhaustion of seasons without a single place of rest.
Can you all find rest? Enough, enough! Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: One day, Master Huìtáng asked a monk, "Where have you come from?"
He replied, "Nanxiong Prefecture. The Master said, "Come out here for what purpose? He replied, "To seek out a venerable elder.
The Master said, "It would be better to return to your hometown. He asked, "I do not know, Master; what is the meaning behind your command that I return to my hometown?
The Master said, "In your hometown, three coins can buy a piece of salted fish as large as a palm. The Teacher said, "I would rather have my body shattered into atoms than [accept such a thing]."
"I will never let another monk’s eyes go blind. Huìtáng was slightly more adept than that. Some fellows would simply say, "It is difficult to forget what one is accustomed to.
What common ground for conversation could there be? He ascended the hall and cited the koan of King Kāśīputra asking Venerable Siṃha about the "emptiness of the aggregates" (skandha-śūnyatā).
The Master offered this verse: "When did the Venerable ever attain the emptiness of the aggregates? King Kāśī merely cut his own spring breeze in vain. The peach..."
After the rain of flowers has fallen, it dyes the flowing waters of a stream crimson.
Master Xue’an Congjin of Tiantong in Siming was a native of Nanxi in Yongjia. His secular surname was Zheng.
He took refuge with Master Puan at Yuanzi Temple, who served as his preceptor for the tonsure. He then visited Xinwen at Ruiyan. One day, he entered the inner quarters to see Xinwen.
The Master was asked about "a flake of snow on a red furnace. As he was about to answer, he suddenly grasped the essential meaning.
He remained there for three years before entering Fuzhou to see Fozhi at Xichan Monastery. When asked, "Where have you come from? the Master replied, "From Siming.
Fozhi asked, "Have you seen the 'Dull Sack'? The Master gave a shout. Fozhi struck him. The Master caught his fist and said, "Master, do not be so hasty. Fozhi—
"Blind fellow! Stand here. At that time, Xinwen was the head of Jiangxin Monastery; when the Master returned, he went to visit him, and Xinwen appointed him as the *karmadāna* (Vina).
One day, Xinwen asked the Master, "A single shout distinguishes guest and host, and the illumination and function act simultaneously. What is 'a single shout distinguishing guest and host'?
The Master then shouted. Xinwen said, "Is this shout the guest or the host? The Master said, "As for the guest, it is always the guest; as for the host..."

The Master [Zhaozhou] said, "From beginning to end, you are the host. Hearing this, the monk laughed and said, "You have lost your eyesight again. The Master then presented a verse, saying: "A single shout distinguishes guest and host;
Yet once more, you have lost your eyesight. I flip a somersault backward and go; Treading upon and killing a dead toad.
Initially, he resided at Lingyan in Yizhen. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Lingyan? The Master said, "The cold spring of Deer-Run soaks the bright moon."
Longdougang was deeply hidden amidst white clouds. A monk asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "At midnight, Mount Sumeru is placed in the nostrils. The monk asked, "What is Chan? The Master said, "Looking up, one does not see the sky.
The monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "The whole body enters the wild grasses. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said—

A thousand layers, a hundred turns. The monk said, "An adept. The Master said, "Withdraw. Ascending the hall, he said: "When the shadow of the golden mallet moves, the Buddhas of the three periods dare not face it head-on.
When the Dharma-ordinance is put into practice, external paths and celestial demons all fold their hands in submission.
Steep and towering, like wood without boards; pure and naked, requiring no contrivance. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, there is no need for doubt. How excellent!"
Let go of both good and evil at once. Then, mixing mud with water, take up the handle and pull the plow;
moving freely in all directions as things unfold, there is no hindrance whatsoever. At such a time, tell me: how does one sing the "Song of Great Peace"? After a long silence:
"The iron boat rests across the ancient ford; the old family style is re-established. He ascended the hall and said: "To turn over within the diamond circle..."
He puts on the nostrils of Śakra; he lets go his hand atop a precipice. He brings forth the eyes of Bodhidharma; going and returning three times, his spirit is not yet exhausted.
Once the pivot of the mechanism turns, its momentum cannot be halted. Holding the tail of a scorpion upside down, he makes the Śrāvakas his servants;

stroking the whiskers of a tiger in the proper direction, he calls the Bodhisattvas his slaves. Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya is not yet born; such is the Dharma and the Patriarchate.
He placed [the monastery] entirely under the charge of Tiantong. How should one manage the seizing and the releasing? After a long silence, he said:

"A holeless iron hammer is hurled right at your face; a pure breeze rises across the heavens and over the earth. On the twenty-third day of the seventh month in the sixth year of the Qingyuan era, he requested a bath, changed his robes, and wrote a verse.
He then set down his brush and passed away. He was eighty-four years old, with seventy years of monastic seniority. His entire body was interred at Xinfeng.

To the left of the stupa, it is recorded that the Chan Master Yue-lin Shiguan of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou—disciple of the late Elder Monk Zheng Chan Master—was by secular surname Huang. He was a native of Hougan in Fuzhou. [He became a] monk...
The monk asked, "When Sanxing’s Way meets a person, it emerges; when it emerges, it does not act for the person's sake. What is your intention here? The Master said, "Wrong.
The monk asked, "Xinghua says, 'When my Way meets a person, it does not emerge; when it emerges, it immediately acts for the person's sake.

What about this? The Master said, "Wrong. The monk said, "Xinghua’s spear and banner stand upright; Sanxing’s liver and gall are laid bare together. The Master said, "You are merely citing [the words]."
[The Master] entered the hall. A monk asked, "How does the Master benefit people today? The Master said, "One blow, one mark. He ascended the hall and said:
"At this very place, all Buddhas turn the Great Dharma Wheel; at this very place, all Buddhas enter Parinirvāṇa.
At such a time as this, where do you see Old Śākyamuni? After a long silence, he said: "Joining palms at the main gate; [entering] the Buddha Hall."
[The Master] burned incense inside [the hall]. Ascending the hall, he said: "This world does not move; that world does not change. It arises where it is;
it is extinguished wherever it is. A-he-he! To see or not to see? A gust of autumn wind blows, and two or three leaves fall.
Ascending the hall again, he cited Chan Master Yangqi’s address to the assembly: "When body and mind are pure, all objects are pure. Pure, pure..."
Pure. Body and mind are pure. Do you still know where the old man of Yangqi has landed? "The fish bought on the boat is especially fine;
the wine purchased after treading through the snow is doubly fragrant."
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Guang of Donggu at Lingyin:
Chan Master Zhigong Yiju of Tianning in Mingzhou ascends the hall. A single phrase prior to the triggering of the mind contains ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations.
Once every three days there is wind; once every five days there is rain. The fields are saturated with water and all things flourish. But tell me, what about Shen...?
"How long are the whiskers of the Iron Ox of the Prefecture? [The Master] struck his staff and descended from the seat.
Chan Master Or-an Ti of Jiaoshan, a Dharma successor of [the aforementioned master].
Chan Master Chi-dun Zhi-ying of Tian-tong in Mingzhou appeared in the world at Yanfu in Chaling County, and subsequently moved to Jinshan.
He served at Lingbao, Ningbo, Jingshan, Shaoxing Ba’en, and Suzhou Lingyan. He returned to reside at Jingshan once more, and was subsequently transferred to Xuedou in Siming and finally to Tiantong.
There, he ascended the hall and said: “Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout—like a dragon leaping from the clouds and a thunderclap startling the hibernating insects.
Those who open their eyes immediately manifest their spirit; those who cannot stir are dead within it. You people, do you wish to...”
“Do you see Deshan and Linji? [The Master] planted his staff, let out a shout, and descended from the seat. He ascended the hall and said:
“The face of the sun, the face of the moon—transforming before the pivot of the occasion. Of the thousands and tens of thousands of people here, who has seen them intimately?
A gust of west wind comes; two or three leaves fall. He ascended the hall and said: “When Mazu ascended the hall, Baizhang rolled up the mat. The elephant king turns in circles; the lion leaps back.”
He proposed a verse on the blue sky that resounded like a thunderclap. In his eulogy on the First Patriarch’s dialogue with Emperor Wu of Liang, he said:

"Raising the first hammer upon Mount Sumeru, The jade gate and golden lock are difficult to open. To strike again from behind is but a weary effort; One should regret having traveled ten thousand miles.
In a verse presented to a master of arts, he said: "The person of no rank is bare-boned; They enter and exit through the gateway of the face."
Who knows? The great void originally shares its longevity with him. You, Yu Jia, must rely on the gentleman to examine this in detail.

He presented a verse to Zhang, the Magistrate of the Prison, which says: "Livingly seized and captured are hundreds of prisoners; The shackles are struck and the locks are beaten as they are questioned of their origins.
If within these one word can effect transformation, One brings to life the dead ends of the past."
The verse by Chan Master Yaoshan of Cizhan in Siming praises the Second Patriarch as follows: "His heart’s desire to study had not yet been fulfilled amidst the blue clouds;

With white hair and at his wits' end on a long road, he was trapped at Shaolin. Upon rising after three prostrations, he made a fundamental mistake; From that moment, receiving echoes and responding to shadows has continued unto this day."
The Dharma Heir of Master Huichuan (Hui-ān) of Guifeng:
Zen Master Meng’an Yuancong of Jing Mountain, Hangzhou. A native of Fuzhou, he attained the essential core of the teachings within Huichuan’s assembly;
the community recognized him as a preeminent disciple. Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: When a monk prostrated before Xuansha, Xuansha said, "Because..."

"I must pay my respects to you. The Master recited a verse: "Because of me, you must pay your respects; do not let out flatulence or discharge excrement, for you would bring trouble upon all people under heaven by mistaking what belongs to yourself.
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: When Zen Master Zhaozhou was on the latrine, he saw Attendant Wenyuan passing by.
Suddenly calling out, "Wenyuan! Wenyuan responded. Zhaozhou said, "One should not speak while on the latrine."
"You speak of the Buddha-dharma. The Master’s verse says: "The Way is luminously clear, yet not spoken; by whom can this principle be known?

A spring breeze comes all at once, and flowers lie scattered across the ground. The verse requested by the parting traveler seeking a monk says: "Before the mountain, the wheat ripens as the rain first clears;
Mulberry and *zhà* trees are green, their colors fresh like willows. Not a hair's breadth remains, and its wind-bone is revealed; Every single thing is simply a comparison."
The Body of the Sage.
A Eulogy by Chan Master Wansong Huana Dalian, Successor of Chan Master Penglou Anhui, on the Image of the Buddha Emerging from the Mountains, which says: "Practice fulfilled and merit perfected."
To the very marrow of his bones, he is utterly impoverished; unable to endure his emaciation, his hair hangs in disarray. His transgressions against the heavens are now beyond counting;
within this *Vaiśeṣika* [confession], he offers this single admission. From the *Zengji xuzhuan denglu*, Volume One.
*The Expanded Collection of the Transmission of the Lamp*, Volume II,
compiled by the former Abbot of Jingshan Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Monastery, the Bhikṣu Wénxiù of Wúxún;
the nineteenth generation after Dàjiàn.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Mit’an Jie of Tiantong:
○ Chan Master Songyuan Chongyue of Lingyin, Hangzhou. His secular surname was Wu. He was born at Songyuan in Longquan, Chuzhou;
thus, he took this as his monastic name. From childhood, he was outstanding and extraordinary, never indulging in play. At the age of two...
At thirteen, he left home and donned the robes for sweeping stupas. He first visited Master Miaogong at Lingshi, and subsequently met Dahui at Mount Jing.

Hearing Dahui praise Master Huagong of Jiangshan as being of direct and swift capacity, he went immediately to study under him. One night, while contemplating the koan "The dog has no Buddha-nature," he attained realization.
He then went to consult Ying’an, who presented him with the koan: "The World-Honored One has a secret teaching; Kāśyapa has a hidden meaning."
The leaves did not conceal [the truth]. The Master said, "You have left the Abbot at a loss. Ying'an shouted a single roar, and the Master immediately prostrated himself.
Ying'an was greatly pleased and regarded him as a vessel for the Dharma; he spoke a verse to encourage him to shave his head.

In the second year of Longxing, he finally received ordination at the White Lotus Hermitage on West Lake in Lin’an. He traveled extensively through the gates of many great elders, yet few could withstand his scrutiny.
Yi entered Min and met Master Mukan Genkō. One day, Mukan raised the koan: "A phrase with no meaning, like a vine leaning against a tree.
The Master said, "Torn asunder! Mukan said, "Langya said, 'What a pile of firewood! What do you say? The Master said, "Adding a point to an arrowhead.
Mukan said, "My elder brother’s response surpasses what I could have given; yet, it is still not it. Some other day, the handle of the whisk."
"It is in your hands. Regarding "guiding others," it is indeed difficult to cause an ordinary person of broad ground to leap directly into the realm of the sages.
Regarding "testing people," if one strikes them as they pass right before one's face, one already knows their very marrow before they have even opened their mouths;
what difficulty could there be? The Hermit raised his hand and said, "I have told you clearly: open your mouth!"
"It is not on the tongue; you shall know it for yourself later. Later, when he met Mimiǎn at Xishan in Quzhou, the Master would ask questions as they arose and Mimiǎn would simply smile.
The Master was so earnest in his pursuit of the Way that he forgot to sleep or eat. He followed Mimiǎn when he moved to Jiangshan Huazang and then to Jingshan.
Once, during a period of private instruction, the Master asked a monk standing nearby, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not..."
Wu. While serving by his master’s side, he attained great enlightenment. He then remarked, "Today I finally understand Master Mudan’s saying: 'The opening of the mouth does not depend on the tongue.
When Mudan moved to Lingyin Monastery, he appointed the Master as the First Seat. Subsequently, the Master appeared in the world at Chengzhao in Wu Commandery;
later he transferred to Guangxiao in Jiangyin, Yeyu in Wufei, Jianfu in Fanyang, Xiangshan in Siming, and Suzhou.
He went to Tiger Hill. In the third year of the Qingyuan era, he received an imperial decree to take charge of Lingyin Temple.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Why have the clear-eyed monks lost their nostrils? Is there a thief, or is there no thief? He ascended the hall and said:

"In general, to uphold the lineage of our school, one must possess the correct eye at the crown of the head and the efficacious talisman suspended from the elbow. For instance, when Baoshou opened the hall, Sansheng pushed forward a monk."
Baoshou struck him. Sansheng said, "If one serves people in this manner, one will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou.
Baoshou threw down his staff and returned to his quarters. These two venerable masters, through their casual jostling and pressing, revealed the very marrow of Linji’s mind.
It was simply that they did not realize that life and death were entirely in the hands of this monk.

Is there anyone who can discern this? In years past, I sought fire and found it along with smoke; today, I carry spring water and return with the moon. On the occasion of the New Year’s Day, he ascended the hall:
"The first day of the new year marks a new dawn, and every matter is manifest. Sometimes I let go, sometimes I cut off [all paths].
Without sparing my two eyebrows, I sit and turn the entire platter over. Buddhist Dharma and worldly dharma are, in their entirety, a single piece."
Since these are both the Buddha-dharma and the worldly dharma, how can they be made into one piece? Simply cultivate a heart of resolve, and you will certainly not be deceived.
Entering the hall, he held up his staff and said: "Entering a field of weeds, one does not discriminate; one simply picks up whatever grass comes to hand.
The ox of Huai Prefecture eats the grain; the horse of Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly. The Administrative Supervisor Zhang of Dushan in Huaining has cast three cauldrons. Piṇḍola...
The Venerable One did not know it; he lost his lapis lazuli bowl. Tell me, where has it fallen? [He] threw down his staff and said: "It is difficult to deceive the eyes of the assembly.
Ascending the hall, he cited Master Baoning Yong, who said: "The Great Square has no exterior; the Great Circle has no interior.
With neither interior nor exterior, saints and ordinary people gather together. Pottery shards and rubble emit light; Mount Sumeru is pulverized. Immeasurable..."
"Regarding the hundred thousand samādhis of the Dharma-gates," he raised his staff and said, "Understand them all right here.
*Sulu sulu, siri siri, svāhā*. The Master said, "This old fellow’s karmic consciousness is vast and boundless; unable to save the boat, he breaks the scoop.
He resided at Lingyin for six years, during which time the Way flourished. Later, he retired to Dong’an. I belong to this lineage.

Even while suffering from a slight illness, he did not cease his preaching of the Way. Suddenly, he personally wrote a letter of parting for the various high officials and ministers, leaving behind two maxims to test his disciples, saying:
"Why is it that a person of great power cannot lift their foot? When the mouth opens, it is not upon the tongue.
He also sent a letter to Guangmu of Xiangshan and Shan'kai of Yunju, who were his Dharma heirs, entrusting them with the Great Dharma. Then...

He wrote a verse, saying: "Coming, there is nowhere from which one comes; departing, there is nowhere to which one goes. In a fleeting turn at the profound pivot, even Buddhas and Patriarchs are at a loss.
He sat in *paryaṅka* and passed away in silence on the fourth day of the eighth month of the second year of the Jiading era. He was seventy-one years old and had spent forty summer retreats.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the slopes of North Peak. Lu You, styled Fángwǒ and serving as a Court Gentleman for Special Duties, composed the inscription for his stupa.
It is said: "Reading the Master’s words, they are steep and towering, looking down upon clouds and rain like Mount Hua at five thousand *zhang* high;
they kick at the heavens and ride upon the void, startling the heart and dazzling the eyes like the surging waves at the Sea Gate of Qiantang;
they cause tigers and dogs to tremble with fear and roof tiles to shatter and fall like the battle of the Han army at Biyang. These may truly be called the Linji orthodox lineage of Ying’an Keqin."
He was a true descendant of Pō’ān. Fàngwēng (Lóngshǒu) truly knew how to speak!
○ The Chan Master Zuǎnshī Pō’ān of Wòlóng in Kuízhōu was born into the Wáng family of Guǎng’ān in Shū. He left home to become a monk under Dēxiáng of Luóhàn Yuàn.
Hearing that the Elder Yuán was residing at Zhāojié, he went there to consult him; their words were in accord, and [Yuán] ordered him to serve...
One day, while passing before the abbot’s quarters, Yuanwu asked, "Is there anyone at the hermitage? The Master replied, "There is no one.
Before Yuanwu had finished speaking, he struck the Master across the chest with his fist and said, "What about you? At that moment, the Master suddenly attained realization.

He left the mountain valleys and went to Dezhou Jujian in Lishui to receive the tonsure; shortly thereafter, he received full ordination and traveled extensively to visit various masters. Eventually, he arrived at Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou.
While sitting through a snowy night, he thought to himself, "I have been traveling as a monk for ten years, yet I still cannot penetrate [the truth].
While he was in a state of deep frustration, he did not notice the bell strike. As he went to the back hall, he looked up and saw the two characters for "Zhao Tang" (Hall of Shining).
His doubts were instantly resolved. Shortly thereafter, he visited Shuian at Shuanglin. Shuian asked, "The Venerable Simha had his head cut off by King Kalinga."
"True indeed. But tell me, why did the bearded man of Western Heaven have no beard? The Master said, "It is not until the Twin Trees that this story can be told.
Shui-an said, "Today I have run into a true adept. The Master said, "The heart does not betray the person, and the face shows no shame.
Shui-an then stepped back. The Master said, "You have been seen through. When Shui-an retired from his post, he went to visit the Master.
Miaoyan met him at Wugu and appointed him as the guest prefect. One day, while Miaoyan was conversing with a monk nearby, he raised the koan:
"It is not the wind moving; it is not the banner moving. Upon hearing this, the Master attained a great awakening. The following day, Miaoyan encountered him before the communal quarters.
The Master said to him, "In no way may you employ any artifice; try to reveal some sign of your realization. The Master responded immediately, saying, "There is a guest in the Abbot’s quarters.
Yun’an laughed heartily. When Yun’an moved to Jiangshan, the Master attended him as a follower for five years, fully grasping the essential points of the teaching.
He then took his leave to return to Sichuan. As he departed, Yun’an sent him off with this verse: "Coming from the south ten thousand miles away, the river..."
Rough and rugged, he rushed through the torrent and crossed the blade-edge to strike open the profound pivot; at the crown of his head, the *zhī* flower blossomed, blinding the Diamond Eye.
His coming and going were like a pearl rolling across a tray. Subsequently, traveling south, he reached Kuimen, where the Minister Yang Gongfu invited him to reside at Wolong.
He took his leave and traveled extensively, visiting Huizang Dun’an at Wushan, Yan at Jingshan, Qi at Lingyin, Wuxian at Mount Jing, and Meng’an Cong at Mount Meng.
All of them appointed him as the First Seat and charged him with preaching the Dharma.
He resided successively at Jianfu in Changzhou, Lingyan in Zhenzhou, Xiufeng and Qionglong in the Wu region, and was invited by Prince Yang to reside at Zifu in Huzhou. This concludes the account.
The layman Zhang, a member of the *zhāijū*, invited him to serve as the founding abbot of Guangshou Huiyun Chan Temple.

He occupied the seat of the Dharma six times, all at the invitation of princes and high-ranking officials; at that time, he was held in great honor. Entering the hall for the formal discourse (*shàngtáng*), he cited an ancient master who said:

"When Yangqi first settled there, the walls of his hut were thin; the entire hall was covered with snow and pearls. [The Master] then said: "Tuck in your necks and sigh in silent lamentation. I recall..."
"Ancestors lived under trees. The Master said: "Yangqi competes for excellence, not for inferiority; Xiufeng competes for inferiority, not for excellence.

When Xiufeng first settled here, there was no distinction between kin and stranger; everyone possessed a pearl from the ocean's depths. Though the lakes and mountains fill one’s eyes, they can never be seen enough—Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of his late teacher, Miamu, who said: "If someone asks about winter..."

Regarding the matter of "coming events": In the capital, they produce "great yellow" (rhubarb). For the sake of one grain of rice, they lose six months' worth of provisions. Xiupeng does not speak thus:
when asked about the matter of winter coming, he says, "In the capital, they produce 'great yellow. One merely seeks one grain of rice, yet gains a hundred years' worth of provisions.
Or perhaps an administrative official might say, "Venerable sir, Venerable sir, do not speak of provisions for a hundred years; you shall only receive six months' worth."
"Not a few. It is enough simply to say to him: "If you can only discern the heart of acceptance, you will certainly not be deceived.
Ascending the hall, he cited Master Dongshan’s saying: "What is Chan? The Jambu tree is on the south side of the sea.
Near, it does not leave the square inch of the mind; far, it is a hundred thousand eight thousand miles away. Ultimately, what is Chan, Chan? The Master said: "Qionglung also has one."
The Place of the Way. What is Chan? The Jambu tree stands on the southern edge of the sea; it supports the heavens and props up the earth, propping up the heavens and supporting the earth.
It cannot be described through clever words; it requires only transmission from mind to mind. Ultimately, what is this "Chan, Chan"? [He] ascended the hall and said:
"Before the fifteenth day, it is as clear as a mirror; after the fifteenth day, it is as black as lacquer. As for the very fifteenth day itself—"
"How is it? [he asked]. "The oriole migrates to the lofty trees, chirping repeatedly; the butterflies dote on the fragrant clusters, flying in pairs.
When the Master was about to pass away, he wrote a letter to bid farewell to those for whom he felt deep affection. He composed a verse, saying: "The final word has already caused me such distress;

having written it out before others, there are a thousand errors and ten thousand mistakes. Having finished writing, he sat upright and passed away. This was indeed the ninth day of the sixth month in the fourth year of the Jiading era.
When the Master was passing away, he stayed at Mount Jing. He left instructions that his remains be discarded beneath the mountain.

The master of the estate, Shiqiao, collected the bones and erected a stupa on a separate peak to the right of the [original] stupa. His age was seventy-six; his years since ordination were forty-nine.
Chan Master Caoyuan Daosheng of Guipeng in Xinzhou was a native of Nanjian. He appeared in the world at Miaoguo in Raozhou, then moved to Guipeng, and later resided at Jianfu in Raozhou.
Over a month later, he passed away. He ascended the hall and said: "The two characters 'Buddha-dharma' are known by everyone.
Yet how can one bring oneself to swallow such lethal poisons as arsenic? Even if you were to penetrate beyond the time before Avidyā (Viyūna), it would still be [nothing more than]..."
"Stupid and crazed, he runs outside; this mountain monk has already been dragging through mud and water.
What should you all do? He lets out a shout. Ascending the hall, he says: "Today is the fifteenth of the eighth month; the weather is half cloudy and half rainy.
How many travelers outside the gate fail to see the full moon facing their doors? It is both laughable and lamentable—how can they compare to those within the temple by West Lake?"
A group of ancient Buddhas, having retired from the assembly and returned to the hall for tea, ascended the dais for the formal discourse: "The spring breeze fans eastward and westward;

the spring rain is neither quite clear nor quite cloudy. Pale whites and deep reds are spread out like brocade; the warbling of orioles and the chatter of swallows play together like the music of flutes and pipes."
Each and every one reveals the wondrous gate of perfect penetration; at every turn, the treasury of the true Dharma-eye flows forth.

Should you direct your mind toward it or attempt to settle within it, you will find yourself as before amidst ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains. Only when you know where to return directly beneath can I grant that you have pierced through it from all sides.
Baizhang descended from his meditation seat and ascended the hall. Snow and rain fell in profusion; water dripped from the eaves. How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Amidst the weeds—
One cannot leap out; it is also a great humiliation. A turtle in the water drills through an iron wall. *Duḥ!* [He] ascends the hall and says: "The moon gives birth to one":

pressing down the silver mountains and iron walls. "The moon gives birth to two": the Earth-Dweller riding an ox through the bustling marketplace. "The moon gives birth to three": the secluded birds at the edge of the house warble their cries.
This is not a web of entanglements or a mere formal proclamation, nor is it a profound discourse on ultimate principle. It is precisely this—*with*...
At such a time, when guest and host intersect, how do you express it in a single phrase? "A single hand hangs down from a precipice ten thousand fathoms high;

within a thicket of a hundred flowers, the udumbara flower appears. Ascending the hall, he said: "At the break of dawn, on the third month morning, the Southern Mountain’s verdant peaks pierce the clouds.
There is no need to seek further for the meaning of the West—outside the window, the sound of the *pobingjiao* bird calls several times. He struck his knee and said, "Excellent!"
The Great Song.
○ Mingtong Kuchan Zijing Chan Master: His secular surname was Gao; he was a native of Changle in Min.
He visited Mukan Yong, Shuian Yi, and Hui’an Ti, and finally met Miyun at Lingyin. Their karmic conditions were perfectly harmonized.
Qie. After a long time, he opened the Dharma at Longxing and Shanglan. He moved to Jiankang Jingzhong, Fuzhou Baiyang, and Fuzhou Taiping Xichan.
In the first year of the Baoping era, by imperial decree, he was promoted to Lingyin and later transferred to Tiantong.

"Sixty-nine years have been but one great dream; let us go back, let us return! Be careful, be careful! He then passed away in a state of profound stillness. His stupa was erected at...
Zixia. ○ Chan Master Deshou of Nangshan Gufeng in Xinghua was of the Chen family of Lianjiang, Fuzhou. He received the tonsure at Fengqiao in Wumen.
Once, he ascended the hall and raised the following case: A monk asked Xuefeng, "What is the first phrase? Xuefeng remained silent for a long while.
The monk reported this to Changsheng. Changsheng said, "This is the second phrase. Xuefeng again ordered the monk to ask, "What is the first phrase?
Changsheng said, "Heaven! Heaven! The Master said: "These two great elders shed tears like this because their hearts are pained.
As for the first phrase, you have not even dreamed of it yet. Suppose someone were to suddenly ask Yishan:"
What is the first phrase? He simply said to him, "The sword has long since departed. Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Master Zhenneng, who said:
"The head-dhūta rock is enveloped by moss; the Peak of Thrown Pens is entangled by *bìlì* vines.
At Luohan Monastery, three novices are ordained each year; at Guizong Monastery, they drink tea after the formal meditation session. Does the assembly wish to understand this? Listen."
I shall cite one verse: The sky clears and the sun rises; Rain falls and the ground becomes damp. I have spoken my heart’s content, Yet I fear you will not believe it.
This was spoken by Chan Master Zhineng Zhiweng, a successor in the Dharma lineage.
The Chan Master Yunwai Yunxiu of Siming was a native of Changguo. Though his physical stature was slight, he possessed an abundance of vigor and spirit.
He took refuge under Master Zhigong (Jugong) and received the tonsure; he investigated the tenets of the Caodong school until he had exhausted its very source and foundation.

He traveled from Chushi (慈溪) to Shimong (石門), then to Xiangshan (象山) and Zhimen (智門), and subsequently to Tianting (天寧). Following this, he was urged by the followers of the Three Schools and the fourfold assembly to reside at Tiantong (天童).
Upon ascending the hall, he said: "Within the bustling red dust of the marketplace, there is the Buddha-dharma of the bustling red dust of the marketplace.
Within the deep mountains and rocky cliffs, there is the Buddha-dharma of the deep mountains and rocky cliffs. Yesterday, I, this mountain monk, went out..."
Within the bustling red dust of city gates, the Buddha-dharma is momentarily forgotten.

When one travels twenty *li* to the Pine Clouds, one encounters the Buddha-dharma amidst deep mountains and rocky cliffs. The assembly, tell me: what is the Buddha-dharma within deep mountains and rocky cliffs?
After a long silence, he said: "White clouds are pale and vast, appearing and disappearing within the great void; the blue..."

Luó Yín climbed straight up to the top of the cold pine tree. As Shè, the Head Seat, the Secretary, and the Librarian were about to ascend the hall for the formal discourse, he struck a circular gesture with his whisk and said:
"The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and is beyond the hundred negations.

He struck another circular gesture and said: "In the practice of ritual, harmony is the highest value; this is what constitutes the beauty of the Way of the former kings. He struck yet another circular gesture and said: [silence].

"A mani jewel that people do not recognize, yet the Tathāgata has personally retrieved from within his own storehouse. Do you all see it? What is seen differs from person to person, with each having their own gains and losses.
Here at Tiandong, there is neither rigidity nor insistence. The Master’s preaching of the Dharma is able to employ skillful metaphors and indirect guidance;
he values bringing himself down to the level of the student to bring them to completion through subtle means. As for those who gallop ahead, leaving the dust behind—even though they are like hawks...

His eyes were like those of a dragon, yet they lacked any trace of peering or spying. Throughout his life, he was neither arrogant nor greedy for accumulation; whatever offerings or benefits he received, he gave them away to others.
Since his passing, he left no remaining assets. Zen practitioners collectively contributed money to escort him to the ferry and bury him at his home mountain.
The Dharma Successor of Chan Master Chidun Ying of Tiantong:
○ Chan Master Jingkou Rujué of Jingshan, Hangzhou, a native of Wuzhou. Initially, when he visited the room of Chidun, the master posed the instructional phrase:
"What is the Buddha? The Master replied, "A rotten winter melon. He then composed a verse, which begins: "What is..."
The Buddha eats rotten winter melon; biting into it, the frosty water permeates his teeth. Although its root and stem have no hollow pit, once a year it blooms but once.
He also composed a verse to present to Chidun, saying: At Mount Zhong, I braved white blades with my bare body;
Several times I have been nearly buried alive. Since the man was lost and the house destroyed, I have realized there is no rank to be found.

Arrangement for the Small Sermon at the Opening of the Summer Retreat. In this school of ours, the true command is fully upheld; it is like a violent wind and torrential rain, surging forward with no one before it to resist.
Like a spark struck from stone or a flash of lightning, one cannot catch up to its swift flight. To raise a thought is to lose the source; to lift the eyes is already to have missed the mark.

This is not a dharma of the present moment; do not give rise to various kinds of thoughts. Even if you practice the three modes of cultivation in alternation and strive to achieve results within a fixed period...
Realization. The second head and third crown; ten thousand props and a thousand supports—only to find one’s breath growing more frantic by the moment.
