From afar, he beheld that in the Eastern Continent of Zhendan there were those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna.

Traveling ten thousand miles from afar, his intent was to cut in line and snatch the market. He has reached the point where the drums resound in the Phoenix Hall and the bells toll in the Azure Pavilion;
yet every turn of the throat strikes a forbidden taboo, and every step taken finds no door. The entire nation finds it difficult to pursue him, and he is now doubly exposed.
The new abbot of Jiangshan, having no choice but to act, has boarded another’s boat and entered another’s domain. A new official does not concern himself with the affairs of the past. It is finished.
"In the end, what of it? [The Master] struck the meditation seat and said: "The watchtower is silent, storing the moonlight of a thousand peaks;
amidst the frontier grasses, the ten-thousand-li autumn is spread. Ascending the hall, he said: "The Five Peaks stand steeply; those who reach them must be true men. A single mirror hangs in the sky;
there is nothing that does not receive its illumination. The ancestral patriarchs' foundation remains as it was; the livelihood of the patch-robed monks has never changed. He then donned his robe.
When there is no place for the hand to grasp, one must pull it up; when there is no door for the foot to step through, only then is it fit to tread.
When the mountain clouds are hazy and the stream waters flow gently, a single melody is impartial and the myriad realms enjoy their work. At such a time, where does the merit reside?
From of old, the chariots and books have shared the same script and tracks; today, the four seas are one family. (Zhiyuan Wuyin)
The Chief Monk of Zichun, Yang Yen-zhenjia, having received an imperial decree, assembled various masters of Chan from Jiangnan to attend court and discuss the Way.
The Emperor asked, "What is the fundamental principle of Chan? The Master stepped forward and replied, "Chan is pure wisdom, wondrously perfect;

its essence is fundamentally empty and still. It is not something that can be known through seeing, hearing, sensing, or cognizing, nor is it something that can be grasped through deliberation or discrimination."
[The student] replied, “I can. The Master further said, “The lineage of the Chan school may be recounted in detail.

The Master said, “The lineage of Chan began when the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, held up a single branch of a golden *pāla* flower and showed it universally to the great multitude.
Only Kāśyapa smiled. The World-Honored One said, ‘I possess the treasury of the true Dharma-eye, the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.’”
He entrusted [the Dharma] to Kāśyapa. From him, it was passed down through successive generations until Bodhidharma.
Looking toward this land of Eastern Zhendan, Bodhidharma saw that there were those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna; thus he crossed the sea and arrived here.

He did not rely on written words, but pointed directly at the human mind, so that one might see one's nature and become a Buddha. This is what constitutes the Chan school. The Emperor praised this, and the Master then spoke with composure, saying: "Chan..."
The teaching and its essence are fundamentally one. It is like hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all returning to the sea, where they share no different taste.
It is also like Your Majesty sitting firmly upon the mountains and rivers as the empire is unified; the four barbarian tribes and the hundred蛮 (man) peoples arrive from every direction.
One must enter through the Gate of Accordant Succession; only upon reaching the Golden Hall and personally beholding the golden countenance can one be said to have arrived home.
If, however, followers of the Teaching merely rely on words and letters without attaining the profound essence, they have not reached it.

They are still outsiders who merely follow and comply with the gate. Even those in the Chan school who have sat through six or seven broken cushions of *pūtaka* grass, yet have not attained realization, are likewise outsiders who merely follow and comply with the gate. This is what is meant by "reaching home" and "coming together.
Thus, those who study the teachings must penetrate the profound principle; those who practice Chan must awaken to their own mind. As it is for us today...
Only by personally ascending the golden hall and beholding the golden countenance once can one truly be called a "man who has arrived home.

The Emperor was pleased and granted him food before he took his leave and returned south. He addressed the assembly, saying: "I originally intended to remain hidden deep within mountain caves, passing my time in seclusion;

yet I did not expect that with the sun shining and heaven looking down, it would be difficult to escape the reach of the supreme transformation. He further said: "With the patched robe covering one's head, all matters [are settled]."

"Stop! At this time, even this mountain monk has no understanding. A disaster struck the mountain once more. The Master said to the assembly, "I have incurred a debt to this mountain," and so he exerted all his strength to rebuild it again.
He filled in the pond at the base of the hall to serve as the site for other buildings, completing them one after another.
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the Gui-si year, he wrote a verse and passed away. He was seventy-five years old and fifty-nine years since his ordination. He was buried at the temple.
On its western slope.
○ Hezhao Iron Mirror Zhiming Chan Master was the son of the Huang family of Changxi in Fudang.
He first visited Baosou Yao at Tianning Monastery in Jiahe; although he received his encouragement, he did not achieve great awakening. Later, he relied upon Yanyuan.

At Jingci Monastery, Xi was appointed to attend upon him; morning after morning he sought instruction and evening after evening he paid his respects, until he attained realization of wisdom. Later, he visited Qingxi Yuan at Huqiu, who commissioned him to serve as the librarian.
Upon ascending to Shuangjing, Zangsou again appointed him to oversee the library. In the *Xinsi* year of the Zhizhi era (1281), the seat of Heshan was vacant, and the Master was invited to fill it.
He subsequently moved to reside at Damei in Siming. In the *Gengzi* year of the Dade era (1300), [he returned to] Heshan.
The elders spoke with one voice, and the Xingxuan Yuan (Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) invited him to return for a second term as abbot.

He ascended the hall and said: "The wilds are shrouded in autumn gloom, and the crickets all sing; the maple forest sheds its leaves, each one a crimson heart. Bodhidharma’s boneless descendant searches for a needle at the bottom of the sea.
When he suddenly finds it, what then? Who says the palaces of the Dragon King are deep? He ascended the hall and said: "Bodhi..."
Polishing it, it does not come to this eastern land; on the official road, few people travel. The Second Patriarch did not go to the Western Heaven;
private wine is drunk by many. Before which mountain is there a great highway? How many have known those who come from the south and go to the north?
It is simply that one block of stone in the middle has never been stepped upon by anyone. Is there anyone among you who has stepped upon it? [He] threw [the staff].
Holding up his staff, he said: "Look beneath your feet. He ascended the hall and said: "Today is the twenty-fifth of the eighth month.
I remember Dongshan leaving Cha-du; he fell into Yunmen’s net. His grievance remains until now, with no place for it to be cleared. He raised his whisk.
"Master Yunmen has arrived! Which mountain’s staff should he receive? Tell me, where does his fault lie?
It lies in playing with people’s sons and daughters. He ascended the hall and said: "If you strive and seek with intent, it will be like donkey-years before you meet him.
If you let go completely, he appears in an instant. Xiangyan heard the sound of a bamboo being struck and thoroughly saw his original face. This is not so.
Question: "Tell me, where can one avoid such heat? [The Master] replied: "Go to the hall to drink tea.

On the fifth day of the eleventh month of the Yanyou Yimao year, he summoned his disciples to entrust them with his final affairs. He asked for paper and wrote in large characters: "Beyond all nets and cages; no room for evasion.
The great ocean’s waves are stilled; empty space is revealed alone. Having set down his brush, he passed away peacefully. He was eighty years old.
16. ○ On the occasion of Chan Master Zhihongjian’s initial residence at Zhenru Monastery in Xinzhou, Mingtong of Siming ascended the hall and said:
"The Buddhas cannot truly preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; the Bodhisattvas possess wisdom, yet their vision of nature is not clear. White.
The clouds have no mind or intention, yet they pour down rain upon the world. The great earth has no sentient feelings, yet it can grow all grasses and trees.
When the ancient worthies proclaimed in this manner, their skillful means in opening the way for humans and devas within the Dharma of the Four Truths was truly unsurpassed.

they recorded it and he entered nirvāṇa at the age of sixty-eight, on the eighteenth day of the third month in the twenty-sixth year of the Zhizheng era. His disciples, following his final testament, interred his entire remains in a stūpa.
Chan Master Xing Gong of Shilin at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou first resided at Shangfang in Anji.

He subsequently ascended to Fabao on Sishi Creek, Longxing Huanglong, and Chengtian in Wu County, before arriving at Jingci. Upon ascending the hall, he said: “With eyes cast across the azure heavens, the winds are clear throughout the ten thousand lands;
with hands extended into the red dust, the sun rises over a thousand peaks. As soon as it is thus, it is already not thus. Therefore—”
"I declare that this Dharma Seal is taught for the benefit of the world. Wherever you travel, do not propagate it recklessly.
Holding his staff horizontally, he said: "Two thousand two hundred and six years have passed since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

I, the śramaṇa Xinggong, now manifest this seal at the head of the Ti and Xia rivers, in a place of pure sounding-bell clarity. There is not the slightest bit of falsehood herein. He struck the ground with his staff.
[The Master] held up his staff and said: "I respectfully announce. Ascending the hall, he said: "In the still mountains, bees labor with heavy pollen;
in the empty woods, the bamboo shoots reveal their bright flesh beneath the sheaths. Leaning on the railing, I unconsciously become dazed and numb, until a yellow oriole calls out once more.
"Si-xi, for speaking thus, you deserve thirty blows of the staff. Why? Because you follow after sounds and pursue forms. Ascending the hall, he said: "A land of waters..."
The waters are broad and the ground is damp with moisture. In the sixth month, the flower mosquitoes have snouts like iron.
Rising at midnight, one laughs until one cannot stop. Why does one not cease this affliction? A single fan by the bedside; for no reason, it has broken again.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "In a village of three households, a cow wags its tail. He then shook his whisk and said, "How far removed is this from that? He then cast down the whisk.
The Master said: "It is fitting to let prisoners remain incarcerated so that their wisdom may grow. He ascended the hall and said: "Xuefeng rolls the ball; Heyang beats the drum;
Bimozhe holds up the fork; Daowu performs a dance. All worthies and sages distinguish themselves by means of the unconditioned Dharma.
He gave a shout and descended from the seat. In his room, the Master gave this instruction: "The entire great earth is this very adamantine true body. Above...
"Where shall the seated one place his leather bag? The plantain tree sprouts upon hearing thunder. Now tell me, is this sentient or insentient?
Beneath Mount Nanping stand three barriers rising like a sheer cliff. For those who cannot pass through, there is a hundred errors for every single mistake;

for those who do pass through, there are a thousand hardships and ten thousand difficulties. Suddenly, someone who cannot bear it might come forth and ask: "If they have already passed through, why [is it so difficult]?"
"It is difficult indeed. Go away and come back tomorrow; I shall examine it with you in detail.
Master Chan Master Binggu Yan of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing ascended the hall and said: "How coldly blows the north wind, blowing against those robes beneath the crags.
The family estate has long been overgrown with weeds; why does the traveler not return? A hundred years of human life—how can they be preserved forever? Yesterday...
The youth of yesterday is now old; I turn my thoughts back to Hanshan. For ten years he has been unable to return, having forgotten the path by which he came. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Even the kalpa-stone may be worn away, but the bonds of affection are difficult to sever. He struck his knee and said: "Beneath the green pines of ruined tombs, paper money is hung year after year.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Cold winds and sparse rains mark the beginning of a new year; in solitude, beside the cold spring at the ancient ravine."
In the warm chamber, the hearth stoves burn pieces of firewood; there is no need to burn paper money to send off the Poor Spirits. Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Imperial Birthday:

Peace reigns in the heart-kingdom, the six states are unified, heaven and earth are vast, and the chariots and books are one. The wind follows the tiger; the clouds follow the dragon. Deep as the sea, high as Mount Song.
Among the myriad spirits, none can participate in the work of transformation; all know that the single breath returns to the great void. (He strikes the whisk once.)
[End of section].
○ Zen Master Jing Yun-geng of Tiger Hill, Suzhou, ascends the hall: "If I do not break it open for you, I fear you will not turn back;
yet if I do break it open for you, I fear you will curse me away in the future. Ascending the hall, the mountain monk says: "If I were truly..."

To raise this up: at the Riverside Pavilion, there is no place for you to set foot. For now, I suppress my majestic light; I have not yet spoken of "transcending the school" according to your capacity.

If, on another day, you can realize that Mount Huqiu is one hundred and thirty feet high and that the Śarīra Stūpa was established during the Sui Dynasty, then I may grant you a point of entry. If you are content to remain inferior, how can I blame you?
The Old Monk ascended the hall and said: "At Longmen, there are no guests; each and every one possesses the principle of having no step backward.
Sparse Mountain was short, yet he sold his cloth-bill three thousand *li* away; lame Yunmen had his leg broken under pressure. You lot simply spend your days drifting along.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall and said: "I observe that the Tathāgata did not come from the past, nor does he go to the future; even now..."
"Not abiding. Now tell me, what is it that is bathed with fragrant water in the Great Hall?

If you can understand this, you will be free to pick up or set down the ladle in your hand as you please. If you have not yet attained this, on this day next year, you will continue as before to splash about recklessly.
Ascending the hall: Cold as ice and frost, fine as rice powder; water cannot wash it away, fire cannot heat it.

When the Queen Mother descends by day, her cloud-bannered flag unfurls; when the cuckoo cries at night, the mountain bamboo splits. Ascending the hall: An ancient said, "To rely on the scriptures to explain the meaning is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three ages;
to depart from a single word of the scriptures is to speak like a demon. Since neither relying nor departing can be found, [what is there to grasp?]
"Ultimately, how is it? [He] struck the meditation platform with his staff and said: "The fisherman looks only at the fishing line; he does not see the reeds facing the red smartweed.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "When Yunyan views the mountains and enjoys the waters, this staff likewise views the mountains and enjoys the waters.
When Yunyan is afflicted throughout his body by illness, this staff likewise is afflicted throughout its body by illness. Yunyan..."
The entire body is liberated and at ease; even this staff is liberated and at ease throughout. He plants the staff and says: "It is easy to cleave open the rivers and mountains;
it is difficult to eliminate love and hate."
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Yun’an Yan of Daochang:
Chan Master Xutang Zhiyu of Jing Mountain, Hangzhou. A native of Siming, he appeared in the world at Xingsheng Temple in Jiahe.

He successively resided at Guangxiao and Mingzhao in Xian, Yanfu and Ruiyan in Wuzhou, Baolin in Wu, Yuyang in Siming, Boyan in Hangzhou, Jingci, and Jingshan—having occupied ten monasteries in total. Within his quarters, the Master gave this instruction:

"Why is it that those whose own eyes are not yet clear take empty space to wear as trousers? Why is it that they draw lines on the ground to make a prison? For what reason do they fail to penetrate this?
This person is nothing more than one who enters the sea to count its sands; why then does he stand on tiptoe upon the point of a needle?

A monk asked, "The single phrase before sound does not fall into the trap of permanence. Turning the position to accord with function—how do we meet it? The Master said, "To inquire, one need not reach out the hand.
The monk said, "But tell me, what of 'Ten Thousand Years for the Son of Heaven'? The Master said, "Auspicious grass grows in a fortunate era."
"Forest flowers bloom in early spring. A monk said, "It reaches the point where the nine provinces and four seas are moved by thunder and stirred by wind.
The Master said, "When one goes out the door, one only fears not being the first to arrive. Ascending the hall, he said: "The spring breeze is like a blade; the spring rain is like a balm.

Within the gate of the patch-robed monks, what need is there for such tedious talk? Ascending the hall, he said: "If words are sufficient, one speaks all day long and yet exhausts the Way. If words are insufficient, one speaks all day long and yet never exhausts it."
To speak of the Way is to exhaust all things. Now, as for the Way and things—whether they are one or two:

if you say the Way is one, why is it that when the mountain is pressed down, the main peak is low? If you say they are two, why is it that "heaven and earth are but a single finger" and "the myriad things are but a single horse"?
If you can distinguish black from white within this, I shall repay you the price of your straw sandals; otherwise, I only wish for the silkworms to thrive next year.

The wheat was ripe; Rāhula’s son was given one coin. For the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said: "There is a person who daily consumes ten thousand taels of gold, identical to this sacred regulation.
It is simply that no one recognizes him. If there were someone who could recognize him, I would grant him the right to consume ten thousand taels of gold daily.
He ascended the hall again and said: "The Two Forests (Erlin) originally have no gateways for people to approach; nor do they establish..."
To leave this matter in the land of nothingness—provided that all of you are like iron entering the earth, transforming together with it, only then can you surpass those who merely carry away dung.

As for such people, I am ultimately at a loss for what to do. Ascending the hall, he raised the example of the ancestral teacher Songyuan, who, when approaching his passing, addressed the assembly, saying:
"Among my long-standing brothers and practitioners on the true path, there are only..."
The method of the black beans cannot be employed; the Way of Linji is about to perish and vanish without a trace—how tragic! [The Master] comments:

"The Great One of Vulture Peak is like one leaning on a staff while riding a horse; though he avoids the calamity of falling, he cannot escape the disfigurement of those who observe from the sidelines."

While the Master was at Jingci Monastery on the day of his formal entry, his exchanges of questions and answers were at an end. Suddenly, an imperial messenger arrived at the gate to deliver an edict.
The Emperor asked: "Why did Zhaozhou travel as a mendicant for eighty years? Why did Xutang reside as a mountain dweller for eighty years?

The Master cited the story of Zhaozhou’s travels to Linji and offered this verse: "Zhaozhou traveled as a mendicant only upon reaching eighty; Xutang returned to reside on the mountain only upon reaching eighty."

Possessing a unique capacity to revive the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, he moved the imperial countenance within the nine-layered capital. When he presented his verses in response to the Emperor’s inquiry, the Sovereign was greatly pleased;
he specially bestowed five hundred *shi* of rice and one hundred rolls of silk, granting him permission to open the hall and settle the assembly.
He later resided again at Yuwang and Jingshan, where he likewise received abundant imperial gifts and honors.
Master Shifan Yan of Siming Tiantong ascended the hall and said:
“I cite the case of National Teacher Dadian, who, when asked by Minister Han [Yu] how many years had passed since his birth, held up his prayer beads and asked, ‘Do you understand?

The Minister said, ‘I do not. Dadian replied, ‘One hundred and eight, day and night. The Master offered this verse: “A single string of *maṇi* beads, confronting one face-to-face; It deceives and ruins—”
The Head Seat suspects that Changli was killed; he has exhausted all manner of wretched stratagems. He fundamentally never knew the Spring and Autumn Annals.
This is the lineage of Chan Master Jinshan Yanshi Kai.
Chan Master Shixi Xin Yue of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou was a native of Meizhou in Western Sichuan. He ascended the hall and, citing a monk, said:
A monk asked Master Jiufeng, "What is the student’s own self? Jiufeng said, "Ask anyone else. The monk said, "If one accepts it as such right now, what then?

Jiufeng said, "Does Mount Sumeru still bear another Mount Sumeru upon its head? The Master composed a verse, saying: What is the student’s own self? Ask anyone else. If one accepts it as such right now, Does Mount Sumeru still bear another Mount Sumeru?
One knows one’s own heat and cold for oneself; when the Patriarch’s meaning came from the West, who else could have asked? To accept it as a whole is to be the whole;
atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, one bears Mount Sumeru. A verse sent off a monk says:

Before reaching the Twin Trees, I see my old acquaintance: The brows arch like a new moon, the eyes span the autumn. Before exchanging words of greeting, you should first ask: Why is it that the bridge flows while the water does not?
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Wudetong of Huazang:
Chan Master Xuzhou Pudu of Jing Mountain in Hangzhou. A native of Jiangdu in Yangzhou, his surname was Shi.

Although he studied secular texts as he grew up, he had no intention at all of remaining in the world. His mother, recognizing his resolve, sent him to rely upon [the master] at Tianning Monastery in the prefecture.
Having left the household life, he happened to meet General Bi again and conversed with him. Bi marveled at him greatly, saying, "This boy is short and sturdy, yet his voice resonates like a bell;
in days to come, he will be a leading 'claw and tooth' within the Dharma. He took him back to Wulin and had him pay respects to Master Zuxin of Dongtang Monastery to serve as his preceptor.
After attending upon Zuxin for five years, he resolved to travel to various quarters to seek instruction. First, he visited...
He received the "Iron Ox Seal" at Lingyin. Thereafter, he traveled extensively throughout Jiangdong, Jiangxi, Hubei, Hunan, and Hubei.
At that time, Wude was propagating the Way at Jianfu in Raoyang. The Master resolved to seek instruction from him, and when Wude moved to Foyan and Huazang, the Master accompanied him.
Once, while entering the inner quarters, Wude asked, "Who is it that does not take the ten thousand dharmas as a companion? The Master replied:
"Under the golden incense burner lies an iron mound. Daide said, "I thought this short fellow had some depth of understanding, yet it is only like this.
The Master bowed low and paid his respects, saying, "I thank the Abbot for providing this testimony.

At the beginning of the Chunyou era (1241–1252), Tiantong Huiguang, Dayue Cishi, Shiyuan Lian, and Huqiu Shishi Diyi all recognized his extraordinary potential and retained him to oversee monastic affairs.
The Provincial Governor Zhao Xin’an invited him to the world at Bānshān in Jīnlíng. Subsequently, he moved to Jīnsān in Rùn, Lùyuàn in Tán, Shūsān in Fǔ, and Chéngtiān in Sū.
During the Jiǎngdìng era, he was widely renowned; upon the petition of State Councilor Jia, he was appointed to Zhōngtiānzhī, and later requested imperial edict to ascend to Língyǐn.
In the Dīnchū year of the Zhìyuán era, he received the command to go to Jìngshān. He ascended the hall and addressed the assembly:
When a heterodox person preaches the True Dharma, the True Dharma is entirely heterodox. When an orthodox person preaches heterodox dharma, the heterodox dharma is entirely orthodox.
(He strikes the staff once. Is it heterodox? Is it orthodox? (He strikes the staff once again. Does he preach it? Does he not preach it?
If you can discern and distinguish this here, then a house of gold is not truly noble; jade food and brocade robes—what honor are they?

[The Master] ascends the hall and says: "The myriad dharmas are the light of the mind; all conditions are but the clarity of nature. Originally there is no person who is deluded or awakened; it simply requires realization today.
Since there is no person who is deluded or awakened, what is it that is realized? [He] strikes the meditation staff once. A thousand words, ten thousand...
No one understood his words. He continued, "Furthermore, it follows the warbling oriole over the low wall. He ascended the hall and cited Master Yunmen’s address to the assembly, which said:
"You all are spending the summer retreat here; I have no desire at all to tell you—just take care of your eyebrows! The Master said:
"Yunmen was like a divine tortoise dragging its tail, leaving no trace behind. But at Lingyin, it is not so: you..."

While these various people here are passing the summer retreat, I, the mountain monk, shall speak directly to you: the mouth is the gate of calamity. Ascending the hall, the Master raised the precedent of Zen Master Linji, who said:
"There is one person who remains on the road for kalpas without ever leaving home; there is another person who leaves home and is no longer on the road.
Which of these two is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans? The Master said: "A rabbit and a horse."
Horned oxen and sheep lack horns; an inch of hair and a foot of a hair-span exist within the vast expanse of heaven and earth. Pan Lang rides his donkey backward; he topples and kills Huang Fancho.
When the Master resided at Mount Jing, he encountered a fire; with his remaining will intent on restoration, his efforts were beginning to bear fruit.

Suddenly, he manifested a slight ailment and requested a brush, writing in large characters: "For eighty-two years, I have steered the bottomless boat; now I have trodden it over and shall return home."
Yuet Yi-tian. His entire-body stupa is located ten *li* east of the temple, on the southern side of Guasiwu.
He was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Xuedou Dayie Qian.
○ Chan Master Jue’an Mengzhen of Chengtian Temple in Suzhou was a native of Xuanchuan. He became a monk at the age of eight and [was ordained] at nineteen.
Having received full ordination at twenty, he immediately set out on pilgrimage. He visited seven or eight venerable masters, but the Master’s mind could not resolve this matter.
Hearing that Wuzhun’s methods were fiercely pungent, he ascended Mount Jing. Whenever he entered the meditation room, he was struck with trembling fear; he could not even remember his *huatou*.
From then on, he no longer entered the room, spending day and night solely in seated meditation. One day, while in the corridor—
While traveling, Xingwen heard a fire-board strike and had a realization. He rejoiced to himself, knowing he had found the location of his original life-spirit (*mìngběn yuánchén*).
Thereupon, he went again into the room. Zhun asked, "Are you a monk who eats porridge and rice, or a monk who studies Chan and the Way?
The Master replied in a loud voice, "I am a monk who eats porridge and rice. Zhun said, "You must eat your fill before you can succeed. The Master said, "Thank you, Master."
He continued his offerings. From there, he found a path and traveled along it; however, regarding the "dog has no Buddha-nature" koan, he found no point of entry.
He then went to Xuedou to see Dayue. Dayue asked him, "What is the matter of birth and death?"
The Master said, "Eyebrows are placed above the eyes. Xie asked, "Why are the eyebrows placed above the eyes?
The Master said, "To speak of it makes one feel all the more unbearable. Xie asked again, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "From Jingshan.
Xie asked, "What is the state of affairs after the fire? The Master said, "The five peaks still pierce the heavens as high as before. Xie asked, "As for that matter, have you ever..."
"Is it broken? The Master joined his palms forward and said, "Fortunately, it has not been touched. He then hung up the portrait of the patriarch and returned to the hall.

The Master knew in his own heart that he had not yet attained complete liberation; his mind remained constantly restless and feverish. One night, late in the evening, as he walked before the Sangha Hall, he saw a crystal lamp and was suddenly and greatly enlightened.
Everything he had previously attained vanished all at once, like ice melting or a fortress crumbling to pieces.
The next day, Xie entered the room. [Xuefeng] raised the question: "What is the Buddha? [Yunmen] replied: "A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves.
Before the sound had even faded, the Master said: "Feel free to leap and bound as you please. As Xie hesitated, the Master went to the center of the hall to pay his respects.
Xie asked: "How did you meet Yangqi face-to-face? The Master said: "You missed it right before your eyes. As Xie again hesitated, the Master moved to the eastern side to attend to a monk.
The interlocutor asked for his greetings. Xie said, "We are still separated by the sea. The Master clapped his hands, laughed loudly, and went out.

After some time, he established the Dharma at Yongqing, moved to Lianyun, ascended to Heshan, and finally reached Chengtian. There, he ascended the hall and said: "To direct the mind toward studying the Buddha is to be drawn into the palace of Māra;
to fix the mind on practicing Chan is to fall into the realm of the five aggregates. Even if you loathe the Buddha and refuse to act as one, you will still be..."
The staff pierces through the skull. If you look at it in this way, there is truly no place for the mind to function.

(He plants the staff on the ground. "Carry your old books back to your old retreat; wild flowers and singing birds are one and the same spring. Ascending the hall, he said: "The green bamboos before the courtyard are lush;
the yellow chrysanthemums beneath the steps are dense. To call them the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is also the function of Prajñā."
Suddenly, someone might come forward and say: "I have seen that from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past down to the present, they have spoken of myriad bodies and functions;

they do not seem as eccentric as Chengtian. Is this perhaps because your wisdom surpasses that of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Or is it merely a fabrication and a product of your own conjecture? [The Master] plants his staff upright and says:
"It is better to gaze toward the evening sky and the sands, where the west wind startles the falcon into a slanting flight. He then ascends the hall and cites National Teacher Shao.
The Master composed a verse: "At the summit of Tongxuan Peak, it is not of this human world; Outside the mind there is no dharma—every eye meets the green mountains.
The Master called to the assembly, saying: "National Teacher Shao has indeed a fine verse, yet it is split into two parts.
I, Chengtian, also have a verse: 'Atop the Double Emei Peaks, Above is the blue sky; In the dead of night, one seizes the black rooster.'"
Reaching out one's hand, one cannot see one's own palm. (He lets out a shout. Entering the hall for the discourse: "The heat of the three summer months is not like the heat of the human heart;
the dangers of the road are not like the treachery of the human heart. Ten thousand bushels of pure wind upon a jade platter—no one knows with whom it leans against the balustrade."
Suddenly, someone came forward and asked, "Venerable Sir, at such a time as this, what is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

To him, he replied, "The heart of a thief is always fearful. During the Zhizheng era of the Yuan dynasty, a Dharma Master of the Xianshou school petitioned the throne to convert the famous monasteries of Jiangnan and Zhejiang into temples for the Huayan teachings.
By imperial decree, he traveled south; upon arriving at Chengtian Monastery on the second day, he...
The Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma. He extensively cited the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, expounding them with great breadth and freedom.

He analyzed the strengths and weaknesses of various masters’ commentaries and exegeses as clearly as pointing at one’s own palm. The presiding lecturers heard what they had never heard before and received immense benefit from the Dharma.

They remarked, "If even the Elder of Chengtian Temple is such as this, how much more so must it be for the Great Master of a major monastery in Hangzhou? Consequently, they returned to present their report.
[The Master] retired before the imperial edict.
○ Zen Master Xiangtan Yong of Huishen ascended the hall and said:
"When Wuzhuo the Abbot went to Mount Wutai and was drinking tea with an old man, the old man picked up a crystal cup and asked, 'Is there such a thing as this in the South? Wuzhuo..."
[The monk] said, "There is none. The old man asked, "What do you usually use to drink your tea? The monk was unable to respond. The Master composed a verse, saying:
Gazing longingly at Mount Wutai, my thoughts linger; Under the bright sun and blue sky, I am bewitched by ghosts. Most painful is one thing that is difficult to comprehend:
When drinking tea from a crystal cup.
○ Chan Master Guān Pǔ’s Verse on Mazu’s Instruction to a Monk to Ask Damei:
“What did you obtain from Mazu, Master, that you have come to dwell on this mountain? The verse says: “Taking only Mazu’s lead blade, He tears asunder the iron netting that blankets the heavens.
In the emerald pond at night, rain beats upon lotus leaves; To this day, he still laments his poverty—having one body is too much.”
The *Pǔshuō* (General Discourse) of Chan Master Cixizé of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai states briefly:

"When a superior practitioner who investigates the mystery or a high-ranking traveler of the Way brushes aside the weeds and observes the wind to arrive at a certain place, they first offer an entry-level confession, saying:
'The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. Then, he calls out: 'Brothers! If birth and death truly exist, from of old..."*
To this day, not a single person has been able to escape birth and death. If it were non-existent, what would one do about the birth and death manifest before one’s eyes?
Birth and death are both existent and non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent. At such a time, is there anyone who slips through the net?
Since there is no way to escape, on the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, you will run right into it before your eyes;
how, in the end, will you manage it? Even though you have worn out your straw sandals, time slips away and cannot be toyed with.
You must investigate until the place of departure is clear, so that it corresponds to the original point of entry; only then will it be correct. It is also said: "Just let it be like this."
Cease! Then where would all the complications just mentioned be placed?
Even if you all were to refuse to accept them at once and clear them away until they are utterly exhausted, I, this mountain monk, nevertheless have an ancient saying to present to you.
I recall Changqing addressing the assembly, saying: "Once you have cleared everything away until it is pure and clean, you must then come forward and seek me out. There is.
If a single blow reaches you, you ought to feel shame and remorse. But if not a single blow reaches you, what then? Xuedou said:
"Having swept everything clean and put it all away, you must still come forward and seek it from me. If there were a blow that reached you, it would be an injustice to you;
if no blow reaches you, I deal with you on equal terms. These two great masters both initially favored the single blow, yet they could not avoid falling into conceptualization.
To deliberate over gain and loss is not the way of Tianfeng. Once you have thoroughly cleansed and settled yourself, you must come forward and seek me out.
If there is a blow for you, it is like adding embroidery to brocade; if there is no blow for you, it is like adding frost to snow.
Tell me, does this benefit others at the beginning or at the end? If you can discern this, then come when the next notice board is hung.
General Remarks.
Yunchao Yan Chan Master of Ruiyan, Successor in the Dharma Lineage.
Chan Master Netang Bian of Wanshou Monastery in Suzhou ascends the hall and says: "When the Elder Śākyamuni was born in the royal palace..."
What a fine newborn child! He leaves people with no choice but to doubt him. Yet, when he declared, "In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored," his failure was complete.
Later, in his cold, shameful state for forty-nine years across more than three hundred assemblies, there was no way to rescue him, nor could he be saved;
there was no way to retrieve him, nor could he be reclaimed. O virtuous ones, do you wish to see him?
Is this not the point where Old Śākyamuni failed? "Right and wrong arise only from speaking too much; afflictions stem entirely from forcing oneself to emerge.
Entering the hall, he said: "You are here, and I am here; when humans and devas meet, both are able to see one another."
At this time, Qingxiu sings a song of Great Peace: "For one string of cash, you can buy three pecks and a half of rice;

for two strings and five hundred cash, you can buy a large bolt of fine silk. "O Zen practitioners, although this is so, there is leftover rice in the kitchen, yet there are hungry people on the road.

He ascended the hall and raised an ancient case: A monk asked an ancient worthy, "When the myriad objects of perception come to invade [the mind], what should be done? The worthy said, "Hang it down..."
[The Master] puts it on. The ancient worthies possessed the skillful means to block the surging waves [of delusion], yet they could not avoid exhausting their minds and laboring their efforts.
Suppose someone were to ask Jinshan, "What is it like when the myriad phenomena come to invade? He would simply say to him:
"Since I have no mind toward the myriad things, what harm is there in the myriad things constantly surrounding me? Entering the hall, he said: "If I were to explain it through for you, hereafter..."
"You must scold me! If I do not break it open for you, I fear you will let the opportunity slip away through procrastination.
Suddenly, if some fellow comes out and says, 'The Elder has fallen into a trap,' simply tell him:
'It is the old monk's own fault. The verse by Master Yaoyun Chao says: People say the Master died long ago; I alone linger, undecided in my doubts. Since—
The nest is empty and the clouds disperse again; though spring is deep, the cuckoo still cries out. A verse sent to Master Tiēbiān says:
"I contemplate the four lines and send them to Chéngtiān; I have rolled them up whole, yet half is missing. It is neither a formal verse nor a poem;
How can it be brought forth before others? A verse sent to Master Wúzhǔn says: "The monkey and the turtle hand over their charge."

It is not opened. When the elder brother calls and the younger brother responds, it seems as though they have forgotten their minds; yet when it comes to speaking of the point of paradox, their hearts and livers cannot be brought along.
In a verse sent by Chan Master Qingxi Yi of Mount Huqiu in Suzhou to a departing monk, he wrote: "The ten thousand folds of Mount Tai enter the eyebrows..."
Blue. Traveling together on the road, each hastens toward their destination. At the clear dawn, the cock crows by the moonlit thatched inn; who is it that rises first to call out, "Elder Brother"?
The Dharma successor of Chan Master Guyuan Dao of Jingci Temple.
The Zen Master Wanshou Gaofeng Yue composed a verse in praise of Bodhidharma, which says: Unfurling his banner and deploying his array, he entered the realm of Liang;

Before even beholding the Emperor’s countenance, he had already surrendered. Though he possessed supernatural powers, they could not be displayed; With effortless grace, he crossed the vast Yangtze River on a single reed raft.
Dharma Heir of Chan Master Wuzhun Shanfeng of Mount Jing:
Chan Master Xueyan Zuqin of Yangshan in Yuanzhou was a native of Wuzhou. Initially, he visited Wuzhun at Mount Jing;
because [Wuzhun] was casting a bell and ordered him to compose a preface for it, the Master composed a verse, saying: "The entire body is but a single mouth. One hundred...
Forged in the furnace and rolled out, he brought the setting sun to its end and further urged the bright moon onto the towers and terraces.
Zhen immediately appointed him to the office of Attendant. From then on, his reputation stirred the monastic community.
He appeared in the world at Longxing Temple in Tanzhou, then moved to Daolin in Xiangxi, Furi in Chuzhou, Husheng in Taizhou, and Guangxiao in Huzhou. Finally, he presided over Yangshan.
Thus he became widely renowned. He ascended the hall and said: "Pure clarity, utterly free from a single speck—this is precisely the flow of true permanence.
Yet even if one were to shatter the mirror, one would still not avoid a scene of total disorder. It is better to eat when you meet with food and drink tea when you meet with tea.

At dawn, standing alone outside the empty courtyard, I leisurely gaze upon several trees of cold plum blossoms. He ascended the hall again and said: "The waters of the sea cannot be measured with a peck; empty space cannot..."
It may be measured. One must not scatter sand upon pure ground; one must not set foot in rotten mud.
These four turning phrases each have their point of descent. But tell me, where do they descend? In the Great Xiangguo Monastery of the Eastern Capital, there is a banana tree;
when the wind blows and the rain beats upon it, it looks like a tattered monk’s robe. [Ascending the hall: "A phrase, no phrase—like a vine leaning against a wall."
A tree. A white heron descends to the field—a thousand dots of snow. A yellow oriole perches upon the tree—a single branch of blossoms.
Having sold his cotton robe three thousand *li* away, he has come from no great distance; why, then, does he set down his mud-platter? He laughs loudly.
"Vipaśyin Buddha long ago set his mind [upon this], yet until this very day he has not attained the wondrous. Entering the hall, he said: "The Chan-tree cries out in clamor. The Way..."
Before the gate the wind howls vast and wide; to ponder this in cold silence is truly laughable. What is there to laugh at?

To casually pick up a pear from Suzhou, only to find upon closer inspection that it is actually a date from Qingzhou. Ascending the hall, he said: "This matter is fundamentally manifest; yet though you seek it, it cannot be seen.
A flawless white jade is originally without blemish, yet it is by polishing that a flaw is created. To grasp it as a substantial reality is to give rise to flickering illusions within emptiness."
Lightning! At first glance it seems trivial, yet beneath one’s feet a crimson thread is added. If you are a student of the Way, look well at this expedient—how so?
Do not look at the fan in the immortal’s hand.
Chan Master Duanqiao Miaolun of Jingci Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Xu family of Huangyan, Tiantai.
His mother was Liu; she conceived him after dreaming of the moon. At the age of eighteen, he received the tonsure at Guangci Monastery in Yongjia.

There, he met Guyuan Dao at Ruiyan, where he heard the kōan regarding "three pounds of flax" and became skeptical of it. He traveled extensively to consult various masters, yet his realization remained unattuned. He thought to himself: "I..."
Being slow of speech and hard of hearing, he thought it better to take up the practice according to the texts. He made it his daily occupation to recite the sutras.

Suddenly, while reading the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, he saw the mountain hall at Yunju and reflected: "Even mosquitoes, gadflies, and ants have no words to speak, yet they are able to perform their tasks.
He attained sudden enlightenment and said: "Zhaozhou’s ‘Cypress Tree’ koan is truly direct and absolute; it cannot be conveyed through words. He returned.
He went to visit Wuzhun at Xuedou. Wuzhun asked him, "Why does a dog have karmic consciousness?
and commanded the Master to provide a response. After thirty attempts, none were in accord. The Master asked, "Is there no expedient means? Wuzhun answered him with the verse composed by Zhenjing.
He immediately stood up straight for a long while. Suddenly, upon hearing the sound of a wooden board, sweat broke out over his entire body; it was only then that he felt a sense of liberation.
Zhuan invited him to Mount Yuyang and Shuangjing, where both monasteries followed him as their teacher. He was then appointed to share the teaching seat.

He entered the world at Jiyuan, subsequently moved to Ruiyan and Guoqing, and finally reached Jingci. There, he ascended the hall and said: "In the mountains of Jing there is jade, but those who obtain it do not find it within the mountains of Jing. In the waters of Chi there is..."

The pearl is not found in the red water by one who merely picks it up; the "True Person of No Rank" possessed by the patch-robed monk is not realized by one whose entry and exit do not occur through the face-gate.
[The Master] suddenly takes up his staff, holds it crosswise, and says: "Do you understand? A stone man crouches at the mouth of the Yangtze River in Youzhou."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: "Ciming kept a basin of water in his room. Across the top of the basin he laid a sword, and upon the sword he placed a pair of straw sandals.
Whenever a monk arrived, he would point them out; if the monk hesitated even for a moment, he would strike him. The Master offered this verse:

"Leaping through the midst of a hundred flowers on a galloping whip—how much elegance and flair there is here! The scholar who failed the imperial examination stole a glance, and his breast was filled with [doubt]."
"What can one do about old sorrows? Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Deshan lowers his head; Jiaoshan nods his head; Juizhi raises a finger;
Xuansha strikes his toe and breaks it. Holding up his staff, he says: 'All of these do not go beyond the tip of this mountain monk’s staff.
How is this to be seen? He plants the staff on the ground and says: 'When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the world. Ascending the hall, he raised an example.
Chan Master Daguan Ying addressed the assembly, saying: "The seven Buddhas are subjects of one's nature; the myriad dharmas are slaves to one's mind. Now tell me, where is the master residing?
He gave a shout himself and said, "All those from the seven Buddhas downward have now shown their heads. Then he gave a nod himself and said: "Yes."

Each person stands in attendance. The Master says: "To call the Seven Buddhas 'slaves of nature' and to point to the myriad dharmas as 'servants of the mind'—Daguan claims for himself a path of transcendence.
Yet when he himself shouts and himself assents, this is still merely the business of slaves and servants;
when has the true Master ever been seen even in a dream? Do you all wish to see him? He sweeps once with his whisk and says: "At dawn..."
A spring breeze stirs the ranks; throughout the gardens, flowers of a hundred varieties bloom. As his end approached, he entered the room with the assembly and finished his duties.
He then requested a brush and wrote a letter bidding farewell to the various mountains and to the Duke of Wei. When the Duke sent medicine as a gift, the Master would not accept it.
The Duke again sent a messenger to ask, "The Master was born at Tiantai; why did you die at Jingci? The Master replied, "The sun rises in the east and sets in the west at night. He then wrote:
He transformed others through verses. His secular age was sixty-one; his monastic seniority was forty-four.
○ Chan Master Xiryan Liaohui of Siming was of the Luo family from Pengzhou in Shu.

From the time his hair hung down in childhood, when he played with other children, he would invariably knead soil and sand to fashion Buddhist stupas and images. One day, at Yuzhang Mountain, Zudeng and...
He departed. His teacher joined his palms toward him, and because of the karmic affinity between teacher and disciple from past lives, his parents permitted him to leave the household life.
Dengshou bestowed upon him the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*. However, this was not his aspiration, so he took his leave and traveled to Chengdu to visit Huai’an Zhao at Zhaojue.

Zhao recognized his capacity and instructed him to travel south for further inquiry. He then went to attend on Zhejiang Weng Yan at Mount Jing, where he heard that Gao Yuanquan was a man of direct path.

Zhizhe personally admired him. When Fanyuan was traveling to Ruiyan on Mount Tai, Zhizhe went along with him. One day, Fanyuan asked, "Do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth exist, or do they not?
As Zhizhe was about to open his mouth to speak, Fanyuan immediately let out a shout. Zhizhe then presented a verse.
Yuan said, "There is no connection. One day, the Master happened to write down the words he had spoken to the assembly regarding the white poplar tree.

Yuan read them and laughed, saying, "You may as well be good at calligraphy and composing verses; however, what can you do about there being no connection? The Master was frustrated and unable to express himself.
Yuan said, "I have offered many skillful means, yet you yourself have disregarded them. The reason lies not here; you must go see Xuedou."
At that time, Wuzu Fayan was the abbot of Xuedou. When the Master went to his quarters to present himself and recount his background, Wuzu scolded him, saying, "Go back to sleep!
Subsequently, he appointed him as an attendant not involved in administrative affairs. One day, Wuzu said to the Master, "The point where you cannot see through lies right at the tip of your nose;
the place where you cannot express it does not leave your lips. Yet, if you try to seek it, it is thousands of miles away."
The Master raised his voice and said, "I thought there would be much more to it. Zhun followed Yuanzhao, the Abbot of Yungai Monastery, as his attendant;

through his composed and respectful inquiries, he mastered the essential points of the teaching. When Zhun resided at Mount Jing, he invited [Yuanzhao] to serve as the Librarian of the Canon and later promoted him to the Second Seat.

From then on, his reputation spread throughout the monastic community. Zhao Guanwen, the Prefectural Governor of Suzhou during the Jiezhai era, appointed the Master as the Abbot of Foding Monastery. The assembly...

When he presided over Jisi Temple, his governance was highly praised. He subsequently moved to Nengren in Dongjia, Donglin in Jiangzhou, and finally to Tiantong, where he achieved magnificent achievements at each location.
On the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, he ascended the hall, held up his staff, and addressed the assembly, saying:
"The Yellow-Faced Gautama was a fierce general of Central India. He took compassion as his bow and arrows, and wisdom as his spear and halberd, leading a hundred..."
His ten thousand heroic soldiers were irresistible; he deployed over three hundred battle formations that were invincible.
Thus, for forty-nine years, he produced over five thousand scrolls of military treatises. Although these works have circulated among the people, not a single character has ever been leaked.
Because he stood as an adversary and an enemy to the demonic armies of birth and death, he subsequently constructed [a fortress] on the banks of the Bahudā River.
There is a great city named Nirvana. Within that city, he first rewards all the soldiers with his body of purple-golden hue, commanding them to gaze upon it until they are fully satisfied.
After repeatedly consoling and instructing them, he further scatters eight pecks and four bushels of pearls and jewels.
His intention is nothing other than this: he surely desires to break open the sturdy gates of birth and death, so as to universally bestow [liberation] upon all beings throughout the entire world.
They shall give rise to the path that leads through the heavens and brings life together, reaching the field of great peace and security and great liberation before they finally cease.
How could it be said that, after more than two thousand years, their aspirations have still not been fulfilled and their merits have not yet been realized?
Since I, this mountain monk, know that their strength is exhausted and their stratagems are spent, I cannot help but draw my sword to assist them. (He strikes once with his staff.)
The waves of the four seas are calm, and the dragon sleeps in peace; the clouds of the nine heavens are clear, and the crane flies high.
Elder Fuyong ascends the hall. He relates how Master Fuyong visited Master Shixing.

When Master Shixing ascended the hall, he took his staff in his right hand and moved it toward the left, saying, "If it were not for my elder brother Fuyong, it would have been very difficult to fully comprehend. He then spoke this verse: "Exhausting all [effort]..."
The spirit of old age remains; cups and dishes appear ever more new. Who would have known that the wine of a village inn could not persuade those who dwell in the imperial towers?
In his later years, he resided at the Huanzhi Pagoda Hermitage. As he approached the end, having instructed his attendants, he asked, "What time is it now?

They replied, "It is the second watch. Thereupon, he relaxed his body as if casting himself down; a moment later, when they looked upon him, he had already passed away. This was indeed the third month of the third year of the Jingding era.
The eleventh day of the month. [He passed away at] sixty-five years of age; forty-seven years of summer retreats.

Chan Master Ning, "Retired Plowman" of Lingyin in Hangzhou, first resided at Chongsheng in Jiaxing, and subsequently occupied Bao'en, Chengtian, Huirui, and Wanshou in Suzhou, before arriving at Lingyin.
He ascended the hall and said: "There is no dharma before the eyes; the meaning lies within the eyes."

[The Master] entered the hall. "After the rain, the mountain colors are emerald; with the warm breeze, the birds' songs are clamorous. He struck the meditation seat once and said, "It is laughable that the old barbarian had no transformative wisdom;
he sat before the peak of Shaoshi for nine years. [Later,] while ascending the hall, he cited the case where a monk asked Xianglin, "What is it like when the year is spent and the age is exhausted?
Xianglin replied, "Old Wang of the eastern village burns paper money at night. The Master said, "Old Wang burns..."

Money. His words are upright and his speech is upright. A brocade wrapping a raw stone; iron encasing a lump of clay. Ascending the hall: A thousand peaks stretch to the horizon, locked in verdant green;
willow catkins fill the sky, drifting like cotton. Pity the True Man of No Rank, who has been sleeping on grass and under the dew all along. *A!* (Silence)
"The three springs have passed by my gazing; when will it be the year of my return?
On the occasion of ascending the hall, Chan Master Bieshan Zhi of Tiantong in Siming raised this case:

When the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana, Mañjuśrī requested the Buddha to turn the wheel of the Dharma once more. The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying: "In the forty-nine years since I began teaching, I have never spoken a single word."
[Zifu] said: "You requested that I turn the Wheel of the Dharma once more. Have I ever turned the Wheel of the Dharma before? He spoke in verse:

"This old man has lived his life telling great lies; He deceives the blind and the deaf by taking non-existence for existence. Only at the moment of death does a single word prove true— Yet even this is merely the 'mealtime bell' for the Acharya."
Master Huanxi Yichan of Siming Tian Tongshan ascended the hall and said: He cited the Sutra, which states:

"The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas; yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him, and he did not attain the Way of Buddhahood. He then offered this verse: "The seal of Vairocana was cast at the beginning of the kalpa;
The ancient inscriptions, though carved with minute detail, remain distinct. How laughable and how tragic that people do not recognize it— Yet they instead harbor resentment."
The characters are incomplete.

Master Ming of Yuepo at Tiantong in Mingzhou ascended the hall and, citing the story of Mazu when a monk asked about the phrase "leaving the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations," offered this verse:
"Leaving the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations— Passing the blame back and forth, how many times has it been done?"
I know. This monk carries a load of bewilderment; he has traded it for two head of fat and muddled things to take home.
○ Fourth, Chan Master Xuedou Hishou Shaotan of Siming was a native of Western Sichuan. He appeared in the world at Fulong Monastery.

Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the matter of the supreme vehicle of the ancestral school? The Master said, "The dripping from the eaves is distinct and clear. The Master then continued:

It is difficult to escape. With eyes wide open, one enters the boiling cauldron with dignity. At this point, how can one attain it?

If you intend to roast the yellow earth until it is soft, you will still fail to disregard the purple clay seal; you cannot avoid treading upon the footprints of the ancients. If you intend to lock the void and seal the dream, [you remain bound].

The roads are blocked and the bridges severed; furthermore, there is fear of remaining entangled within the thicket of complications. It would be better to offer up a little according to one's capacity and act in accordance with the exigencies of the times.
[He] picks up his staff: vertically it exhausts the three periods of time, horizontally it spans the ten directions.

[He] leans on the staff: the blue-eyed yellow-headed ones cannot understand it. Wild plum blossoms, the wind stilled, their dark fragrance floats forth. He ascends the hall: "In the second month, spring is said to be at its end. Shao...

The flowers are as rich as wine; the orioles sing in the willow rain. The butterflies play in the sea-blossom breeze. If you understand this as an objective realm, it is like crossing mountains to seek the tracks of ants.

at sunset, weeping for the end of the path. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: One night’s awakening, three loads of earth—before his feet have even crossed the threshold, the bones of his hands...

"The wild goose flies into the vast darkness; what can the fowler do? [The Master] ascends the hall and says: "If one can give rise to a single vital mechanism and utter a single appropriate word, there will not be a single cloud for ten thousand miles.
The blue sky deserves a blow of the staff. Without waiting for the spring breeze to intentionally open it, the dark fragrance is already upon the plum blossoms.
He sends this verse to the Abbot of Tianmu: "The old man of eighty has grown new teeth; he chews them thoroughly..."
The void spits out tea seeds, scattering them toward the trees by the Linglong Cliff; branch after branch, leaf after leaf, they are all *tánhuā* (pariṣekapuṣpa) blossoms.
Chan Master Kexiang of Xuefeng on the Steep Bank in Fuzhou ascended the hall and said: "Cao Shan once had a monk ask him: 'When snow covers the thousand mountains, why is the solitary peak not white?
Shan replied: 'You must know there is the extraordinary within the extraordinary. [The monk] asked: 'How is this so?'"

"This is the difference within difference. The Master said, "It does not fall into the category of the colors of the various mountains. The Teacher offered this verse: "Within words, 'this' and 'that' carry profound mystery;
All seek to distinguish the correct from the biased within words. Alas, they neglect the single imperial highway, Which lies vast and submerged before the bright moon.
The verse for receiving guests at Yupu (Fisherman’s Harbor) says: "Beyond the mountains of Wu, in front of the mountains of Yue, There is rice to fill the hunger..."
Sleeping on a mat; reaching this point, one is able to find rest. Yet the Imperial Capital remains separated by but a single tide of the boat.

The Master composed a verse: "In my life, I never wished to encounter a Buddha; Yet upon the tips of my ten fingers, the azure countenance appears.
