[Chang] provides a verse on the story of Linji’s visit to Huangbo: "By the plum tree, spring is already three-quarters spent; The playful butterflies and wandering bees have heard nothing yet.
How strange that the pure fragrance has leaked forth so lightly— A single branch slants down against the bamboo fence.
He offers a verse for a monk being sent to see Jianfu Zeshan: "To which direction does the Master go to pay his respects? At Jade Terrace (Yují), it is difficult to point out the way."
There was a certain "Dull Bagman" from Changting who has now appeared in Raozhou as the Dharma successor of Chan Master Xiaoyin Yun of Longxiang.
Chan Master Jueyuan Huitan of Tianjie Temple in Yingtianfu was of the Yang clan of Tiantai; his mother was surnamed Jia. She dreamed of swallowing...
Mingzhu became pregnant, and when she gave birth, [the child] had a broad forehead, full cheeks, a flat crown, and large ears; his physical characteristics were most extraordinary.
In his youth, he relied upon Faguo and Dajun of Yue to study the supramundane teachings. Upon reaching adulthood, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under Jiaogong of Goryeo and listened to the *Mohe Zhiguan* under Chenggong of Shangzhu. Subsequently, he abandoned them both. At that time, Guang...
Zhizhe was in Central India; the Master went to visit him. Zhizhe asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from traveling the mountains.
Zhizhe said, "As for that which you used to press down under your bamboo hat while wandering everywhere to seek instruction—how is it now?
The Master said, "I presented it to the Master before I even entered the gate. Zhizhe said, "Why do you not bring it forth right now? As the Master hesitated, Zhizhe immediately—
"Hai! At that moment, the Master attained a sudden, profound realization. One day, Zhizhi opened both hands and showed them to the Master, saying, "I have spread my hands wide;
why do you refuse to accept this? The Master said, "Do not come here to obstruct me. Zhizhi said, "Come closer and I will explain it for you.
The Master immediately covered his ears and walked out. Zhizhi nodded in approval. Later, when Guanzhi was appointed by imperial decree to lead Longxiang Temple...
He served as the founding abbot. The Master followed him to serve as the keeper of the treasury and subsequently shared the teaching seat.

In the *Xinwei* year of the *Zhishun* era, the Imperial Secretariat issued a mandate for the Master to take up residence at Zutang on Mount Niutou. In the *Guiwei* year of the *Zhengding* era, he ascended to Qingliang.

His spiritual conduct became known to the Imperial Preceptor, who conferred upon him the title "Pure Enlightenment and Wondrous Practice" (*Jingjue Miaoxing*). In the *Yiwei* year, he moved to Baoning, and in the *Bingma* year, [Emperor] Taizu Gao...

When the Emperor established Jianye as his capital, the Master went to pay his respects at the imperial camp gate. Seeing that the Master was of imposing stature and exceptional character, he sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly a monk of both merit and wisdom.
He then appointed him to preside over Jiangshan. In the year Dingyou, the Longxiang Monastery was granted the name Great Tianjie Temple;

by imperial decree, the Master was summoned to serve as its abbot. The Emperor personally inscribed the six large characters "The First Zen Forest of Tianjie" and displayed them above the gate to honor the school.
"Ultimate," the Master said, pointing toward the monks within his quarters. "Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, there is no room for you to chew and swallow;

there is no room for you to pursue or turn toward. Do you understand? The monk was at a loss. The Master said, "If you have not yet clarified three, eight, and nine, it will be difficult to avoid self-murmuring.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "The spring breeze sweeps on, the spring days linger; the yellow oriole sings upon the branches of a hundred flowers. Within this, there is the infinite."
[The Master] said, "In the end, who do you allow to know? Before he had finished speaking, a monk suddenly asked, "What is it like when the mind, intellect, and consciousness cannot be suppressed?
The Master said in a stern voice, "Who is it that cannot be suppressed? He ascended the hall and said:

"Before the first day of the sixth month, the myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images speak Chan on your behalf. After the first day of the sixth month, an eight-sided grindstone rolls through the void. Today..."
Precisely on the first day of the sixth month, the person of no rank stands bare-boned and stark. The golden-maned lion knows how to turn its body;
the hornless iron ox sleeps at Shaoshi. The ten sages and three worthies know nothing of it; Hanshan and Shide laugh themselves to tears.

Ascending the hall: "Arriving in the Western Heaven in the morning, returning to the land of Tang in the evening—the mirror is present before the movement of the mind, yet I dare not grant my seal of approval.

Baoning has opened wide his eight characters; is there anyone who cannot restrain or control it? He descended from the seat. Ascending the hall: "It cannot be gathered by being embraced; it cannot be dispersed by being pushed away.
It is not uniform when categorized, nor is it confused when mixed. Ceasing illumination and forgetting conditions, throughout the ten directions..."
Severing [all ties] while seated. Waving the hand across the river—seeing this, one must accept the ambiguity with all one's might.
To have attained even half of Jiangshan’s [teaching], and to uphold it in such a manner—even in a donkey’s year, you have not yet dreamed of it. Entering the hall: This is simply a ready-made koan.
Among the assembly, there are many who understand it, yet few who do not misunderstand it. Therefore, gold and brass are not distinguished, and jade and stone are not differentiated. Longhe...

"In this matter, one must simply distinguish clearly. If there were one monk named Zhang with long arms and another named Li with large eyes—if everyone were like the Dharma school of Bodhidharma today—whom would you have to carry the burden?

*Huh!* [He] descended from his seat. He ascended the hall and said: "The Sutras have masters of the Sutras; the Treatises have masters of the Treatises. Longhe has now opened up a single thread of the Way."
The section is concluded. Holding up his staff and striking it once, he said: "Tell me, what chapter and verse is this? He ascended the hall and said:
"Before King Vipaśyin and after Maitreya Buddha, there is a ready-made public case that I do not dare to break open for you.
Why? Because my heart does not betray others, and my face bears no shame. He ascended the hall and said: "To propagate the school of Yangqi... (He sat.)
The position of Nanquan’s bowl; the life-root of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the very nose of the patch-robed monks. (He plants his staff and says:

"Bought cheap at the eastern market, sold dear at the western market. To the assembly: "In years past, when Wenyuan attended Zhaozhou, he preached the Dharma on the latrine and was not easily repaid."
When the single thought of returning the light becomes clear, the frost is pure and the moon fills the tower at midnight. In the first year of the Zhida era, the Imperial Palace was newly completed.

As the Emperor was about to ascend the precious throne, he issued a decree for the Master to lead twelve hundred monks to open and read the Tripitaka, thereby solemnizing the ground of pure awakening.
The Master ascended the seat to preach the Dharma; the Emperor personally led his ministers before the dais.

Upon hearing [the news], he looked on with great joy and bestowed inner treasury silks as a gift. In the spring of the first year of the Hongwu era (Wushen), the Shanshi Yuan (Court for the Propagation of Goodness) was established;
by imperial decree, the Master was appointed to lead the affairs of the court. He was divested of his purple robes and gold-embroidered square cassock. The imperial edict stated, in brief:
"Since I first began my enterprise, I have charged you to rectify the school. Your virtuous influence has revitalized the Dharma-gate, and this auspicious fortune..."
For his assistance to both the state and the family, he was specially granted the title of Great Chan Master Yanfan Shanshe Liguo Chongjiao.

At that time, scholars in academic robes claimed that Buddhist monks were parasites upon the world and petitioned the Emperor to eliminate them. The Emperor showed this memorial to the Master, who replied:
"Confucius regarded the Buddha as a Great Sage; by this we know that a true Confucian would certainly not disparage the Buddha. He was not mistaken.
"The Buddha was certainly not a true Confucian. The Emperor likewise declined to grant his request, as he believed that the Buddha's teachings secretly supported the sovereign’s governance.

In the sixth month of the summer of the Gengxu year, during a court deliberation regarding a subordinate official from the Western Regions, the Emperor—because that realm highly esteemed the Buddhist vehicle—specially commanded the Master to go there, decreeing that the Minister of State Zhao [Name] serve as his deputy. The Master received the command and departed that very day.
Setting out on his journey, he showed no concern or attachment for his robes or alms bowl. In the autumn of the Xinhai year, he rested at the kingdom of Siṃhala (Sengqieluo).
Its king received the Master at the Buddha Mountain Monastery (Foshan Jingshe) and performed the rites of a disciple toward him. On the ninth month, he manifested a slight ailment.
On the twenty-sixth day, having bathed and changed his clothes, he urgently summoned the Minister and said to him: "My illusory karmic conditions have ended here; I cannot return."
"Life has ended," he said. He then instructed those around him to remain steadfast and sat upright. When midnight had passed, he asked, "Is it dawn yet?
They replied, "It is not yet. After a short while, he asked again. They replied, "The sun has risen. Thereupon, he passed away peacefully. His secular age was sixty-eight;
his years as a monk were fifty-three. The King provided for his funeral, cremating the coffin and collecting the relics, including his teeth and tongue.
His remains were interred at the stupa of a Pratyekabuddha in that country. In the winter of the Jiǎyín year, the Minister of State Zhao [Surname] returned to court and reported these matters.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor sighed with admiration and issued an imperial decree for Zonglé, the Abbot of Tianjie Monastery, to enshrine the Master’s robes to the left of the Yuhua Terrace.
○ Chan Master Yongzhen Yuanliang of Lingyin, Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Ji’gan, was a native of Wu County in Suzhou.
He was the third son of Fan Wenzheng Gong and the ninth-generation descendant of Shangshu Youcheng Gong, whose name was Chunli.
His father was Bohe, and his mother was Lady Zheng. They had two sons: the elder was Shuyu, and the younger was the Master himself. At the age of fifteen, he followed [his teacher].
He received the *mì* tonsure at Yingfuyuan in Li. He studied the Tiantai teachings and contemplations under Dharma Master Ze of Beichan.
Because of the encouragement of Tianping Zhushan Shi Zhan, he was urged to follow the Chan school; thereupon, he went to see Guangzhi at Longxiang.
Guangzhi asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From Beichan in Suzhou. Guangzhi said, "The Three Vehicles and the Ten..."
[Zhizhe] said, "I shall not ask about the teachings of the two divisions. What is the matter of traveling on foot? The Master hesitated; Zhizhe then shouted. The Master bowed and withdrew.

The following day, he saw [Zhizhe] again and was about to pose his question when Zhizhe shouted once more. The Master lowered his head. Zhizhe said, "To seek it through thought is to fall into the second place.
Thereupon, the Master attained realization and attended upon him at his side. After a long time, he mastered [the teachings].
Having grasped the essential principles, he went again to pay his respects to Master Shi-shi Ying at Yuyang Monastery. Master Shi appointed him to oversee the collection of the teachings.

In the Renwu year of the Zhizheng era, by order of the Xuanzheng Yuan, the Master was invited to take charge of the world at Zisheng Monastery in Jiaxing, and subsequently moved to Tianzhang Monastery in Yue.
He moved to Zhongtianzhu in Hangzhou and ascended to Lingyin Monastery, where he addressed the assembly, saying:
"At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, when monks travel east and west, if the tip of your staff brushes against someone who understands the Buddha-dharma, it will be a disaster.
The Buddhas of the three periods cannot grasp it; the patriarchs of successive generations cannot grasp it; the old monks of the world cannot grasp it."
"Ho! He said again, "If one can recognize the source upon the tip of a single hair, then even ten thousand taels of gold will be worth spending.
Why then did Yunmen say, 'Return to me the payment for ninety days' of rice'?
This is because the furnace contains much dull iron, and the door of a skilled physician is filled with patients. There is yet another matter beyond this."
In the interim, there were other deliberations, and the Dharma school of Bodhidharma was swept away entirely.
On the sixteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Hongwu era, he passed away. One day prior, he said to those around him, "Tomorrow at the hour of the snake (10 a.m.), I shall depart.
When the time arrived, he bathed and sat upright. His attendant monk requested a verse, whereupon he wrote: "This year I am fifty-five; I have shattered the void."
Empty drum. Not crossing the pass of birth and death, what need is there to seek out Buddhas and Patriarchs? In an instant, he passed away in silence.
○ This was Chan Master Lǎn'ān Tíngjùn of Jìngcí Monastery in Hángzhōu; "Yòngzhāng" was his courtesy name. He was originally from Lèpíng in Ráo, surnamed Dǒng.
He left the household life under Mǎijí of Dàyún Monastery in his hometown. At the age of twenty, he shaved his head and received the precepts.
He was fully equipped with the necessary provisions. At twenty-five, he traveled abroad, visiting various monasteries across Mount Lu for a long time.
Eventually, he went to the region of Zhejiang and met Yuejiang Yin at Heshan in Wuxing. Yin said, "I have already seen you before you even entered the gate.

The Master replied, "The phoenix does not always dwell in the wutong tree. Yin said, "Not so, not so. The Master harbored doubts about this, and served him as an attendant for a full year without [Yin ever speaking again].
At that time, Guangzhi was propagating the Way in Zhong Tianzhu (Central India) of Hangzhou. The Master went to pay him a visit. Guangzhi extended both hands to show them to him;
the Master immediately prostrated himself. Guangzhi asked, "What do you see? The Master replied, "A fine steed, as soon as it falls to the ground, has its heart set on a thousand li.

Guangzhi sighed in admiration and said, "You are of the lineage of Huanglong and Foyin. Guard and uphold this well yourself. Later, Dongyu of Lingyin Monastery appointed the Master to serve as the head of the administrative office.
The Record Office states: At the beginning of the Tianli era, Emperor Wen established the Great Longxiang Jiqing Monastery at his former residence in Jinling.

Guangzhi served as its founding abbot and invited the Master to occupy the position of First Seat. There, the Master expounded and implemented the Pure Rules (qinggui), issuing commands to the vast assembly.
Consequently, his Dharma assemblies reached their full splendor. In the second year of the Zhizheng era, by selection of the Xuanzheng Yuan, he resided at Baima in Suzhou.
He subsequently moved to Zifu in Wuxing, where he constructed the Great Hall, the Mountain Gate, the Sangha Hall, the kitchen, the storehouse, and the Abbot’s quarters;
in barely five years, these were all fully completed. He was then transferred again to Nengren in Shaoxing and Zhongtianzhi Jingci in Hangzhou. During the present dynasty...
In the first year of the Hongwu era, monks and Daoists from western Zhejiang gathered in Jinling for corvée labor and taxation; the Master was among them and stayed at Mount Zhong.
On the twenty-third day of the fifth month, he sat upright as usual and remained silent for a long time. The attendant monk thought the Master intended to depart.

He prostrated and requested a verse of farewell. The Master stared at him with wide eyes and said, "If the conditions for remaining have not yet ended, one stays; if the conditions for departing have ended, one leaves.
What need is there for a verse? After a short while, he passed away. His dharma-brothers from the Tianjie Jueyuan Temple, including Master Tan, diligently managed the funeral arrangements.
His secular age was seventy, and his years as a monk were fifty.
○ Fourth, Yuyang Juezhao Chongyu: A Chan master of the Chen clan of Pilin. He served Master Xiaolin Xiao of Shouchang Temple as his teacher.
He visited Jizhao at Mount Jing and Duanya at Mount Tianmu, but found no resonance with either.

Upon meeting Guangzhi at Zhongtianzhu, and later at Longxiang, their spiritual faculties finally converged. He was appointed to the monastic administration and charged with overseeing the Tripitaka library. From then on—
This further encouraged him to apply himself with vigor to the Way; for thirty years, his side did not even touch his mat.
He emerged into the world at Nan Chan in Taiping, was later transferred to Yuan Tong in Jiu Jiang, and finally reached Yu Wang. There, he ascended the hall and said:

"Before the vast chaos had been divided, and before heaven and earth had taken their positions, there was a single phrase that the Buddhas of the three periods did not know and the Patriarchs of the six generations did not understand. I, the old monk..."
What a pity that today, when he should manifest it directly before us, he simply spreads his two hands and says, "Ha! Ascending the hall, [the Master] said:
"In the past, Master Jiantang brought forth a dead cat’s head and set up shop in the mountains; he haggled for a price that reached the heavens, yet no one would buy it.
To this very day, it has been blown upon by the wind and scorched by the sun until its stench permeates the sky. This mountain monk cannot bear to let it go."
The strength of one's arms is heavy; this is the way to go upward. Is there no one who can set a fixed price? To see what is right and not act upon it—what bravery is there in that?
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The scriptures state: 'Pure and originally so, how did mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
I, this mountain monk, say: 'Pure and originally so'—what do you call 'mountains, rivers, and the great earth'? If you were to turn toward the scriptures..."
If you attain awakening upon hearing these words, it is like pressing sand to extract oil; if you seek a seam within the painted waves, how can you ever reach the ultimate?
The earth slants toward the southeast; the heavens slant toward the northwest. [Ascending the hall: "O virtuous practitioners of Zen!
There is no mystery, there is no subtlety; there is no Buddha and no Patriarch. From morning until evening, as you walk up and down the east and west corridors—"
"Has there ever been anything that has tripped up your heels?
Chan Master Zhongbin Kechi of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Shangsu, was a native of Linhai in Taizhou.
His surname was Xu. At the age of thirteen, he received the full precepts under Mingyan Taigu Xi at Tiantai.
Having heard that Wuji Ben was propagating the Way at Jiangxin, he went there to pay his respects. Wuji asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from Tiantai.
Wuji said, "The Stone Bridge was split into two pieces last night; do you know of this? The Master replied, "I left Huading Peak recently. Wuji said, "That is what I am asking you."
At Shiqiao, the Master said, "I arrived here ten days ago. Xuanji was delighted. After some time, he went to visit Guangzhi at Longxiang, where he served as the Director of Records (*neiji*).
He then paid his respects to Jizhao at Mount Jing, where he served as the Librarian (*dianzangjiao*). From then on, the monastic community’s perception of him changed.

He emerged from seclusion at Wufeng in Siming, moved to Damei, and was promoted to Jingci. Entering the hall, he said: "Let us set aside questions and answers for a moment; before you have even entered the gate—"
We have already met one another; the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace have been repaid all at once.
If you still persist in viewing and listening, you will inevitably require further annotation. Bodhidharma said: "I came to this land from afar / To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings.
/ One flower opens into five petals; / The fruiting occurs naturally. Years have passed and circumstances have long since changed; for those of later generations—
The style of the Sun family is boundless; it has stirred the body and mind into a single tangle of hemp thread. Today, Wufeng cuts them all off at once. Do you understand?
"Fifteen days after the hundredth day approaches Qingming; the Yuanxiao festival is surely on the fifteenth of the first month. [He ascends the hall.]
The vast sky is boundless; the bright sun flies by. The human heart is restless; white hair urges one toward home. These principles of reality are manifest and unchanging through all time.

Beneath the three rafter-poles and before the seven-foot mat, you should apply yourself to introspection and examination. Entering the hall [he said]: Greed, anger, and ignorance; precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
How can a lump of clay or a clod of earth be made into something complete? If you lose your money in the river...
The Master entered the hall and said: "At the Crane Pond and Vulture Peak, in the monasteries and gardens of the coastal lands;
on the path of Caoxi and before the peak of Shaoshi—everything is as level as a palm and as straight as a string. It is all right here. Those with ears hear it; those with eyes see it."
His hearing and seeing were vivid and clear. [He asked: "What is this, right here and now? After a long silence, he said, "Vaguely Yue Province; faintly Yangzhou.
On the seventeenth day of the eighth month in the twenty-fourth year of the Hongwu era, he passed away. He was eighty-three years of age and had been a monk for sixty-nine years.
Chan Master Zongle, whose style name was Litan and courtesy name was Quanshi, was a native of Linhai in Taizhou. He belonged to the Zhou clan;

his father was Ji-fu and his mother was of the Ge clan. From the moment he first learned to sit up, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), which caused his parents and relatives to regard him with wonder.
At the age of eight, he was sent to study Buddhism under Guangzhi at Zhong Tianzhu Monastery in Hangzhou. Upon merely glancing over the scriptures and books, he mastered them.
[He] recited [the precepts]. At fourteen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination. Zhi founded Longxiang Jiqing Temple in Jinling, and the Master went with him. One day, Zhi asked:
"What is the meaning of the National Teacher’s calling the attendant three times and the attendant responding three times?
The Master said: "Why do you dig into flesh to create a wound? Zhi said: "I thought you were extraordinary, but it turns out you are just like this. The Master gave a shout.

When Zhì held up his staff as if to strike him, the Master shook out his sleeves and departed. From that day on, [Zhì] attained the profound mysteries. After some time, he went to visit Yuánsǒu at Jìngshān;
their words accorded perfectly, and Yuánsǒu appointed him to oversee the secretariat. Not long after, he emerged into the world at Shuǐxī in Xuān, remaining there for over twenty years.

After all his [previous] positions had been abolished, he was appointed to the Zhongtianzhu Temple in Hangzhou and later transferred to Mount Jing. Emperor Taizu, the August Founder, inquired about matters concerning ghosts and spirits;
the Emperor issued an edict for monks of learning and conduct from the two provinces of Zhejiang, and the Master was ranked foremost among them.

He was lodged at Tianjie Monastery, where his responses were in accord with the Imperial will. Subsequently, when a Great Universal Salvation Assembly was established at Mount Zhongshan, the Master presided over it.
The Emperor commissioned him to compose hymns for praising the Buddha and further instructed him to preach the Dharma to spirits and deities.

When the Taizu ascended the dais to listen, he marveled at his excellence and commanded him to reside in the celestial realm, honoring him with great favor. At that time, both the monastic and lay communities turned toward his transformation, and the Dharma assemblies flourished in their peak prosperity. He ascended the hall and said:
In suffering and pleasure, in adversity and favor, the Way is found therein. When there is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither adversity nor favor, where is the Way?

[The Master] held up his staff and said: "Throughout the hall, the wind of boundless white artemisia blows; clearly it does not arise from the autumn river. He ascended the hall and said: "There are twelve months in a year.
For nine months, one travels through prefectures and counties, enjoying the waters and gazing at the mountains. Look closely..."
The period has come to an end. During the three months of the summer retreat, it is precisely the time to rest and cease.
For me, a mountain monk, to announce this is like washing a clod of earth in the mud. (He strikes the whisk. "A fragrant breeze comes from the south;

the halls and pavilions grow cool. On the Winter Solstice, he ascended the hall: "The first yang returns, and the myriad species revive. The Duke of Lu writes of clouds upon his terrace; the Han dynasty..."
To add thread to a maiden’s loom is to clutter the valleys and fill the ditches when it concerns the dissemination of worldly truth;

to further deliberate upon it as if it were the Buddha-dharma is to fall into pits and moats. Why? Because a carriage does not push sideways, and there is no logic in making crooked judgments. Ascending the hall: It is the severe cold of mid-winter.
Heaven is cold, and people are cold. The hearth fire is lit again and again; drawing up my feet, I sit upon the meditation mat. There is a phrase already present and complete.

"Great snow fills Chang'an. [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended. Entering the hall, he said: "To speak of mind, to speak of nature, to speak of the wondrous, or to speak of the mysterious—all these are merely the saliva and spittle of wild foxes.
To wield the staff, to shout, to brandish the fork, or to dance with the bamboo—these too are the livelihoods of ghosts."
Holding up his staff, he said: "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon it long ago; yet until this very day, he has not attained its wondrous essence.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Today is the first day of the third month. The past has already perished; the future has not yet arrived; the present does not abide.
From this root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. Striking the whisk, he said: "Swinging on a swing upon the tongue of a tiger; [jumping] within the eye of a *jiaoming* (a tiny insect)."
The night market was opened. Whenever His Majesty visited or summoned him for an audience within the inner palace, he granted him tea and a meal.
Furthermore, having composed a collection of poems modeled after those written by the Master, he bestowed them upon the Xitian Shanshi Chan Master Bandida as he arrived at court.

Upon seeing the Master, [the Emperor] sighed in admiration, saying, "Truly, he is a compassionate vessel for those in the sea of suffering. Once, when the Master was afflicted by illness, the Emperor visited him in person to offer his condolences and dispatched physicians to examine him.

In the spring of the Ding-si year, he received an imperial decree to join Pu-fu and Ru-qi of Hangzhou in annotating the *Heart Sūtra*, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for circulation among the people.
Because there were missing or scattered texts among the Buddhist scriptures, the Taizu (Emperor Taizu) commanded the Master...
He led thirty disciples to the Western Regions to seek them out. He obtained the *Zhuāngyán Bǎowén Wénshū* (Mañjuśrī’s Adorned Jewel Text) and other scriptures.

In the third month of the fifteenth year of Hongwu, he returned to court. In the sixteenth year, the Office of Buddhist Records (*Sēnglùsī*) was established, and the Master was appointed as Right Street Overseer (*Shànshì*).
Whenever there were matters concerning the Dharma gate, his fellow officials did not dare to speak; only the Master spoke up with vigor. Later, because of [the matter of] the Elder...

The official’s memorial regarding his affairs incurred reprimand, so he went with him to Chafeng in Fengyang to build a temple. The construction was completed in three years, and by imperial decree, the temple was granted the plaque "Yuantong" (Universal Penetration).
In the autumn of the nineteenth year, he was summoned to return to Tianjie Monastery. Upon being introduced for an audience, the Emperor bestowed a poem upon him containing the lines:

"Leshan, having departed from here, who shall ask about Chan? Morning and evening, I constantly think of you as being before my eyes. Two years later, the old temple was destroyed by fire; the Master—
Taking the restoration as his personal responsibility, he led Master Chun of Zhushan to petition for its reconstruction outside the Zubao Gate.

The Emperor said, "It may be done. Thereupon, the Master exerted himself without showing any sign of weariness. Upon completion, the Master cleared a room at Santaba Hermitage and inscribed its plaque with the characters "Pine-Tree Dwelling" (Songxia Ju) to serve as a place for his retirement in old age.
In the summer of the twenty-third year, an imperial edict was issued for him to reside there once again.

He was granted the title Tianjie (Heavenly Realm). The Emperor decreed that he should forever uphold the fundamental principles for one hundred and twenty years. In the twenty-fourth year, he again presided over the Right Street.
After residing at Shanshe for some time, he was granted leave to return to Chafeng due to his advanced age. He then proceeded to the palace to pay his respects and take his leave.
The Emperor said, "In solitude you gaze upon the bright moon; at ease you face the white clouds. Go forth!
He departed for Shifo Temple on the banks of the river. Suddenly he manifested illness; having summoned his disciples to offer them final instructions, he passed away peacefully.

His cremation yielded immeasurable *śarīra* relics. This was the tenth day of the ninth month. His secular age was seventy-four, and his monastic age (*varṣa*) was sixty. His remaining bones were enshrined.
He was buried to the right of the Guangzhi Pagoda at Tianjie Monastery.
○ Chan Master Zongchang of Fanglin at Tianjie Monastery in Yingtian Prefecture, whose alternative name was Huanyun, was the son of the Mao family of Linhai in Taizhou.
He addressed the assembly, saying: "An ancient worthy said that this body and its lifespan are like a horse passing through a crevice; what leisure is there for intervals?"
"Sentient delusions constitute miscellaneous affairs. Great assembly, when you put on your robes and eat your meals throughout the twelve periods of the day, is that not a miscellaneous affair?
When you burn incense and prostrate before the Buddha, is that not a miscellaneous affair? When you read the sutras and practice seated meditation, is that not a miscellaneous affair?
Tell me, which of these is the matter of one’s own fundamental allotment? After a long pause, he said: "I do not dare to slight you; you all..."
"All shall become Buddhas.
Chan Master Daochun Yaya of Jiuyan on Mount Tiantai composed a verse on the Buddha’s Attainment of Enlightenment, which says: "Stately and alone, revealed before the kalpa began;
Ten thousand miles of blue sky, with the blazing sun suspended. Only upon beholding the morning star at night did he suddenly awaken; At the crown of his head, he deserves a blow from the staff."
Three thousand blows of the staff.
[This concludes the section on] Chan Master Zhongfang Lun of Baoning, successor to [the lineage].
Chan Master Xiaoyan Xinian of Fengsheng in Gourong ascends the hall and says: "Not not. Is it not is? It is different."
To miss by a hair’s breadth is to lose by a thousand *li*. Zhaozhou’s tea. Luling’s rice. Jade chopsticks prying open the tiger’s eyes;
a golden whip striking out the phoenix’s marrow. A-he-he! Who recognizes that King Yama is a ghost? Entering the hall:
One mouthful of needle, three feet of thread, Jinzhou cloth, Yangzhou silk. Zhaozhou said, "I was making a..."
The cotton robe he wore weighed seven *jin*. He closed his door to fashion the carriage, yet when he stepped out, it fit perfectly with the ruts. He sent this verse to his fellow practitioners:
"Shamefully, I am a mountain dweller; I gladly endure hunger and cold. A triple-strand bamboo belt cinches my waist; On four walls, the frost gathers like mist. My *kāṣāya* is not a single piece;
My paper quilt is completely tattered. Laughing on my bed, I turn over; Outside the gate, the sound of a carriage passes by. [He] looked up...
Looking up at the rafters of the hall, one knows there is not a single thing in the mind. A newly cleared patch of fallow land; after the rain, the radishes have grown large.
The Dharma Successor of Zen Master Linquan Lin of Lingyin:
Zen Master Mushi Wenqian of Hongfu Monastery in Taizhou. He was born into the Fang clan of Changle, Fuzhou. From childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and quick-witted.
He was able to recite from memory any text he read upon a single glance. At the age of eleven, he received the full precepts from Zizheng at Anguo Temple in Shaowu.

He traveled through various regions until he reached Jiangshan, where the dharma seat of Tanfang was then extremely flourishing; there was also a head seat named Suo Tieshan, who was likewise a native of Min.
He was renowned as a man of long-standing virtue. The Master consulted him on the essentials of Chan and instructed him to investigate the koan of "The Dog Has No Buddha-nature.
After some time, he attained a realization and went to see the Master, saying, "Zhaozhou has been caught by me! The Master said, "What about the word 'No'? He then struck him with his fist.
The Master said, "Apart from this one punch, where would you have fallen? The Master then raised his sitting cloth and gave him a blow.
He said, "What more is there to add? He replied, "I grant you thirty blows. He then visited Mount Jinshan and retired from public life.

Later, when he was appointed to serve as the *jishi* (record-keeper), he heard of the spiritual influence of Liaohan at Lingyin and went to visit him, saying, "I have come from afar to pay my respects;
I beg the Master for a reception. Liaohan said, "Before you even entered the gate, I already knew your mind. The Master said, "It is like using the wind to fan a fire."
He did not exert much effort. Huanchu asked, "Where have you recently come from, Secretary? The Master replied, "Jinshan.

Huanchu said, "When Jinshan and Jiaoshan compete for the title of 'foremost,' which is this [your current state]? The Master said, "I would not refuse to tell the Master, but I fear you will not believe me.

Huanchu nodded his head in agreement. He subsequently appointed him as the administrative secretary (*zhongji*). Later, he issued a decree from the Xuanzheng Yuan to appoint him as the abbot of Jueci Temple in Tai, and later transferred him to Hong.
Fú. In the spring of the fifth year of the Hongwu era, Emperor Taizu Gao issued an edict summoning ten monks of high virtue to a Dharma assembly at Mount Zhong.
Master Yan was selected for this. He was summoned for an audience below the Wulou Hall and granted a banquet.

The following day, the Emperor visited Mount Zhong and proceeded to Chongxi Temple. Yan’s presentation of the teachings met with the Emperor’s approval, and His Majesty was greatly pleased. Subsequently, he was moved...
Suffering from a slight illness, he said to his disciples, "I am departing today. Someone asked, "What about the Master? The Master replied, "Do you call me deluded?
The questioner asked, "If one is deluded, this can be deluded, but that cannot be deluded. The Master spoke in a stern voice, "What 'this' and 'that' are there?
When the assembly requested him to leave behind a verse, he took up his brush and wrote in large characters: "There is a world to be..."
To renounce is the view of sentient beings; that there is no world to renounce is the view of the Tathāgata. Having toppled Mount Sumeru, space has neither front nor back.

Thereupon, he sat upright and passed away. The Imperial Preceptor Jin of the Heavenly Realm was summoned to the inner palace, where he reported in detail the reason for the Master’s passing and recited his final verse.
Emperor Taizu personally transcribed it, expressing profound admiration and praise.
[He passed away] long ago. His cremation yielded immeasurable relics. He was fifty-seven years old; his [monastic] age was forty-six.
○ Chan Master Mozhong Qiqi of Suzhou’s Huqiu [Mountain] was of the Tiantai clan. Having resigned from Wanian [Monastery], he lived in seclusion at Shiqiao Hermitage.
For many years he sat in meditation, unaware of human affairs. In his later years, the Senglu Si (Office for the Registration of Monks) nominated him...
He resided at Yunyan for barely one year. By nature, the Master was simple and aloof, and he was unskilled in worldly affairs; thus, the gentry and commoners treated him with ordinary indifference.
Yet, when he passed away, his radiance was magnificent and extraordinary, leading all to sigh in endless admiration. This was the twenty-third year of the Hongwu era.

When the Master was about to pass away, he burned his own drafts of former Dharma discourses. He recorded only the verse he had once composed for the occasion of sending Master Heng to reside at Qionglong, which says:
"Upon the summit of Mount Qionglong floats an iron ship; It directly reaches the ten-thousand-acre autumn of the Southern Lake.
In vain do we speak of the National Teacher’s inherited legacy; Now we meet a Bodhisattva who continues his illustrious path. The spiral-tufted peaks are fine for crowding the eaves; The Dharma..."
Rain-fed springs of sweet water flow around his dwelling. Do not say that the Patriarchal intent has not come from the West; before a word was even opened, the response had already been given.
Chan Master Tánshí Dèqí of Huírì Monastery in Chángshú, Sūzhōu—whose secular surname was Hú and whose family name was Wéishān—was a native of Tàicāng.
He entered the monastic order at Xingfuyuan. Initially, he met Yuanweng Xin of Tianchi in Huzhou.

Upon arriving at Zhongtianzhu in Hangzhou, Liaohan took an interest in his earnest devotion to the Way and appointed him to the position of Attendant. He was subsequently promoted to the post of Librarian.

When Liaohan moved to Lingyin, he went there to pay his respects and was eventually assigned as the Second Seat. Having studied under him for a long time, he fully mastered the Master’s final teachings.
He remained there for some time before returning to Daikura, where he constructed a hermitage called Jōe and resided. He lived together with several fellow Zen practitioners;

from morning bell to evening drum, their Zen recitations followed a constant routine. The common people of the district flocked to him with unified reverence. When scholar-officials visited his door, he would speak only of Zen and not of worldly affairs;
if they were unable to grasp his essential point, he would invariably cite the *Nirvāṇa-samavasaraṇa-parivarta* (Enlightened Nature) and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

An analogy for this opening: whenever anyone listens to his instruction, they do not fail to feel a spontaneous surge of faith. In his later years, the fourfold assembly exhorted him to open the Dharma-sun of wisdom.
Although he did not encounter the opportune time [for widespread propagation], he was able to take up the path of the Dharma as his own responsibility.

Regarding the pure regulations of the monastic community and the formal procedures for ascending the hall: "The Great Way has always emerged from the ordinary; why use the calculating mind to measure it? When thirsty, drink."

When thirsty, one drinks; when hungry, one eats. In cold weather, one faces the fire; in heat, one seeks the cool. Within the halls of Huiri Temple, the entire assembly ascends the dais at dawn to chant the sutras.
When the gruel is finished, the board is struck and they sit in meditation. After the meal, they pace back and forth along the corridors. Tell me, is this ordinary, or is it not ordinary?
If it were a golden-haired lion, it would see the error from three thousand miles away. [End of Excerpt]
The Hall Master cited Zen Master Zhenjing, who said: "In the second month of mid-spring, the weather gradually warms;

as the season arrives, the myriad things vie for their loveliness. Do not wait for the peach blossoms to awaken to the Way; once you step outside, the fragrant grasses will already be lush. The Master said: "Speaking in such a manner still carries a trace of lingering attachment.
At Huiri’s place, it is not so. In the second month of mid-spring, the weather gradually warms; as the days grow long, it is precisely the time to take a nap. Long... [text ends]
Even as he slept one night upon his bed, the full moon rose from the mountain peak. After a long while, he said: "Since the passing of Ziqi, those who truly understand have been few;
often my playing of the seven-stringed zither has been in vain. Eventually, at the Yuanjue Hermitage established by the lay patron Gu Renda of Jiading, the Master was about to pass away.
He said to the abbot, Shen Shiyin: "I have a cassock that no one is worthy to receive."
Ling said, "Alas, I have incurred the offense of my teacher's school. Having finished speaking, tears fell from his eyes. After a long while, he passed away peacefully.
During the cremation, an extraordinary fragrance permeated the air; everyone marveled at it.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Guding Ming of Mount Jing:
Chan Master Xiangyuan Renshu of Mount Jing, Hangzhou. He was born into the Chen family of Linhai, Tiantai.

At the age of twenty, having heard of the reputation of Jizhao at Mount Jing, he went to rely upon him and received the tonsure. When Tanfang succeeded to the abbacy, he appointed [Renshu] to oversee the inner quarters.
Record: Upon returning east to Yǐn, he arrived at Yùwáng Monastery, where Xuěchuāng appointed him to the post of Shūjì (Secretary).
Mìomíng was the abbot of Zhōngtiānzhú in Hángzhōu; the Master went to visit him. Mìomíng asked, "Did you bring the śarīra from Yùwáng with you, Secretary?
The Master spread his two hands and said, "What is this? Mìomíng said, "A clumsy *tathatā*. The Master said, "You have missed it right before your face. Mìomíng then took up his bamboo staff.
He struck him, saying, "Not so! Not so! The Master broke into a sweat like rain and said, "This time I have seen through this old fellow.

Hui-ming later moved to Mount Jingshan. The Master went there again to study under him, and was appointed to the second seat. By imperial decree, he was authorized to propagate the Dharma at Mount Tianmu.
His elder brother, Da-que, looked upon Miao-ming and received the lineage from him. The first year of the Hongwu era...

In his later years, by imperial decree of the Shanshi Yuan, he resided at Jiahe. In the fifth year of Tianning, an edict was issued for eminent monks throughout the empire to assemble for a Dharma assembly on Mount Zhong;
the Master was included among them. He entered the audience at the Fengtian Hall, where he was granted a seat and provided with a meal.
Subsequently, he took up residence at Jingshan. Ascending the hall, he said: "The mind is not the Buddha; wisdom is not the Way. Those who understand it thus will find their entire lives fulfilled."
For those who do not understand it in this way, there will be joy throughout their lives. Bodhisattvas of the highest vehicle have faith without doubt;
those of middle and lower capacity will surely laugh upon hearing it. (He strikes the meditation staff. Do not laugh. A wooden horse neighs in the night wind; at dawn, the morning light is lost.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: Qianfeng addressed the assembly, saying, "If you raise one, you must not raise two; to let pass one move is to fall into the second.
Yunmen stepped out from the assembly and said, "Yesterday someone came from Tiantai and went on to Jingshan."
Qingfeng looked at his attendant and said, "Tomorrow there shall be no communal labor. The Master [Yunmen] took this up and said:

"Qingfeng was like Xiang Yu, holding an army of four hundred thousand, meeting Han Gaozu at Hongmen. Had it not been for Yunmen sniffing the earth to recognize the opportunity, how could one have seen the former followers turn their spears and cast off their armor?
Qingfeng looked at his attendant and said, 'Tomorrow there shall be no communal labor. His failure here is many."
[The Master] ascends the hall. There is one phrase that reaches your very flesh and picks at your sores; there is not a single phrase that allows you to flee from its shadow at midday.
When it is neither thus nor otherwise, what then? After a long silence, he said: "Lying across the body to face the universe—who is the one who emerges?"
Because County Magistrate Liang Gongfuan urged Master [Feng]fu to construct a Buddha hall, the timber had already been prepared but the work remained unfinished.
Suddenly, he said to his disciples: "When I first came to reside on this mountain, I dreamed that Jizhao gave me nine pairs of chopsticks.

Now nine years have passed; my karmic conditions have come to an end. He wrote a verse and passed away on the fourth day of the sixth month in the Gengshen year of the Hongwu era. His body was cremated.

A vertebral bone, over an inch long, formed the likeness of a Buddha, with eyes and brows clearly defined. Those who beheld it were struck with wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Relics like pearls adhered to his remaining bones; they were enshrined in a stupa named Guiyun (Clouds Returning) at the foot of Mount Lingxiao.
While he resided at Mount Jing, Song Gong Lian, the Hanlin Academician, presented him with ten verses, the final one of which read: "The lamp of tranquil illumination is transmitted."

Reaching the Subtle Brilliance (Miaoming). Now the Seal of Authenticity belongs to the Senior Brother. He shall take the Eastern Sea as oil to kindle the flame and continue the lineage of fragrance until reaching the City of Transformation (Huacheng).
Chan Master Tianyuan Qingjun of Linggu Monastery in Yingtian Prefecture, whose courtesy name was Sui’an, was born into the Li family of Huangyan.
His father was Yi and his mother was Ying. In his youth, he studied at the local village school; he was exceptionally brilliant and insightful. Yet, he was not content to remain in secular life.
At the age of thirteen, he went to rely upon Miaoming at Mount Baota in Mingzhou. After more than a year, he shaved his head and received full ordination.

When Miaoming moved to Zhongzhu, he invited the Master to reside in the office of attendants. Upon Miaoming’s promotion to Mount Shuangjing, the Master was again appointed as the Secretary (Jishi). The Master redoubled his efforts, sitting in meditation to investigate the ultimate truth.
While practicing meditation, he did not forget the matter of "pointing upward. One day, while reading the *Recorded Sayings of Dahui*, he reached the passage:

"To call it a 'bamboo stick' is to hit [the mark]; not to call it a 'bamboo stick' is to turn one's back. Suddenly, he attained awakening and immediately informed Ming. Ming asked, "How is my hand like the Buddha’s hand?
The Master replied, "Shut that stinking mouth! Ming laughed heartily. The Master continued his reading the following day.
He profoundly investigated the meanings and purports of such scriptures as the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Vimalakīrti*.

Subsequently, he returned to Siming and remained for five years at the Zu-’an (Ancestral Hermitage) of Master Fozhao at Yuyang Monastery. Finding the scenery of the East Lake and its green mountains exceptionally serene and sublime, he went there to hang his staff and reside.

In the first year of the Hongwu era, he first responded to the request of the Prefectural Governor and took up residence at Wanshou Monastery; after only three years, he again sought out [a new location].
The second was the abbot of Linghe Hermitage, who lived in a thatched hut on his native mountain and named it Suian (Hermitage of Following).
In the fourth year [of the Hongwu era], Emperor Taizu Gao Huangdi issued an edict to hold a Great Universal Deliverance Assembly at Mount Zhongshan, summoning ten *śramaṇas* of realized virtue;

the Master was one of them. Upon the completion of the ceremony, he returned to the mountain, having received most generous imperial gifts. In the fifteenth year, the Office of Buddhist Records (*Senglù*) was first established.
The Director summoned the Master, Jueyi, who had been appointed by imperial decree at the age of nineteen to preach the Dharma at the Great Vegetarian Assembly at Linggu Monastery.
Auspicious light manifested, illuminating the groves and valleys; ten thousand eyes beheld it and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
At that time, the incumbent abbot of Linggu, Xiwu, had previously resigned due to illness. Emperor Taizu commanded the Master to fill the vacancy and personally composed ten poems for him.
In the second chapter, [the Emperor] honored his conduct. He further issued an edict to the Office of Monastic Records, appointing the officials Hongdao Yijian and Shou to serve him.
Renzong, Lelie, Hanlin Academician Liu Sanwu, and Dong Lun all composed verses in harmony to present as gifts to the Master. Soon after, these were submitted in response;
when Taizu reviewed them, he praised them as excellent. At that time, a great snow was falling, yet Taizu sat at his desk, and the Master again came through the snow to visit him.
The Emperor composed a poem in the morning to praise him, containing such lines as "The Buddha-sun increases its brilliance" and "The myriad phenomena unfold;

his entire body enters again into dreams. From then on, the Emperor’s reception of him became increasingly generous. He frequently received imperial edicts to compose verses in response. One day, he respectfully presented a poem titled "In Reverent Harmony:
Thinking of My Parents and Yearning for My Homeland. The Emperor praised it with deep admiration and bestowed upon him two thousand five hundred *bojyo* (treasure notes).
The Master did not regard [the funds] as his own; he submitted them to the throne for the expenses of the Wan-gong Pool (Ten-thousand-Worker Pond).

Furthermore, the various Princes treated him with great courtesy, bestowing upon him handwritten poems, gāthās, and rare treasures. His reputation for the Way spread far and wide, and scholars from all quarters gathered like clouds and water;
the Master exhorted and encouraged them according to their individual capacities, bringing many to spiritual accomplishment. On the Buddha’s Birthday...
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case: When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth;
he walked seven steps and looked around in the four directions, saying, "In heaven above and on earth below, I alone am honored.

Yunmen said, "If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him dead with a single blow of my staff and fed him to a dog, just to ensure peace throughout the world. The Master offered this verse: Pointing to heaven...

Pointing to the ground, he declared it the foremost; from this, ten thousand calamities and a thousand misfortunes emerge. Yunmen’s staff was too short—what can be done? The disaster reaches his descendants with no end in sight.
On the occasion of the opening of the retreat and the formal expression of gratitude to the Head Seat, the Master ascended the hall and said:
"I cite Master Yunmen, who once remarked: 'Countless dead people lie upon level ground; those who pass through the thicket of brambles are true adepts. At that time, there was a monk..."
Xuchun said, "If that is so, then the first seat in the hall has some merit. The Master said, "What do you call a thornbush forest?
And why would one need to pass through it? Little do you realize that the thornbush forest is itself the seat of Bodhi.
From time immemorial, one has never been separated from it for even a moment. Walking, one is within it; standing, one is within it; sitting, one is within it."
He is within; he lies down within; he rolls up, spreads out, appears, and disappears, moving vertically and horizontally through transformations with complete mastery.
Thus it is said: "Responding to conditions and meeting with stimuli, there is nowhere he does not pervade, yet he eternally dwells upon this seat of Bodhi.
Nevertheless, when the World-Honored One entered the house of Indraśaila, was that the same as this moment or different? Ultimately, water must flow toward the sea.
He departed. Upon reaching Touyun, he sought out the mountain to return. He presented a verse to Attendant Quan, which said: "A broken smile reveals his full capacity;
The twenty-fold black staff has not yet released him. When meeting people on the road ahead, do not speak of this in error; To gain an advantage is to suffer a disadvantage.
On the thirtieth day of the fifth month in the Ren-shen year of the Hongwu era, he entered nirvana. Five days prior to that, he had discarded his robes and ornaments.

He bid farewell to his friends, exhorted his disciples, and took leave of his colleagues; he wrote a verse to bring about their transformation. He was sixty-five years old in the cyclical year of Ch'un-ch'iu (Spring and Autumn) and fifty-one in the year of Hsia (Summer).
His disciples performed the cremation and collected his remains to be interred to the left of the Miaoming Pagoda at Shuangjing.
Chan Master Wanjin of Baitan at Tianjie Monastery in Yingtian Prefecture was the son of Yao of Wujun; his mother was Su.
When the Master was born, a wondrous fragrance filled the courtyard. Upon reaching the age of five or six, he had a square forehead, a round face, and a complexion as fair and radiant as jade.

The Governor of Zhuo cherished him. He would often carry him upon his carriage, returning home to play with him as if he were a precious jewel among his wife and concubines, wishing to adopt him as his own son;
however, his parents were reluctant and would not grant him. By the age of seven, he was exceptionally brilliant and perceptive; having looked at a book only once, he could immediately memorize it.
One day, he requested of his mother, "I am troubled by the impermanence of worldly phenomena; I wish to seek the Dharma that transcends the world. His mother said:
"Leaving the household life is extremely difficult; since you were young, you have not been able to endure it. [The Master] replied, "My heart finds joy in it myself;

I imagine there is no suffering. Thereafter, he requested permission repeatedly. His parents, knowing his resolve could not be overturned, allowed him to become a disciple of Master Daoyuan Yan at Baoji Temple in Wuxian.
Upon his tonsure and reception of the full precepts, Daoyuan became the head of Dezang Monastery in Jiahe, and the Master served as his administrative director (*gang*).
Wuwei soon left and went to visit Miaoming at Shuangjing. Upon seeing him, Miaoming regarded him as a vessel for the Dharma and kept him in his service.
One day, Miaoming said, "When Deshan saw Longtan, why was it only when [Longtan] blew out the paper candle that he suddenly attained awakening?
Wuwei replied, "Do not try to deceive me. On another day, [Miaoming] raised the case of the Tathāgata having a secret teaching. Ca...
He did not conceal his shortcomings. Before the sound of [the master’s] voice had even faded, the teacher immediately raised his own voice, saying, "Master, spare your eyebrows!

One day, hearing a boulder fall to the ground, his mind became vast and open, and he suddenly forgot all intellectual understanding. Mingyi appointed him as the Record-keeper (*jishi*). From the Rear Hall, he was subsequently promoted to the Front Hall.
From then on, his reputation grew exceedingly great. In the year Yiwu of the Zhizheng era (1355), he entered the world at Ruiwang Monastery in Suzhou.

He was transferred to Tianning Monastery in Jiahe. Upon hearing of the Master’s Way, the Imperial Preceptor, the Great Treasure Dharma King (Dabao Fawang), conferred upon him the title Chan Master Yuantong Pujie.
Having lost his father in childhood, the Master had only his mother remaining; he therefore built the Guyun Hermitage to the east of the city to provide for her care.
In the first year of the Hongwu era, the Shanshiyuan (Institute for the Welfare of the World) was established to oversee the Buddhist teachings. The Master was appointed as its director.
He was invited with ceremonial gifts to serve as abbot at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou, but he did not accept. Subsequently, by imperial decree, he was summoned to preside over Tianjie Monastery.
Responding to the summons, he arrived at the capital and had an audience with Emperor Taizu Gao Huangdi in the outer court.
He was granted generous rewards and immediately ordered the inner palace to escort him into the monastery, where he was served a meal from the celestial kitchen.

Thereafter, his frequent audiences with the Emperor were mostly in accord with the Sovereign’s wishes. He ascended the hall and said: "Heaven and earth share the same root as I; the myriad things and I are one body.
The lantern is simply the lantern; the pillar is simply the pillar. When did they ever become one body? Nanquan said, "People of this age..."
Seeing this single flower is like being in a dream. Furthermore, how is it so? Do not mistake Zhi Dun’s crane for Wang Xizhi’s goose.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Huangbo addressing the assembly, saying: "All of you here are nothing but fellows who eat dregs of wine.
Traveling on pilgrimage like this, how could you have reached this day? Do you know that within the Great Tang Empire there are no Chan masters?"
At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "As for those in various quarters who guide their disciples and lead the assembly, how do they proceed? Baizhang said, "It is not that they lack Chan;
it is simply that they lack a teacher. The Master [Dongshan] said, "The paper from Tanzhou has been received; one document is hereby acknowledged.

In the spring of the fifth year, an imperial decree summoned ten eminent monks of the three schools along with two thousand of their followers to establish the *Guangjian Fa Jin* (Great Universal Dedication Dharma Assembly) at Mount Zhong.

He appointed the Master to oversee the affairs of the *zhāi* (fasting retreat). The Master was able to spiritually fulfill the Imperial will; all its rites, regulations, and protocols were worthy of being transmitted for posterity.
Later, as his mother’s age advanced, he recommended Master Le of Mount Jing to serve as his successor, returning himself to Xihuo to attend to his mother.
That winter, an imperial decree was issued to rebuild the assembly at Zhongshan as before. The Imperial carriage visited the site, and an edict was proclaimed.
The Master preached the Dharma; among the dukes, marquises, and common officials, there were none who did not submit with joy.

The Emperor, recognizing that the Master’s talent and wisdom were preeminent, urged him to abandon the monastic life and assist in the administration of government. The Master firmly declined and thus desisted. One day, he said to his disciples:

"I have karmic causes from former lives that must surely be requited. He abstained from food and drink for seven days and passed away in accordance with the natural course of things, on the twelfth month of the sixth year.
On the twenty-fourth day, the shrine was opened after sixty days had passed. Upon viewing him, his countenance appeared as if alive;

his fingernails and hair had grown long. During the cremation, his prayer beads, cranial bone, teeth, and jaw remained unburnt. He was forty-seven years of age and thirty-six years of *dharma-lu* (seniority).
His disciples enshrined his sacred remains and the various indestructible relics at Tianning Temple.
Chan Master Wanshou Benkong Tanxiang of Suzhou, upon ascending the hall to express his gratitude for the Dharma robes bestowed by a donor, said:
"To see is easy; to recognize is difficult. The flower’s root is originally brilliant; the tiger’s body is inherently striped. To recognize is not difficult; to see is not easy.
Dry wood accompanies the person; wherever the stage is set, one performs the play. At Mount Zhong, the Great Being Daolin picked up the scissors at the end of his staff.

The void was cut into pieces, scattered and fragmented. Then, the Buddha-mother Māyā, unable to restrain her laughter, struck it perfectly upon the point of the golden needle and within the path of the jade thread, restoring it to a single whole. The blue remains blue;
the white remains white; the red remains red; the green remains green—all are spontaneous. They contend for corners and seize positions, crowding together.

The flowers cluster like brocade, so that the Buddhas of the three periods—past, present, and future—each sit upon one side in the *Saṃpuṣpita* World, praising in unison: "How marvelous! How marvelous! How rare! How rare!
Because they see that people are shameless and do not gather them, they have run away into the staff of this mountain monk. Raising up his staff, he says: "If you call this a..."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time are this very staff; if you call it a staff, it is also the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time pass through the staff, and the staff passes through the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
At such a moment, if there is one—whether monastic or lay—who possesses the eye of discernment and can emerge [from this state], I grant that your lifelong study of the Way is complete.
If this is not yet the case, let this staff break it open for you. (He strikes the ground with his staff and says: "The wondrous flowers of Bodhi are everywhere adorned;
wherever one dwells, there is constant peace and joy. (Having finished his expression of thanks, he speaks another verse: "Rolling out from amidst a thicket of brocade and embroidery."
Wide open atop the peak of Mount Sumeru—observe where his wondrous functioning and spiritual powers lie. The eagle-eye and dragon-vision are subtle beyond conjecture.
Ascending the hall, the Master raised the case: Once a monk asked Yunmen, “What is the student’s own self? Yunmen said, “Wandering through mountains and enjoying the waters.
