Leaping halfway down the cliff, he felt no suffering whatsoever. He said to his fellow practitioners, "I am going to Jiangxi to see Xueyan.
His companions said, "You have betrayed the old master’s bitter blows! They pulled him back with all their might. The Master then made a vow:
"If I do not realize the truth within seven days, I shall certainly depart. Thereupon, he resolutely fortified himself against the wall, forgetting both sleep and food. At night, he...
He climbed a tree and stood in the dew until dawn. Before his appointed time had come, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
He rushed to Siguan (Deadman’s Gate) and cried out: "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow; once the sun shines upon them, not a trace remains.

From this point on, he no longer harbored doubts regarding the Buddhas and patriarchs, nor did he distinguish between north, south, east, or west. The following day, on the mountain peak, he ascended the hall and said: "I have spread a vast net that covers the heavens."
"Beating the phoenix and netting the dragon, he never once encountered a single shrimp or crab. Today, a tiny gnat has flown in.
Thirty years from now, he will stand atop a solitary peak and cry out at the top of his voice. But tell me, what does he cry out? Raising his whisk, he said:
"The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow. Then, together with his mother, he entered Mount Shangbo in Wukang to establish a hermitage.
He lived in a thatched hut. After five years, he returned to the mountain, where Master Feng shaved his head and gave him the name Liaoyi.

In the year Yiwu of the Yuanzhen era, Master Feng passed away, and the Teacher likewise withdrew into obscurity; nevertheless, wherever he went, the fourfold assembly honored him, and he never once accepted an invitation to preside over a monastery.

All the monks referred to him as "Elder Liaoyi. In the third year of the Taiding era, yielding to the persistent requests of the assembly, he returned to the ancestral temple and remained there for one year.
This was the Lion Orthodox Lineage Chan Monastery. In his quarters, the Master would deliver a turning word, saying:
"Set aside speech and silence, movement and stillness, and bring forth a single phrase! He also said: "When this one breath does not return, where will you establish yourself and sustain your life?
On the eve of the New Year in the first year of the Yuantong era, he suddenly said to his disciples: "There is one matter that is exceedingly great; do you all understand it thoroughly?"
[Muzhou] said, "Hmm. After a long silence, he remarked, "Tomorrow is New Year's Day. On the night of the sixth day of the first month, he said, "I, the old monk, am going to Tiantai tomorrow.
A practitioner asked, "I will follow the Master. The Master replied, "Even if you were to gallop like a horse, you could not catch up.
The next morning, he passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture. He was seventy-two years old; he had been a monk for forty-nine years.
His whole body was buried at Yunshen Hermitage behind Lion Rock.
○ Chan Master Punna Zuoyong of Zhong Tianzhu in Hangzhou was a native of Dinghai, Mingzhou.
He inscribed the following on the painting "Li Yuan Visiting Yuanze": "When we met before Mount Tianzhu, Master Yuan recognized Dharma Brother Ze. Indeed..."

Yet his character was truly extraordinary; even twelve years ago, he already seemed like this master. The Master once composed verses on the theme of mountain dwelling in response to those of Chan Master Yongming Shou;
their spirit and intent were comparable, and in terms of poetic craftsmanship, there were instances where the Master’s work surpassed the original.
At the time of his death, he composed a verse and passed away while seated. After the cremation, a great many *śarīra* relics remained.
In the Fulin Hall on Mount Baiyun at Chuzhou was the "Pseudo-Chan Master" (Jia Chan-shi), a native of Kuocang in Quzhou.

His surname was Ye, and he was born during the Xianchun era of the Song dynasty. Having lost both parents at an early age, he entered the monastic life at Mount Chenfeng in the prefecture when he was seventeen years old.
He honored withered trees as his teachers. Two years later, he shaved his head and received full ordination. He first visited Fengge at Mount Tianmu.

Fengge asked, "What is your name? The Master replied, "It is provisional. Fengge asked, "Is your nature provisional? The Master replied, "Since even my nature is not real, how could it be provisional?
Fengge ordered him to attend the hall. The Master burned off a finger, vowing that he would not rest until he had clarified this matter.
He did not descend from this mountain. Later, while in his room, he heard the story of Zhaozhou’s “dog has no Buddha-nature” and attained realization. He presented a verse, saying:
“Zhaozhou’s one ‘no’— When spring warms, the flowers bloom all at once. Even if you understand it thus, It is but adding more grit to your eyes.”
Feng said, "Not yet. The Master said, "This time I no longer doubt the tongues of all the old monks under heaven. Feng then gave a shout. The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Feng deeply approved of him. He served him diligently for ten years. After he took up residence, his Dharma influence spread widely, and many were those who received his guidance and realization.
In his later years, he retired to a single room, remaining in profound silence and finding joy within himself. One day, he called his younger brother.
His disciple Zhiguang said to him, "I am about to depart. Having written a verse, he cast aside his brush and passed away in stillness.
He was sixty-nine years old; it was the fifth month. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa at the foot of the Fulin Monastery.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Xugu Ling of Mount Jingshan:
Chan Master Zhuyuan Zhengyuan of Mount Jing, Hangzhou. His clan was the Ouyang family of Luling.
He followed his maternal uncle, Master Qing of Meixi, at Gan Zhu Temple in his native village. Qing’s disciple, Siji, shaved his head for him. One.

A man skilled in physiognomy passed by him and said, "Master, you are a man of five deficiencies; yet in the future, you will surely preside over a great Dharma center and become a teacher for humans and devas.
At the beginning of the Yan-you era, he ascended Mount Jing-shan. There, he encountered Fo-jian during a session on entering the room. Fo-jian raised the case of Deshan seeing Longtan:
"Why was it that at the moment [Longtan] blew out the paper candle, Deshan attained awakening? The Master replied, "A scorched brick strikes through the ice to the very bottom. Fo-jian [approved].
[The Master] asked, "After being struck, what then? The teacher said, "The moon in the empty expanse of the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool;

only after repeatedly scooping and searching will one come to know it. Yuanjue [Jian] asked, "What do you know? As the teacher was about to respond, Jian struck him. The teacher suddenly attained awakening and was subsequently appointed to attend to him at his side.
When Jian passed away, Yuansou succeeded him on the seat and ordered the teacher to serve as the *shuji* (record-keeper). The fourth year of the Taiding era...

In his youth, he entered the world at Guanyin Monastery in Shanghai. He later moved to Xingsheng Monastery in Jiahe, where the Imperial Preceptor issued an edict bestowing upon him the title "Buddha-Wisdom, Compassionate Illumination, and Universal Response.
In the second year of the Zhizheng era, he presided over a monastic center on Mount Hu. In the fourteenth year, he moved to Lingyin Monastery.
After he had resided there for three years, Mount Jing was destroyed by war. Prime Minister Da Shi raised an army to restore it as its abbot.

During the following year, while clearing away rubble and overseeing the construction of the Buddha Hall and the Dragon King Hall, his illness flared up before the work was complete, and he was on the verge of passing away. He then wrote a verse of farewell to bid the assembly goodbye.
He again sent a letter to the Chancellor and passed away after completing it. His age was seventy-one; he had been a monk for fifty-five years.
○ Chan Master Liaotang Yuanzhao of Yangshan in Yanzhou was of the Xu clan of Nanchang.
He took ordination under Master Hai, a ninth-generation descendant of Lord Yue of Qu’an at Dayun Temple. There were no internal or external classics that he did not master. Upon reaching—

In the *gen* year of the *kōshin* cycle, he received ordination through the examination of the scriptures. He first visited Master Nul of Chiryeong; although Chiryeong repeatedly prodded him to awaken, he had not yet attained realization.
He then went to see Master Mugam at Angsan Mountain. Mugam raised the koan: "A monk asked Zhaozhou, 'Does a dog have Buddha-nature?
Zhaozhou said, 'No. What was the intent of the ancient? The Master replied, "I have recently departed from..."
Cuiyan Jian asked, "Ultimately, what was the intention of the ancients? The Master replied, "Last night I stayed at the reception hall before the mountain.
Jian was delighted and left him with the keys to the storehouse. Not long after, he departed to travel through the Two Zhe regions.

When Dongyan of Tiantong invited him to share the seat and preach the Dharma, and when Fojian moved to Mount Jing, the Master went there again for further study and was once more appointed to share the seat. He subsequently took up residence at Jingzhong.

He returned to Yangshan, where his Dharma teachings flourished greatly. On the day he manifested parinirvāṇa, he exhorted his disciples to strive diligently in cultivation; immediately thereafter, he passed away with a serene countenance.

His remains were enshrined in a coffin for seven days, during which his facial features remained as they had been in life. When cremated, the smoke formed five colors, and suddenly the flames shone like white lotus flowers.
Once the fire was extinguished, the śarīra relics were as numerous as beans, and even his cranial bone and teeth remained undecayed.
A pagoda was erected at Meizhou to enshrine [the manuscript].
○ Chan Master Jueyin Bencheng of Xingsheng Monastery in Jiahe was a native of Chongde; his style name was Daoyuan.
The master once composed the *Xingxue zhiyao* (Essentials of the Study of Nature) in ten fascicles. Wanling Zhu Shuzhi, Gu Bian, and Duan Tianyou (style name Jifu) all wrote prefaces for it.
[This work] was placed before [the reader]. The preface by Duan states: "This compilation elucidates the nature and mind with the utmost detail and precision. It further says:
"For those of our Confucian school who wish to pursue a study that reaches the ultimate root and source, this book must not be left unread.

Within it, the "Chapter on True Nature" states: "Because the nature and mind are fundamentally one, they are called *tathatā*. *Tathatā* is the single, true source of the mind. (The term "one-true" refers to...)

Since the nature (*prakṛti*) and the mind (*citta*) are of one source, and the mind-nature is entirely suchness (*tathatā*), which is unchanging, it is called the "nature of true suchness" (*tathatā-prakṛti*). It is also called the "mind of true suchness" (*tathatā-citta*).
Nature has no form; the mind has substance. The mind takes nature as its essence (*ātman*); nature takes the mind as its sovereign. Therefore, as for their essence, they are both the same essence.

Therefore, it is said that the essence of nature (*xingti*) is also called the essence of mind (*xinti*). In their functioning, both function together: the mind is the "capable user" (*nengyong*) and nature is the "object used" (*suoyong*).

That which is capable of using is wisdom (*zhi*); that which is used is principle (*li*)—this is what is meant by the perfect interfusion of wisdom and principle (*zhili yuanrong*). If that which is capable of using were not the object used, true wisdom would have no means to manifest;
if the object used were not that which is capable of using, the substantial reality would have no means to be revealed. Thus, the mind does not stand without nature.
The nature is without mind and does not function; therefore it is said that "principle and wisdom penetrate each other, and essence and function share a single source.

(To speak of *tathatā* [Suchness], mind and nature cannot be separated from one another. "True" means truly real; "as-it-is" means as-it-always-has-been. Because it is real, it is unchanging and non-different, without even a hair’s breadth of private delusion. Because it is constant, it is spontaneous, without the slightest trace of artificial effort.

It is also called the *Tathatā-dharmadhātu* (the Dharma-realm of Suchness). (This refers to essence and function sharing a single source. As for the *dharmadhātu*, it is the essence of the One True [Reality] and the foundation of the myriad transformations. True...
It is like the One of quiescent essence; it is the myriad of True Suchness transforming according to conditions. The One is the myriad, yet there is nothing that does not flow from this Dharma-realm;
the myriad is the One, yet there is nothing that does not return to this Dharma-realm. Principle and phenomena interpenetrate; all are the wondrous function of the single mind.

(The identity of principle and phenomena means that every thing is the one Dharma-realm, and the Dharma-realm is the nature. Wondrous function is the function of the mind; the function of the mind is emotion, which is also called the totality of the mind.)

As for the essence of mind and nature: in their quiescence they are one, but in their functioning they differ. The reason why they are sometimes identical and sometimes distinct is that the mind undergoes arising and ceasing;
thus it is said that when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise, and when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.

The mind possesses both the true and the delusive, whereas the substance of nature is solely one (the mind has the designations of "true mind" and "deluded mind," while nature has no such category as "private" or "delusive").
The deluded mind is that which moves in opposition to its true nature; therefore, it is called the mind of ignorance (*avidyā*).

This ignorant, deluded mind arises and ceases in an instant, like clouds suddenly appearing in the sky or dust suddenly settling on a mirror. Yet, while these clouds darken and the dust obscures, they merely veil the exterior.
The substance of the "Heavenly Mirror" is fundamentally without increase or decrease (the gathering and dispersing of clouds and dust represent the arising and ceasing of the deluded mind;

the Heavenly Mirror is ever as it is, for the true nature is immovable). This is because the mind can turn according to objects, whereas the nature undergoes no change. The mind may be good or evil, but the nature is pure and without admixture.

(The master of the body and all affairs is the mind. The substance of the nature is eternally still. When the mind follows the nature, it proceeds according to principle and is thus good; when the mind follows emotion, it attaches itself to the breath and is thus not good. The mind is the initiator.)

Functioning thus, while emotional states (*citta*) may be good or evil, the essential nature (*dharmatā*) is eternally quiescent. It is also termed *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). "Dharma" takes the meaning of providing a standard and sustaining reality;
only that which is perfectly correct and impartial is fit to serve as a model. If there is even the slightest partiality, it is no longer the Dharma.

Therefore, this essence of true nature has, from beginningless time, been a profound and serene *tathatā* (suchness), pure without the slightest obscuration. Thus it is said: "In the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust can be received."
This is what is called the true essence of Great Enlightenment and the fundamental source of all living beings.

*Ode on Modifying the Path*, composed by Chan Master Konghai Liangnian of Zhongzhu, Hangzhou, upon the completion of the two side-gate plaques for the Thousand Buddhas Hall and the painting of the Fifty-three Pilgrims on the wall at Jingci Temple: "The Thousand Buddhas have been bound high upon the hall; the hundred cities..."
Mist and water are swallowed by a single hair. Even if there were another path that pierces the heavens, it would still fall within the second gate of the Southern Mountain.
On the Mid-Autumn Festival, Chan Master Benzhi of Lianfeng Qianfu Temple in Ningzhou ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha at Vulture Peak pointed to the moon;
Caoxi spoke of the moon; Hanshan compared himself to the moon; and Mazu enjoyed the moon. This whole crew is nothing but playing with shadows."
Within the shadows and light, you have not yet seen the true moon. But what, then, is the true moon? [He draws a circle with his whisk and asks:
"Do you understand? There is nothing to compare it to; how can I tell you? Ascending the hall, he said:

"If one discusses this matter, it is like looking at a horse riding from behind a wall; by the time you blink your eyes, you are already thousands of miles away. [This refers to] Gaoting seeing Deshan.
Waving his hand across the river, he then strides off crosswise; already eight *ke* late, yet you still wait for him to raise his brows and blink his eyes.
Raising a whisk or striking with a mallet—what use can these serve? A person of keen intelligence would simply shake out their sleeves and depart from this very spot.

Xifeng has a staff, but it has not even reached the point of being eaten by you. Entering the hall: At the hour of *Chou*, when the cock crows, one looks with sorrow upon rising and finds oneself still leaking flaws. The skirt...
Not even a vest is there; the form of the *kāṣāya* is but a mere semblance. The trousers have no crotch; the leggings have no opening.
On his head, three or five pecks of green ash. He hoped to practice cultivation to benefit others, yet who would have known he would turn out to be such a wretched fellow?
Old Zhaozhou is much like a family of long-established lineage; his wealth and status are indeed intoxicating, yet it is simply that he does not conform to the wind.
The flow has become excessive. Today, Xifeng does not "heat" his eyelids; he simply wishes for future descendants to know it themselves.
[This concludes the record of] Chan Master Anding of Daochang as a Dharma heir.
Master Shiwu Qingqi of Fuyuan in Jiaxing was born into the Wen family of Wenshu, Suzhou. He received the tonsure under Yongwei of Chongfu Temple.
One day, a monk passed by his door and said, "I am about to ascend Mount Tianmu to see Master Gaofeng."
The Master joyfully set out with him to see Feng. Feng gave him the koan "The myriad dharmas return to one" to investigate.

For three years he made no progress, so he took his leave to travel and study under various masters. Feng said, "In Wenzhou there is the Blind Donkey; in Huai, there is Ji’an. You should visit them; you must not delay.
The Master then went to see Ji’an at West Peak in Dayang. Ji’an asked, “Where have you come from? The Master—
The Master replied, "Heaven’s Eye. Tianmu asked, "What instruction does Heaven’s Eye provide? The Master said, "All dharmas return to the One. Tianmu said, "This is a dead word.
What kind of pestilence has afflicted you that it makes you speak like this? The Master earnestly requested further enlightenment.
Tianmu said, "Where there is a Buddha, do not stay; where there is no Buddha, pass quickly by. What is the meaning of this? The Master answered several times.

"It does not accord. Yuanwu said, "This too is a dead word. The Master was unaware that sweat was pouring down his back. Later, while entering the room for instruction, Yuanwu took up the previous conversation to interrogate him.
The Master replied, "When one mounts a horse, one sees the road. Yuanwu rebuked him, saying, "After six years here, you still hold such a view?
The Master, filled with indignation, abandoned his studies and departed. On the road, he suddenly looked up and saw a pavilion; at that moment, he experienced a sudden, expansive awakening.
Xing returned and said to Huan’An, “‘Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell’—this is a dead word.
‘Where there is no Buddha, run swiftly past’—this too is a dead word. Today I have realized the living word. Huan’An asked, “How so?
The Master replied, “On the Qingming festival, the rain has just cleared; the yellow oriole speaks clearly upon the branch. Huan’An nodded in approval.

Before long, the hermitage was moved to Daochang, where he was appointed to serve as the Librarian (Cangdian). The Abbot said to the assembly, "This man is a golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net.
Subsequently, he met Yue Tang Yin at Lingyin Monastery, who invited him to occupy the second seat.
Thereupon, he established a hermitage on Mount Xiawu at Tianhu; he personally performed all manual labor, including gathering firewood and grass. There remained a legacy from an ancient master...

Feng was fond of composing poetry about mountain dwellings during his leisure from meditation; these were widely circulated throughout the monastic communities. When the Guangjiao Prefecture invited him to reside at Fuyuan on Danghu, the Master resolutely declined.
Someone remarked, "To propagate the Dharma is of primary importance; why do you seek only your own perfection? Upon this, the Master suddenly rose up to accept the invitation.

After seven years had passed, his Dharma seat flourished greatly, and his reputation reached the imperial court. The Emperor bestowed incense and ceremonial cloth to honor his excellence, and the Empress further granted him a robe of gold-threaded brocade.
When he ascended the hall, he said: "Before the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the nights are short and sleep is insufficient;
after the fifteenth day of the fourth month, the days are long and hunger is more than enough. It is precisely on the fifteenth day of the fourth month—this is the source of blessings."

The Chan practitioners within this temple have their meals sufficiently provided and their sleep as well; they sport in the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment and dwell in the samādhi of the Wisdom of Equality.
I dare ask you all: by what cause do they reach such a state? When the fragrant breeze enters the door, it naturally brings coolness;
when the lake water reaches the gate, it has no intentional purpose. He passed away after writing a verse at the moment of death. His disciples collected his remains for cremation.
The bone-relic stupa was enshrined at Tienhu (Heaven Lake). His disciple Yu Taigu was a native of Goryeo;
his king honored him as State Preceptor and dispatched an envoy to divide the śarīra relics so they might be returned to the kingdom to construct a stupa.
Changzhou Jingci Pingshan Chulin Chan Master was the son of Wang Shi of the Renhe family; his mother was Huang Shi.

After the Master was born, one morning a monk passed by their house and, holding a wooden carved image of a Buddhist monk about a foot tall, presented it to his parents, saying, "This is the very child you have borne.
Having finished speaking, the monk vanished without a trace. His parents were filled with wonder.
She said, "This child must surely possess the seed of Buddhahood. Thereupon, she abstained from meat and pungent vegetables to protect him.

When he was twelve years old, she had him undergo the tonsure at Guangyan Monastery in the district. Once he had received full ordination, he told his mother, "I wish to travel to the four quarters to study.
His mother replied, "This is a matter within your own domain. She prepared his robes and sandals for him to set out, and before many days had passed, he returned again.
Upon returning, he saw his mother, who said, "One who studies the Buddha-dharma should maintain a non-retrogressive mind;

why do you falter so? The Master was deeply moved and began to reflect upon himself with great earnestness. He immediately went to Jinhua to visit Ji’an at Xifeng. Upon seeing him, Ji’an recognized his potential and ordered him to serve in the private quarters.
One night, while attending to him, Ji’an took paper and clear wax to make a substitute for a candle. He then held it up to show the Master, saying, "Dragon..."
"Tan said, 'I have blown it out; how do you understand this? As the Master was about to answer, the Hermit suddenly covered his mouth with his hand. Thereupon, the Master had a sudden realization.

Not long after, the Hermit moved to Daochang on Mount Hu, and the Master followed him there to serve as the Librarian. On the winter solstice, the Master held the whisk (presiding over the assembly), and the students posed more than a hundred questions.
He answered each question as it arose, like an arrow hitting the bullseye, until the entire assembly was awestruck and submitted. Later, the Hermit passed away."
The Master went to see Xugu at Yangshan. On one occasion, a Zen practitioner requested that he compose a verse for a tea ladle;

upon seeing this, Xugu was filled with joy and surprise, and appointed him to the second seat. He subsequently took charge at Daci and Jiahe. When Zhang [surname] of Danghu established a temple called Fuyuan, he invited the Master to serve as its founding abbot.
He later moved to Zhongtianzhi. The Imperial Court selected him to reside at Jingci, where students gathered in great numbers.
When the number reached ten thousand, the donor also came toward the wind. He renovated the halls and images, making them all new.

He examined and instructed scholars, exhorting them according to their capacities, and further established a Pure Abode (Vihāra) pagoda complex as a plan for his final years. One day, the Master said to those around him, "My worldly ties have likely come to an end.
He was carried in a sedan chair into the city to bid farewell to the Chancellor, and upon returning, he arrived at the Pure Abode.
He went to seek a bath. Having finished bathing and written a verse, he passed away peacefully. This was on the first day of the fifth month of the *zheng* cycle year of *xinchou*.
His worldly age was eighty-two; his years as a monk were sixty-six.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Lingyun Tieniu Ding:
Chan Master Juexue Shicheng of Bore Monastery in Yuzhang. His secular surname was Liu, and he was from Jishui.

At the age of seventeen, his paternal uncles forced him to engage in trade. While traveling and staying at Sanquan Mountain in Daye, Xingguo, there was an extraordinary monk named Wuxiang who possessed supernatural powers.
[The Master] possessed the knowledge of past lives. Seeing [Wuzhuo], he called out to him, saying, "Do you still remember our former companionship at Huangmei?

The Master was bewildered. Wuzhuo urged him, "Exert yourself in the study of Buddhism to return to your former practice. The Master immediately abandoned his business and followed him to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Wuzhuo further instructed him in the art of exiting the spirit (*chushen*).
The Master said, "If the spirit departs while the body remains, it may be carried by others to fire or water; when the spirit returns, where will it find lodging? Wuzhuo replied, "Know that..."

Fazuzu (Buzúxué) abandoned his studies and departed. Liren (Lízhēn) underwent tonsure while still in his physical body. After some time, he went to Wuxing to see Master Mōngshān Yìgōng and Master Ānhuì Xìnggōng.
He returned to his native village to see Master Xǐyá Jiègōng. When Jiè passed away, he went to Xiāngnán to see Tiěniú.

After several rounds of questioning and cross-examination, he finally attained a state of sudden, clear realization, as if all his lingering obstructions were cast off. Tiěniú subsequently retained him and assigned him a seat beside his own at Hongshan.
Ling Jingren built a hermitage called Prajñā-janman on Vulture Peak. Cai Shishi Deng Shiqi also donated his residence to serve as a hermitage, where the Master stayed and traveled between them.
Students gathered there in great numbers; masters from the Western Regions, Goryeo, Yunnan, and Japan all turned toward him with deep admiration.
Officials, scholars, commoners, and people of all ages followed one after another along the roads.

His family painted his likeness and enshrined it for worship. Whenever they trimmed their nails and hair or lost teeth, people scrambled to seize them, and from all of these, *śarīra* (relics) were obtained.
He passed away on the twenty-third day of the tenth month in the Renwu year of the Zhishun era. He was seventy-three years old by secular count and forty-two years by monastic seniority.
Three years later, when his entire body was exhumed from its sand burial, his countenance appeared as if he were alive; even his nails, hair, eyebrows, and beard had grown long.
Each was also over an inch in length. They were adorned with fragrant clay and brought to be enshrined in the hall. A stupa was constructed from finely ground stone to enshrine them.
[He was] a Dharma successor of Chan Master Fangshan Bao of Jingci.
Chan Master Wu Jian Xiandu of Mount Huading, Tiantai, was the son of the Ye family of Xianju, Taizhou.
His family had followed the profession of Confucian scholars for generations. He received the tonsure from Master Gutian Hou at Tianning Monastery in the prefecture;

after receiving full ordination, he visited Fashan at Ruiyan, where he fully mastered the essential points of the teaching. Thereupon, he traveled to Mount Huading to seek out the site of Gao’an’s former residence.

He lived in a thatched hut. After some time, his spiritual influence spread widely, and all considered him to be a reincarnation of Gao’an. Scholars from all quarters vied with one another to gather around him.
People remarked that it was impossible to support a large assembly without fields, so many came offering deeds of land; the Master rejected them all.

Throughout both winter and summer, he wore but a single robe, and as for food, he took whatever was necessary to satisfy hunger, regardless of whether it was coarse or fine. Addressing the assembly, he said: "The wind is cold..."
Cold! The sun shines brightly. *Campaka* flowers bloom, their fragrance filling the road; in a single night, spring grass has grown by the pond.
How pitiable, how laughable is Old Gautama—forty-nine years he spoke, yet never reached the point. Aha-ha! [He] strikes the meditation seat and descends.
A verse on dwelling in the mountains says: "A single pine tree, a wisp of smoke; A full moon, a pool of spring water.
If one were to depict this in a painting, One would add a *dhūta* monk sitting by the rock. And again: "Once, while picking wild vegetables, I passed over the western ravine."

The path was so overgrown with weeds that it seemed lost from waist-high; the spring rain teased out the sunshine until the day grew pale. The cuckoo’s cry ceased, and the bamboo pheasant took up the song.
During his cremation, suddenly from his chest a clear water gushed forth like the pouring of a pitcher, yielding śarīras as large as beans, their brilliance dazzling the eyes of those present.
Master Jingtang Gu of Tianning Monastery in Jiaxing ascended the hall. He cited a monk’s question to Master Yunmen: “What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
Yunmen replied, “Water walking on the eastern mountain. The Master offered this verse: Water walking on the eastern mountain— Directly proclaiming it for you.
Within stillness, heaven and earth are vast; In leisure, days and months are long. He ascended the hall. [The Buddha...]
All dharmas are taught for the sake of transcending all minds. Since I have no mind at all, what use have I for all dharmas?
At the gates of the six sense organs, it is empty and desolate; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, it is empty and desolate.

From where do the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars come? (He lets out a shout. Ascending the hall: One is not one, two is not two—before the flash of lightning has even formed.

The Dharma Successor of Chan Master Huirì Tánshí Xǐ:
The Elder Shòuzhuō was surnamed Xià; he was a native of Jiāding in Sūzhōu. In his middle years, he relinquished worldly attachments to enter the Way under Tánshí.
During the period of Jinghui, Master Shi went to follow him to investigate the essentials of the mind. Shi was given the koan "The dog has no Buddha-nature" to contemplate.
He investigated it through the night until he forgot both sleep and food. Soon thereafter, he received the tonsure and donned the black robes.

From then on, he invariably participated in the retreats held at various monasteries; these were known as the retreats of Shao-long Hermitage at Shuangjiang. One night, during the fifth watch, he heard the crowing of a cock.
He attained sudden and great enlightenment. Although he had never known a single stroke of a character (*dīng*), he spoke this verse: "For many years I sat in a heap in the corner by the wall;
When the yin reached its limit and the yang arose, I walked out. One night at the fifth watch, the cock crowed to announce the dawn; At daybreak, the red sun ascended the high terrace.
After his death, when his body was cremated, his tongue remained unburnt.

[Zhaozhou] used [his foot]. Was it simply because that is the natural way of things? Huayan kicked over the rice table. Zhaozhou said, "That was too crude.
Huayan said, "What do you mean by 'crude' or 'refined' here? Zhaozhou stopped. The next day they went together to another family’s vegetarian feast.
Zhaozhou asked, "How does today’s offering compare to yesterday's? Huayan again kicked over the rice bowl. Zhaozhou said, "It is well; it is just that—"
Huizhao said, "Too coarse. Changqing said, "Blind fellow! What 'coarse' or 'fine' does the Buddha-dharma speak of?
The Master said, "One person walks at the bottom of the deep sea; one person stands atop the high mountain peak.

At that time, when I saw Changqing kick over Huizhao’s rice table, I let out a thunderous shout to make them both retreat three houses. Is there anyone among you who can come to the rescue of these two elders?
All at once! The momentum of a thousand mountains ceases at the foot of the peak; the sound of ten thousand streams vanishes upon the sea.

Chan Master Nichuan Shun of Jingci Monastery in Hangzhou ascended the hall. Holding up his staff, he said: "The staff stands upright—mountains."
[The Master] stands the staff upright and says, "The staff is upright; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all at once upright.
He plants the staff on the ground and says, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are smashed to pieces. Where do you all find a place to settle your bodies and establish your lives?
He leans on the staff, lets out a shout, and descends from the seat. Ascending the hall, he cites a monk who asked Yunmen, "What is..."

The voice was low. His nostrils remained high and prominent. One might have thought this was a verse on Mount Ya, yet it was a hymn for East Mountain.

He struck his whisk and descended from the seat. Ascending the hall, he said: "The willows by the six bridges; the lotuses for ten li. They are constantly turning the Great Dharma Wheel within the eyes of all people.
He took up his staff and said: "One, two, three, four, five. Five, four, three, two, one. Crossing the waters."
Not Piercing the Clouds. Prajñāpāramitā.

He first resided at Beichen Monastery in Fuzhou and was selected for Yunju. In the *jiashu* year of the Hongwu era, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing.
One day, the Master asked a newly arrived monk, "In my place here, tigers and wolves block the path and thorns pierce the sky.
What urgent business brings you, Venerable One? The monk replied, "I have come specifically to pay my respects to the Master. The Master said, "The single phrase upon entering the gate—"
[The Master] did not ask [the first monk]. He then said, "Tell me, where did you get those straw sandals on your feet? The monk hesitated, and the Master gave a shout.

Dharma Heir of Chan Master Shuzhong Yun of Ruiyan:
Chan Master Juding Yuanji of Linggu Monastery in Yingtianfu, also known by his pen-name Yu’an. He was born into the Chen family of Huangyan, Tiantai.

His father was Yidao and his mother was of the Ye clan. At the time of the Master’s birth, auspicious dreams were obtained, and consequently, it was vowed that he would be renounced for the monastic life.

At home, at the age of fifteen, he was already capable of composing poetry and prose. He entered Jing’an Temple in his district to become a śrāmaṇera, where he relied upon Master Diyuan Yu to study the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*.
Upon meeting Master Kuǒngshì Ruìyán, he received full ordination under him and subsequently served as his attendant, mastering all the essential points of the teachings.
When Kuǒngshì retired to reside at Yonglè in Cíxī, the Master attended upon him there, thereby gaining further [instruction].

"Among the monks, who is this Ban Gu or Sima Qian? In the sixteenth year of the Hongwu era, he emerged from seclusion at Ningbo.

the rivers and lakes praised his filial piety. In the twenty-fifth year, the Prince of Shu summoned the Master to preside over Daci Monastery in Chengdu, but he declined the offer with vigor and did not accept.

The Master’s appearance closely resembled that of Master Xián, the "Wine Immortal" of Chéngdōng Chán; some even claimed he was a reincarnation of the Wine Immortal.

When the Master paid homage to the latter’s portrait, he composed a verse which said: People say my appearance resembles the Immortal Elder; Moreover, my surname is the same as his. Are you him? Are you I?
Do not engage in idle debate. Use a bamboo sieve to catch the northwest wind. Furthermore, when once burning incense sticks, there was a verse that said:

"A single thread of smoke scatters the fragrance of the *Avataṃsaka*; The jeweled nets and cloud-palaces all appear before one. If you can simply exhaust the dust within the inch-square mind, The perfuming of hearing does not reside at the tip of the nose."
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Nanchu Yue of Mount Jing:
Chan Master Jianxin Laifu of Lingyin Monastery in Hangzhou, a native of Yuzhang, whose courtesy name was Puan. He ascended the hall and said:
A horse’s jaw and a donkey’s jowl are one wondrous mark of the True One. Crows cawing and magpies chirping are one wondrous voice of the Buddha.
Holding up the whisk, he said: "Tell me, what kind of mark is this? Striking the whisk, he said: "Tell me, what kind of sound is this?"
"You people, if you take form and sound to exist, this is the view of eternalism; if you take form and sound to be non-existent, this is the view of nihilism.
Even if you manage to cast off both existence and non-existence, you are still only halfway there. You must further penetrate through the ultimate barrier above before you will succeed.
But tell me, how do you penetrate this ultimate barrier above? After a long silence, he said: "From now on, I shall not return; I have returned."

"It is already attained. Amidst the five tides of wind and moon, who is there to contend? He ascended the hall and said: "Above, it is not in heaven; below, it is not on earth; in between, it is not in man.
He held up his whisk and asked, "Tell me, why is this in my hands?
With the whisk, he struck the meditation seat once and said, "It is shattered into a hundred fragments. Is there anyone here who can turn their body and cast it out from within this?"
"Is it the breath? On the short night and long road, do not carry a torch; let everyone blow it out and walk in the dark. Entering the hall, [the Master said:
"The ancients said, 'With one mouth, swallow the Buddhas of the three periods; with one breath, turn the entire Great Canon.
When examined closely, this is much like creating trouble where there was none. At Chafeng, it is not so: if you have a mouth, just swallow your spittle; if you have breath, just nurture it."
Divine! How could one have the leisure to swallow the Buddhas of the three periods within one's belly? What spare time would there be to turn the entire Great Canon?
One seeks only to avoid trouble and pass the time, sparing oneself the labor of the mind and effort. Why is this? When all is fully realized, there is nothing further to realize;
even at the point of the most profound mystery, one must still utter a reproach.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Kuang of the Tian Tong Orthodox Lineage:
○ Chan Master Zhu Fang Mulian of Daochang Monastery in Huzhou, also known by his pen-name Xiuan-an (Humble Hermitage). He was a native of Dinghai in Siming.
His father’s surname was Qian. In his youth, he relied upon Master Xingxuan at Fulong Temple on Mount Dayu to become a śrāmaṇera.
After more than a year, he went to Wutai Temple to receive full ordination. While traveling through Western Zhejiang, he first visited Master Zhiquan of Lingyin Temple.
Master Quan asked, “Where are you from? The Master replied, “Mingzhou. Master Quan said, “I have heard that there are three Buddhas in Mingzhou; is this true? The Master answered, “One.”
"Since you do not even see one, how much less could there be three? Quan said, "Are you not a native of Mingzhou?
The Master looked at a monk standing nearby and said, "This old fellow is drunk again. Quan said, "Sit and drink tea for now. Later, he went to Jiangshan to see Zhenzong.
One day, Zhenzong asked him, "Do you remember the verse your own teacher wrote on hearing the rain? The Master replied, "I remember it. Zhenzong said:
"Try to bring it up and see. The Master brought it up, saying, "Drops dripping before the eaves are perfectly clear; deluded sentient beings recognize them as sound.
Zong stopped him with his hand and said, "If you do not call it 'sound,' what do you call it?

The Master said, "I certainly will not call it 'Wan-tuo-qiu' (a bowl falling off a hook). Zong said, "Seeing the person is not as good as hearing their name. The Master said, "You have tripped over the barrier of Yuanwu."
"Does Master Ya know? Zong then made the gesture of a palm strike. The Master stepped back and said, "In the future, you will strike people wrongly.
After a long time, he received an order from the Xuanzheng Yuan to take up residence at Shimen, and subsequently moved to Baoduo Puci.

In the tenth year of the Hongwu era, by imperial decree, the monastery was promoted in status; the Buddha Hall and all other buildings were constructed to double the scale of the original regulations.

In the eleventh year, he received an edict to collate and edit new commentaries on the Three Classics. In the fifteenth year, the court newly established an administrative office for monks and Daoists;
the community elected the Master as the Chief Administrator (Dugang) of the Sangangsi, and there were no monks within the jurisdiction who did not obey him.
He exhorted them to do good. The *Qinggui* of Wuxing had become as coarse and transformed as that of Lu. Entering the hall, he said: "The entire Tripitaka was not spoken by the Yellow-Faced Old Man;
pointing directly at the human mind was not transmitted by Master Bodhidharma. He then held up his staff.

The horns of an ox are three inches long; the horns of a rabbit are eight feet long. The Shepherdess by the seashore, the Juniper Flower by the Ju-ma River, and the Stone of the Wife Who Waits for Her Husband.

Entering the hall, he said: "An ancient worthy said: 'If Śākyamuni had not appeared in the world, and Bodhidharma had not come from the West, the Buddha-dharma would pervade the world, yet those who discuss the profound would not open their mouths.
When the ancient worthy spoke thus, he saw only the sharpness of the tip of the awl."
He saw that the chisel-head was square. Longfeng, however, was not like this:

"If Śākyamuni had not appeared in the world and Bodhidharma had not come from the West, two or five fallen petals would have broken through the moss before the steps. He ascended the hall and cited Master Baoning Yong’s address to the assembly, saying:
Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking of it. To speak of it is for "horns" to grow. [The Master said: "The assembly has grown horns!
Is this an ox? Is this a horse? The Master said: "Big or small, Bao-ning does not even recognize oxen and horses.
Since horns have already grown, what difficulty is there in distinguishing them? Nevertheless, you all must not be careless or hasty. For seventy years...

On the first day of the sixth month, he manifested slight illness. On the morning of the twelfth, after finishing his correspondence with the various mountain monasteries, he passed away within a short while.
Chan Master Lanjiang Qingyong of Juyan in Kunshan, Dharma heir of Chan Master Longxiang Tanfangzhong. A native of Tiantai, his secular surname was Liu. Initially, he followed [Master] Jifu...
Master Yuǎn studied the Tiantai teachings; he then went to rely on Master Xiāng at Shuǐnán in Yuèlín. After a long time, he traveled to visit Master Zhòngfāng Lúnpó at Bǎo níng in Jīnlíng.
There, Lúnpó interrogated him with the "Great Suí" dialogue (*Tàisuí huà*). For half a year, he still did not attain realization.
One day, while walking along the Hùlóng River, he experienced a sudden and profound awakening. He then celebrated this, saying: "The nostrils of Dàsuí have been placed within me."
"Excellent! Zhongfang said, "This is indeed good, yet it cannot be considered sufficient. Once the Master had departed, I kept these words in my mind and did not dare forget them for even a moment.
While passing through the market town of Jing Shan in Huzhou, I suddenly forgot that I was moving a single step.
Only then did I realize there is no Buddha to be attained and no sentient beings to be saved. Hehe! I laughed aloud. Thus it was.
He was seen bestowing broad compassion upon Mount Jiangshan, where he was appointed to the office of Attendant and subsequently entrusted with the keys of the treasury.

He later traveled to Lingyan in Wuxing, where Master Yuyong invited him to share the seat and preach the Dharma. He emerged from seclusion at Cuiwei in Changzhou and was subsequently transferred to Xianci in Lake District.
Jingjue of Tianjie Monastery invited him to occupy the position of First Seat; he was further appointed to Jianyan in Kunshan. When a monk asked about the World-Honored One holding up the flower—
"Kāśyapa smiled—what was his intention? The Master said, "In the World-Honored One’s hand, a flower is red;
on Kāśyapa’s face, both eyes are azure. A monk asked, "The Patriarch faced the wall, and Shen Guang severed his arm—how about that? The Master said:
In those days, there was Liu Zhi who used poison; today, Huik'e has attained peace of mind. A monk asked, "As for 'dividing the skin' and 'dividing the marrow,' what about that?
The Master said, "To grasp the meaning before the pivot is still a stagnation; to know where to return upon hearing the words is likewise delusion.
As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout. Ascending the hall, he said: "The very mind is Buddha; neither mind nor Buddha—this is not it."
The mind is not the Buddha; it is not a thing. A stone woman’s liver and intestines are wrapped in brocade;

a Persian’s nostrils protrude with golden studs. Protruding into empty space, they meet head-on. Ascending the hall, after concluding the story of Baizhang and the wild fox, he let out a wild fox cry and said, "Fox!
Then he descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, [he said: "That which is summoned by feeling transcends mountains and rivers yet is not distant. By conditions..."
When there is a divergence between what one hears and sees, and when there is a gap in one's faculties, one should seek the cause within oneself rather than blaming others.

To employ the method of the black bean, swallow the *lilikipeng* (the thorny chestnut). Ascending the hall, he said: "The pure practitioner does not enter nirvana; the precept-breaking bhikṣu does not enter hell.
When the twelve railings have been leaned upon in turn, at the gateway to the sea, a single point of green lies in the distant mountains. This was composed by the Master on occasion.
Verse: Briefly stated, there is no worldly affair worth pondering; I only regret that the nights in the human world are not long. One awakens from sleep and the sky is already bright;
The western wind fills the courtyard with the fragrance of osmanthus. Verse on the Ferryman: On the south bank and the north bank, voices join one another;
The living path is blocked, stretching a thousand miles. It relies entirely upon the person within to exert effort; A single turn of the prow and the boat sets forth.
He then returned home. Not seeking others, he spoke in verse: "Ordinarily, the handle has been in my hand; throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, its use has been manifold.
Suddenly, when the itch was reached and scratched, the whole body could not contain its joy. He passed away at Songjiang.
Chan Master Weian of Songyin exerted himself in carrying out his funeral affairs.
He was a Dharma heir of Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben of Tiantong.
○ Chan Master Yuanchang of Qianyan at Shengshou Monastery on Mount Fulong in Wuzhou, styled Wuming, was from Xiao County in Yue.
The Mountain Man’s surname was Dong. He followed his paternal uncle, named Tanfang, to study Buddhism at Famen Yuan in Fuyang.

Whenever he saw the titles of the various scriptures, he could immediately recite them from memory. At the age of nineteen, he received the tonsure and traveled to Wulin to study the Vinaya at Lingzhi Temple.
The Vinaya Master asked, "In the coming and going of these eight dharmas, there is not the slightest discord; what does this mean? The Master replied, "Why do you not ask about the ninth dharma?
The Vinaya Master said, "To ask about the Vinaya and receive an answer regarding Chan—you are truly a vessel for the Mahayana.

When the Chancellor’s office hosted a meal for the monastic community, the Master entered with the assembly. Zhongfeng was also seated there; seeing the Master from afar, he called out to him, saying, "You..."
"How do you spend your daily life? the Master asked. The teacher replied, "I do nothing but recite the Buddha's name. Feng said, "Where is the Buddha now? As the teacher hesitated, Feng rebuked him.
The teacher then prostrated himself and requested instruction. Feng bestowed upon him the koan of the dog having no Buddha-nature. Subsequently, he went to Lingyin to practice Chan.
There, Master Xueting Chuan summoned him to serve as the head scribe (*neiji*). Shortly thereafter, he returned to the Dharma [seat].
Having served as gatekeeper for ten years, he suddenly sighed with a deep lament: "Throughout my life, my spirit and ambitions have filled the heavens and the earth;
how is it that I have now become a *xījī* (vinegar fly) in a jar? He went again to Lingyin Monastery and sat in meditation without touching his mat for three years.
Upon hearing the cry of a cock, he attained realization. He hurried to see Zhongfeng, who again rebuked him. The Master returned home in indignation. As the night drew toward stillness—
Suddenly, a mouse overturned the cat’s food bowl; the vessel fell to the ground with a loud noise. He was struck by a sudden awakening, feeling his body leap several *zhang* into the air.
He went again to consult Feng, who asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master replied, "A mouse ate the cat's rice. Feng said, "Not yet.
The Master said, "The bowl falls to the ground, smashing the monastery's bricks. Feng then slightly... [smiled].
The Master laughed and said in blessing, "May you protect and uphold [the Dharma] well. Thereafter, the Master lived in seclusion at the Eastern Hermitage of Tianlong.

A snake would come to his seat every day; the Master preached the precepts of returning to the faith to it, whereupon the snake raised its head, bowed its neck, made the gesture of prostration, and departed.

From that time on, his reputation and influence grew daily. The Provincial Governor, Prince Dehuang, dispatched an envoy to urge the Master to emerge from retirement and assume the leadership of various monasteries.

They also vied with one another in joyfully inviting him, but the Master declined them all. He then crossed the river to Mount Fulong, where he planted his staff at the edge of a cliff and issued a warning:
"If there is a spring on this mountain, I shall stay here. Suddenly, a mountain spring overflowed, appearing the color of white milk.
He then took up residence beneath a great tree. Lou Junru, Xu, and other prominent local families built a dwelling for him to live in. Shortly thereafter...
The site of the old temple was known as Shengshou. Monastics and laypeople alike venerated it, flocking there from all directions.
Prince Zhennan personally inscribed the temple plaque to bestow upon it, along with the *saṃghāṭī* robe and the honorary title "Master of Universal Response, Great Eloquence, and Wondrous Wisdom.

The Zizhengyuan further petitioned the Eastern Court (the Emperor) on his behalf, commanding me to compose the title: "Great Zen Master of Buddha-Wisdom, Perfect Clarity, Vast Illumination, Boundless Universal Benefit."
[The Emperor] bestowed upon him that title along with a robe of gold brocade. A monk asked, "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his slaves;
I wonder, who is he? The Master said, "A broom growing from a heap of refuse. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Go ask the janitor.
Another monk asked, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the True Eye? The Master said:
One day, Master Song Gong Jingliao visited the teacher. The teacher asked him, "I have heard that you have read through the entire Tripitaka;
is this true? Jingliao replied, "It is so. The teacher said, "Do you read it with your ears, or do you observe it with your eyes? Jingliao replied, "I observe it with my eyes."
The Master said, "As for that which is able to see with the eyes, whom do you take it to be? Liang Yang raised his eyebrows toward him.

Thereupon, they looked at each other and smiled. He addressed the assembly, saying: "It is easy to turn mountains, rivers, and the lands back into oneself; it is difficult to turn oneself back into mountains, rivers, and the lands.
He then held up his whisk and said, "Speak a single phrase before your parents were born! He then ascended the hall.
Pointing to the incense burner, he said, "The assembly, the incense burner has finished preaching the Dharma for you all. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The autumn wind is cool; the autumn night is long. The traveler who has not yet returned yearns for his native land. Assembly, what is your native land?"
"Hai! Fortunately, you are at home; there is no need for bitter reflection. On the fourteenth day of the sixth month of the Dingyou year of the Zhizheng era, he wrote this verse:
"A lifetime of idle talk; today, the failure is complete. One phrase roars through the heavens—the Eye of the True Dharma is extinguished.
He threw down his pen and passed away. His remains were interred in their entirety at Qingsong Monastery.
○ Chan Master Wize Lintu of Shishilin in Suzhou was a native of Luling. While he was in the quarters of Huanzhu, a newly arrived monk happened to ask:
"When the Great Matter is not yet clarified, it is as if one has lost one's parents; when the Great Matter is already clarified, it is likewise as if one has lost one's parents.
Before the question had even ended, Huan struck him. As Wize stood by his side, a state of intense doubt suddenly arose within him. Thereafter—
He presented his understanding repeatedly, yet none of it accorded with [the Master’s] intent. One day, he suddenly laughed to himself and said, "Today, I can no longer deceive myself.
Huankan examined him and said, "I shall not ask whether you have understood or not; for now, tell me, what do you call this 'Great Matter'?"
The Master replied extemporaneously: "The pillar swallows Lion Rock; the lantern laughs until its mouth is split in half. Huan-ken then instructed him, saying:
"You must sit and cut off all ties in a state of absolute solitude; thirty years hence, I shall not have disappointed you. He then appointed the Master to head the board of monks.
The Master declined with all his might, but Huan suddenly descended from his seat and prostrated himself once; the Master hurriedly [accepted].
Shen-shen said, "Master, this prostration you have just made is cast into empty space. Huan said, "But you yourself are not outside of empty space.
He then struck the bell to escort the Master back to his quarters. From that time on, Huan would often say, "In the hall, there is a Head Seat (shouzuo)."
The old illusion may now be set aside. Once the illusion was stilled, the Master established a hermitage in the city of Suzhou named Shizi Lin (Lion Grove).
He addressed the assembly, saying: "What is the Buddha? Three catties of hemp. What is the Buddha? That which is inside the Buddha hall.
What is the Buddha? A dried-up dung pellet. For three large copper coins, I bought a fried cake; I eat it right into my belly."
At that very moment, he was no longer hungry. He addressed the assembly: "What is there within the mountains? On the peaks, there are many white clouds. A-he-he!
These are the common property of the community; who would dare to possess them privately? Nevertheless, though it is so, they can only bring joy to oneself;
they are not fit to be presented as a gift to others. The Master once compiled the essential passages from the various commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and merged them into a single work.
One work, titled *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation), was published as woodblocks and circulated in the world.
[The lineage of] Chan Master Píngshān Lín of Jìngcí Temple:
○ Chan Master Zhǐān Dèxiáng of Zhì’ān Temple in Yìngtiānfù, a native of Hángzhōu, appeared in the world at Long... in the prefecture.
Huā moved from Sūzhōu’s Tiānpíng to Hángzhōu’s Bào guó, then ascended to Jìngcí and Jìngshān, finally reaching Tiānjiè. At Jìngshān, Fāng Wénchéng ascended the hall and said:
"A span wide, it is a brand-new sun and moon; ten feet deep, it is a separate heaven and earth.
Those coming from the east and west, those coming from the south and north—all meet here together. But tell me, where does 'not' [exist]?"
Where do you meet one who neither comes nor goes? He lifts his staff and strikes it once: "A crane flies through a thousand fathoms of snow;
a dragon lies coiled in a pool of ice."
The Twenty-fifth Generation after Dajian (Daikō):
Zen Master Shengshou Qianyan Chang, Successor of the Dharma Lineage.
○ Wansong Heshang of Sheng’en on Mount Dengwu in Suzhou, whose name was Shiwei; he was from Jinyi in Leqing County, Wenzhou.
His mother was Zheng. She dreamed that two figures, one Confucian and one Buddhist, entered her bedchamber; by dawn, she had given birth to two sons, the younger of whom was the Master.

A light illuminated the room, and the people, finding it strange, wished to abandon him, but his paternal aunt raised him. While still in swaddling clothes, whenever he saw a monk, he would immediately smile and join his palms.
At the age of eleven, he received ordination at Yongqing Monastery in Yue, taking the lecture master Sheng as his preceptor. Sheng then conferred upon him...
While reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he suddenly attained a realization regarding the fact that all phenomena have been so from the very beginning. He subsequently traveled to various regions;
having received full ordination, he went to Tiger’s Well to study under Master Zhigan. Zhigan assigned him the koan of Nanquan’s “Three Is Not” for investigation.

Thereupon, he went to the old ruins of Foji Temple on Mount Dapeng and established a hermitage there to dwell. Day and night, he pursued the ultimate meaning of the koan he was investigating, almost forgetting to sleep.

After staying for some time, he went to Huading to pay his respects to Wu Jian, but they did not reach a point of mutual accord. Hearing of Qianyan’s spiritual transformation, he went to see him immediately.
One day, while entering the room for instruction, Qianyan asked, "Do you wish to receive the precepts? The Master immediately covered his ears and left.
The next day, during a communal work session of cutting pine trees, the Master picked up a round stone, made the gesture of offering a pearl, and said, "I request the Master to set a price."
Yan said, "Not worth half a penny. The Master said, "Blind! Yan said, "I am blind too, and you are blind too.
The Master said, "Blind! Blind! Yan then withdrew. On the Buddha’s birthday, Yan ascended the hall and said, "Today there are all manner of auspicious events."
"First, the World-Honored One’s birth; second, the clear skies of the celestial realm; third, a great donor preparing a vegetarian feast.
If you people can recognize where this old monk’s tongue falls, you could digest ten thousand taels of gold a day.
The Master moved from west to east, pointing one finger to heaven and one finger to earth, saying: "The God among Gods! The God among Gods! Śākyamuni!"
"Kāmler, who is first and who is last? Yanhe replied, "This man from Wenzhou is acting quite recklessly. Thereafter, he was invited to occupy the position of the Rear Board (Houban).
From that time on, the fame of the Head Seat Wei spread in all directions. Before long, he returned once more to Foji Temple.
Later, Yan sent him a verse and further instructed him, saying: "Your karmic conditions lie in Western Zhejiang; you should go there to transform and guide others. The Master arrived at Gu...

The black ants of Su were drawn to him as if by white silk. He established four sites of practice (*dharma-cakra*), and those who received from him the precepts of taking refuge and the full ordination were beyond counting.

Upon hearing his name or catching sight of his shadow, there was none who did not place their hands upon their foreheads in reverence. Those who painted his likeness to offer worship were exceedingly numerous;

was this not because he shared a karmic affinity with the people of Su from a former life? As he approached his end, he bathed, changed his robes, took up his brush, and wrote a verse before passing away. His entire body [was enshrined].
His stupa was enshrined on Mount Niepan to the right of Sheng’en Temple. He lived seventy-nine years and fifty-nine *zhì*.
○ Chan Master Wéi’ān Dé’rán of Sōngyǐn in Sōngjiāng was of the Zhāng clan of the commandery.

Having attained awakening upon hearing the proclamations of Qiānyán, he subsequently succeeded him on the seat. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Deshan’s staff, Linji’s shout—pick one up and set it down!"
"Side! Bring forth a single phrase from beneath the heels of everyone here! [The Master] drew a line with his staff and said, "Vipaśyin Buddha set his mind upon this long ago;
until this very day, he has not attained the wondrous. He ascended the hall and said: "The river moon shines; the pine wind blows."
"What shall one do during the long, clear nights? Master Yongjia has already spoken his full mind on this.
"Does the assembly know where he lands? [He] strikes the meditation staff. "The kalpa-stone may have a day of wearing away; gold has no time of decay.
In his later years, he lived in seclusion at Songyin, and people consequently called him Master Songyin. Officials, scholars, commoners, and monastics from distant regions and foreign lands...
His teachings flow like water rushing into a ravine. The Hanlin Academician Jingliao inscribed his *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings), stating:

"His language is steep and abrupt—like copper gates and iron walls, or sharp swords and long spears. Not only is it impossible to find a foothold, but there is not even a crack through which one might exploit a weakness.
Alas, how formidable! Can one not believe the words of the Hanlin Academician?"
*The Supplemental Record of the Transmission of the Lamp from the Expanded Collection*, Scroll Six:
*Supplement to the Five Lamps Meeting Their Source*,
Compiled by the Former Abbot of Jingshan Xingsheng Wanshou Chan Monastery, Bhikṣu Wénxiù of Wújùn.
The Seventeenth Generation Successor of Dajian (Dajian Huizhao) below:
Chan Master Donggu Guang of Lingyin, Huzhou, whose dharma heirs include Mingji Zu.
[He was] a native of Wuxi, Chang County, and was a contemporary of You Yu, the Attendant Reader.
(余六切。盛也) [Yù liù qiè. Meaning: "abundant. He was profoundly virtuous. Initially he resided at Benjue Temple in Jiahe; later he moved to Lingyan in Suzhou and Huazang in Changzhou.
However, he stayed longest at Wanshou in Zhongwu, where his assembly numbered over seven hundred, causing the Dharma-way to flourish once again.

By imperial decree, he was appointed to Yuyang in Mingzhou, and by special edict, he was transferred to Lingyin. A monk asked: "When one borrows function to clarify the position, how is it? The Master—

Before the question was even asked, the monk said, "When one clarifies merit by borrowing the position (*ji-wei ming-gong*), what is it like? The Master said, "The sun covers the whole earth, yet it is as black as lacquer.
The monk said, "At this very moment, is it clarifying the position by borrowing merit, or borrowing merit to clarify the position?
The Master said, "It is very much as if you have never had a meal. The monk said, "When a student reaches this point, there is no way to advance and no door to retreat."
The Master said, "You are but a grass-robber. The monk said, "Today I have been caught in the act. The Master said, "Thirty blows shall be reserved for another time.
He ascended the hall and said: "The nature of awakening is wondrously luminous; fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous. In the frosty forest, the jade phoenix gives birth to its fledglings;
at the moonlit door, the golden cock crows at dawn. From the beginning, this has been but our single family style. Truly, with whom can it be shared? Arrive!"
"He did not arrive. He looked up without raising an eyebrow; he lowered his head and clapped his hands, laughing. Entering the hall, [the Master said]: "Myriad pipes cry out as the pine wind howls;
a thousand forests shed their withered leaves. The old barbarian with missing teeth has gone away, leaving no trace. He took up his staff, held it upright, and said:
"Is it still seen as it comes now? He then returned it to its original place and said, "Since you all do not understand, I shall go back to Shaolin.
The Small Assembly Lecture for the Year-End: When misfortune reaches its limit, prosperity arrives; the fragrance of plum blossoms is transmitted. The warming power of spring fills the valley;

as the position shifts, the end of the season is reached. The sound of the pine wind passes through the cold night hall. The seasons are distinct, and coming and going follow their measure. It may truly be said:
When the exhaustion of Tāngtú merges with the Way and penetrates the Source—how is it at such a time? The golden hoe does not move the earth; the numinous sprouts grow wherever they are.
On the fifth day of the first month of winter in the first year of the Bǎoyò era, he manifested nirvana. He wrote a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
A fragment of cloud gathers in the eastern valley; the full moon hangs over the ancient ford. Startled by the cold, white birds take flight; one sleeps at night beneath a shadowless tree.
[This concludes the section on] Chan Master Zu’an Jìan, Dharma Heir of Xuedou.
Chan Master Chang’ung Rujing of Tiantong in Mingzhou ascends the hall and, citing the story of Bodhidharma meeting Emperor Wu of Liang, says:
The Verse of Causality says: The golden crow flies up onto the jade balustrade; The pitch-black Kunlun faces us directly.
In the end, these cannot be transmitted; Falling flowers and flowing water are utterly groundless.
Chan Master Yuanzhou Cihua Puan Yinsu, Dharma Heir of Chan Master Huanglong Muan Zhong.
He was the son of the Yu family from Guanchun County.
At the age of six, he dreamed of a monk who pointed to his heart and said, "In the future, you shall attain self-realization. Upon waking, he related this to his mother, who looked at him.

There was a single spot of bright red upon it, much like a cherry bead found in the world. Because of this, his parents permitted him to leave home under the Venerable Master Xian of Shoulong Monastery.
At the age of twenty-seven, he shaved his head. The Master’s appearance was imposing and his intellect was sharp and wise;
Venerable Xian took a liking to him and urged him to recite the scriptures. The Master said, "I have heard that the original intent of all Buddhas values nothing more than awakening."
To merely count beads and grind ink in one's mind is of no benefit to the practice of the Way. He traveled far to Lake Xiang to visit Daomai Muan, asking, "All phenomena return to the One;
where does the One return? Zhong held up his whisk, and the Master attained realization. Later, he returned to his place of training.

There was a man named Cihua from a neighboring temple whom the assembly invited to serve as abbot. As the temple had no permanent endowment, the Master spread out his quilt and used paper money [to provide for the community].
Wearing robes, eating gruel, and practicing dhyāna, he happened to read the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) and attained great enlightenment.

His entire body was covered in perspiration, and he said with joy, "I have now personally reached the realm of the Avataṃsaka. He spoke this verse: "It cannot be formed into a ball, nor can it be pushed apart;
Why seek Mount Nanyue or Mount Tiantai? At the gateway of the six sense-faculties, no one understands— Thus, the barbarian monk has come for no reason at all. In his daily life...
A verse says: "Numinous and wondrous suchness is no different from the great void; it fashions the myriad things without being obstructed by spatial directions.

Those who admire the Way and turn toward its breeze grew in number daily. The Master preached the Dharma according to what was appropriate for them. When there were those with illnesses, he used grass as medicine.

If he gave it to them, they were immediately healed. There were even cases of pestilence where people did not even exchange greetings; yet when he wrote out a verse and gave it to them, all were completely cured.
Someone asked the Master, "What practice have you cultivated to attain this? The Master then drew a line in the air and said, "Do you understand?
The man replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak of it. One day, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "All..."
"The Buddha does not appear in the world, nor is there any nirvana. Those who enter my chamber will surely be able to achieve profound resonance with the mystery. Guard and maintain this well;

do not let it decline or be lost. Having requested a bath and changed his robes, he sat in the full lotus posture and passed into stillness on the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Qiandao era.
He was fifty-five years old and twenty-eight years of monastic life.
The Dharma Heir of Chan Master Huazangmin:
Chan Master Shiqiao Kexuan of Mount Jing, Hangzhou. He was the son of the Xu family of Jiading, Sichuan.

He was the teacher of Master Biefeng Yin and the younger brother of Master Juzhou Tan; Tan was also his uterine brother. People of the time said that Master Xuan’s Chan was identical to that of [Master] Yin.
His poetry rivaled that of Master Tan. In the Dinghai year of the Jiading era, he was appointed to Mount Jing by Chancellor Luoguo.
Entering the hall, he said: "Three times nine is twenty-seven; at the hedge-top, the pí-pí-li is blown. Alas, those with clear eyes do not recognize one another face-to-face.
Jushi raised his finger; Luzu saw people and turned his back to the wall. Do you understand? Today is the month of December."

1. The Master contemplated that monks from the four directions, clad in cloud-like robes and with calloused feet, were coming to him; yet, by the end of their journey, they had no place to eat or rest.

Thus, he built a dwelling upon the Double Stream (Shuangxi) to provide for those who lacked such provisions. Emperor Ning bestowed upon him the two great characters "Huacheng" (Transformation City) as an honor.
Consequently, he constructed a multi-storied pavilion to display them above. Furthermore, the Emperor granted the Master the title "Furi" (Buddha-Sun). [The text continues with] Yang of Meishan...
You have clearly composed a record of Huacheng Monastery that is quite detailed. The Master passed away and was interred in a stupa behind the monastery.
[The Dharma heir of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao of Jingshan:
Chan Master Liaoming of Jingshan, Hangzhou, a member of the Lu clan of Xiuzhou. He was tall in stature with a large belly. His Way...

He was of robust and imposing appearance. In the *Xinyou* year of the *Shaoxing* era, he accompanied Miaoxi during his exile to Hengyang. The local prefectures and counties provided extremely strict guard and escort;
the Master carried his cangue through the perilous journey, enduring hardships without ever showing the slightest slackening.

Once they arrived at the place of banishment, the number of monastics who followed him to seek the Way never fell below two or three hundred people. Miaoxi, concerned that provisions for meals were insufficient and fearing further calamity, repeatedly urged [the Master] to...
He ordered them to leave, but the Master would not comply. He would always carry a wicker basket on his shoulder to beg for alms.

By evening, dozens of people would come to carry his rice, flour, firewood, and vegetables; these provisions were arranged in rows as they returned home. Although his family was large, there was never anything lacking.

In this manner, seventeen years passed as if they were a single day. The flourishing of the Dharma-heir lineage was such that half of those who received the transmission while he was in exile were due to the Master’s efforts.
In the year Guihai, he took leave to travel to Western Zhejiang to beg for alms, vowing to return on the Shangyuan festival the following year.
Xifa sent him off with a verse, which said: "Laozu is the Great Chan; his boldness is beyond all comparison. Having realized the mystery within mysteries,"
He became the master among masters. Barefoot, he ran through the long streets, covering hundreds of li in a single day.
His physical strength was so fierce that he feared neither cold nor heat. For two or three years, he did nothing but this every day; everyone considered him a madman.
He merely smiled. While the autumn sun was blazing hot, he suddenly came to take his leave of Miaoxi. Carrying a mere *zhū* of incense into the bustling marketplace, Puhua truly knew himself.
With a *jílì* staff slung over his shoulder, his spiritual vigor could not be restrained. As he departed, he offered you these words of parting.
"You must now take this to heart: before the Upper Prime (Shangyuan) of the Jiazi year, you shall surely return here.

Furthermore, he requested a eulogy for the image of Miaoxi, which says: "Even if one were to paint it perfectly, it would still be but a flow of the eternal and unchanging. Puhua turned his chopsticks and rice-bowl upside down;
scratching where the itch lies, he reached the place of ultimate clarity. There is a final word that cannot be restrained when the moment arises. *Du!* And yet—"
Master Yaoxu was noble and spirited in his character, with sharp and agile mental faculties. In his responses and applications of means, he invariably took joy in the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*).
Consequently, he earned the reputation of being a great Chan master within the monastic communities. After some time, he emerged from the mountain to reside at Toudi in Shuzhou.

It happened that the cattle at the various manors of Toudi had been struck by an epidemic, and nearly all had perished. The Master transformed two hundred oxen to fill their place, and for several consecutive years, there was a great harvest.
The harvest was twice the usual amount. He moved his residence to Changlu, where monks gathered like the spokes of a wheel, and the monastic community was transformed.
In the first year of the Longxing era, he received an imperial decree to reside at Mount Jing. On his way, he passed through the Kaihua Monastery in Guangde Commandery;

the head monk, Zongyan, requested a verse to commemorate its reconstruction. The Master took up his brush and wrote: "This Head Monk Yan, His wondrous faculty is ever in hand. He strikes the gavel..."
Where it strikes, it blocks the mother-born mouth; if one can grasp it beyond words, three times three does not make nine.
The head monk transmits it thus, letting out a great lion’s roar. All Buddhas do likewise: with a shout, Mount Sumeru runs away.

He builds a great Brahma-palace reaching the heavens, enduring for a thousand years and ten thousand ages, rubbing the stars and constellations. He offers this verse on the story of Zhaozhou examining the old woman: "Gan..."
Within the halberds lies the foundation of Great Peace; it is only by not using weapons that this is attained.
Without the strength to lift a cauldron or pull down a mountain, even the black steed *Wu'ei* would not easily be ridden across a thousand li.

Previously, Wang, Prince of Yang, had dreamed of a monk of great stature, walking with a strange, slow gait, saying he wished to transform a manor in Suzhou. Upon waking, he found it extraordinary. The following morning, the Master suddenly appeared, walking on foot with staff and sandals.
When he arrived, the King saw that it was no different from his dream. He immediately summoned his attendants, burned incense, and prostrated.

After the tea ceremony, the Master spoke first: "Your Majesty possesses vast estates; you might grant one estate in Suzhou to provide inexhaustible benefit for the worship of the Buddha and the feeding of monks at Mount Jing.
The King did not yet give his consent or refusal. When the meal was over, the Master departed, with nothing further to say.

When these words were spoken, there was a great clamor both inside and outside [the palace]. Rumors spread that the Wang family had donated a manor in Suzhou to Jingshan Monastery, and this eventually reached the ears of Emperor Xiaozong.
It happened that Wang entered the court, whereupon he spoke to the Emperor, saying, "I have heard that you, Excellency, have donated a manor in Suzhou to Jingshan.

I shall grant a remission of its tax obligations. Wang expressed his gratitude. Upon returning home the following day, he sent a letter to Jingshan; at that time, the Master [Zhenxie Qingliao] had already... for two... [days].
He passed away several days prior. Since then, whether awake or asleep, the Master has appeared before him and said, "Among the six perfections, the perfection of giving is foremost.
To begin well and end well is what constitutes true excellence. Thereupon, the King bestowed his manors and serfs upon Mount Jing.
