The annual revenue of this monastery was twenty thousand *hu*. The Master had a great affinity with both monastics and laypeople; wherever he went, offerings were bestowed upon him in clouds.
Throughout Jiang, Zhe, Hu, and Xiang, he was hailed as the reincarnation of the Bagua Monk.
The Chan Master Wude Caishi of Jingshan in Hangzhou was born into the Yang family of Fuyang. Having lost his father in childhood, he entered the monastic order under the monk Keping.
Keping was skilled in medicine and wished to transmit his craft to him, but the Master said, "I have left the household life to seek the supramundane Dharma;
how could I devote myself to the arts of healing and sell my own soul? Thereupon, he focused single-mindedly on Chan study and was not swayed by anything else.
The paths diverged. At that time, Huìdōng of Dàochǎng and Chán Gǎo were serving as models for the monastic community.
The Master traveled from Zhejiang into Fújiān and served under these two masters for a considerable period; yet, although he achieved significant insights, they were not ultimate.
He left them and went to Bǎizhàng in Jīāngxī, where he met the attendant Zōngjiàn, a respected friend of his. During a night conversation, they discussed the excellence of various regions.
Liu Jian said, "If one does not explore the tiger's den, how can one obtain the tiger's cub? You have vowed to accomplish the Great Matter; if you do not see Miaoxi, where will you go?
At that time, Miaoxi had been exiled to Hengyang and was residing in the mountain hall of Huayao Temple. The Master went to follow him there.
One day, while entering the room for instruction, Miaoxi asked, "Why does the person inside the hut not see what is outside the hut? The Master replied, "A catfish."
Xuanji climbed up a bamboo pole and struck him once swiftly with a bamboo rake. At that moment, the Master’s lifelong doubts were completely dissolved like ice melting away.
Xuanji often called the Master "the man from Hangzhou. Because the hall was cramped and overcrowded, the Master built a hut in the forest to live in.
Xǐ visited him and found his quarters desolate, containing only a single couch. He then asked for a brush and inscribed the two characters "Wú" (No) and "Ān" (Hermitage) upon the wall;

the Master took these as his monastic name. Xǐ moved to Méiyáng, while the Master returned to the region south of the Zhe River. After some time, he emerged from seclusion at Běishān in Yízhēn and was subsequently appointed to Zīfú in Shàoxīng.
In the year of Xīnyǐ, he succeeded Yìng'ān as abbot of Wànshòu in Zhōngwú. In the autumn of the first year of Qiándào, [he went to] Jìng...
When Chan Master Shanming Da passed away, Chancellor Qian Gong, who had long admired the Master’s reputation, petitioned the throne for him to serve as the abbot.
In the following spring, the Imperial carriage of the Retired Emperor Gaozong visited the mountain; he commanded the Master to ascend the seat and preach the Dharma.

Delighted, the Emperor bestowed upon him ordination certificates, gold, and silk. The Master subsequently constructed the two pavilions, Yuzhen and Longyou. Upon hearing of this, the Emperor personally inscribed the character "Long" (Dragon).
The three characters "Youge" (Wandering Pavilion) were bestowed upon him. In the summer of the fourth year, Emperor Xiaozong summoned the Master to the imperial court for an audience at Xuande Hall.

The Master first addressed the Emperor, saying, "My late master Zonggao was favored by Your Majesty, and that grace has now extended to this humble monk. The Emperor replied, "I have long heard of your master’s reputation; it is my regret that I did not meet him while he was still alive.
The Master then discoursed extensively on his Way, and the Emperor praised and sighed in admiration without ceasing. In the fifth year...
In the sixth month, he fell ill. On the twenty-sixth day, he summoned his disciples to bid them farewell, wrote a verse of parting, and passed away.

He was fifty-four years of age and thirty-nine years since his ordination. His disciples buried the Master behind the Southern Pagoda. When the Emperor heard of this, he lamented for a long time and bestowed upon him the posthumous title of Chan Master Wudeng;
the pagoda was named Jiguang (Tranquil Light).
Zen Master Yun’an Zuqing of Jingshan, Hangzhou, ascended the hall and said: He cited the case where a monk asked Yangqi, “What is the Buddha?
Yangqi replied, “A three-legged donkey prancing on its hooves. The monk asked, “Is it not this very thing?
Yangqi said, “The Elder of Hunan. The Master offered this verse: Yangqi’s one donkey—its eyes shine like...
A flash of lightning! Treading upon and killing all people under heaven—what need is there to speak of "three legs"?
Chan Master Yuanzhou Yangshan Yuan was a native of Ganjiang. After receiving the full precepts, he became courageous and resolute in his pursuit of the Way.

Hearing that Miaoxi resided in Meiyang, he went to rely upon him. He served diligently with the kitchen duties, exerting himself with rigorous austerity. When Miaoxi observed his capacity, [he recognized his potential].

Shi was sharp and quick-witted; he found this extraordinary. Consequently, during a small assembly (*xiaocan*), he heard [the Master] cite: "The mountain master Xiu fully possessed the dharmas of an ordinary person (*pǎnfú*) yet the ordinary person did not know them;
he fully possessed the dharmas of a sage (*shèng rén*) yet the sage did not realize them. If the sage had realized them, he would have been an ordinary person;
if the ordinary person had known them, he would have been a sage. Suddenly, there was a point of resonance. Later, [the Master] presided over Xiangfu in Quzhou, and then moved to Yuanzhou.
Yangshan took up his duties for seven days and then performed the ritual of offering incense according to the Yunmen tradition.

The head seat led the assembly in a prostration, requesting instruction on the great matter of birth and death and the swift nature of impermanence, saying, "We humbly hope that you will compassionately reveal the causes and conditions.

The Master replied slowly, "If you wish to investigate and clarify birth and death, you must directly observe where birth arises from during the four postures of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining."
"Where does one who comes to die go? Ultimately, what is the true face of birth and death? After a long silence, he did not rise from his seat;
he remained still and passed away like a cicada shedding its shell.
○ Chan Master Yunwo Xiaoying of Ganshan was born with karmic affinity in Hongzhou. He was erudite and possessed vast learning, and was skilled at composing literary works.

Chapter. Having long been intimately associated with Miaoxi, what he has attained is immeasurable. Upon hearing that his fellow practitioner Dun’an had been invited to share the seat at Mount Jing, he sent him a *geya* (verse) saying:
"Mount Jing rises abruptly, its peaks piercing the clouds and mist; Dun’an dwells upon its summit, severed from worldly ties.

He grasps the bamboo whisk and shares half the seat; Yet he hurls poisonous breath toward men and gods. The Master [Miaoxi] has the "Cloud-Lying Discourse" (*Yunwo Jitan*) and the "Climbing Vines" (*Luo*).
Two records of his travels, the *Huyan lu*, were circulated in the world.
○ Chan Master Dabe Jian of Tongjiang lived in seclusion at the Bore Monastery in Min County, Fuzhou.
In the Jia-yin year of the Shaoxing era, he was eighty-four years old. Da Hui resided at Yangyu, separated from Bore by only a body of water.

Although the Master was old, he remained profoundly dedicated to investigation. One day, when he entered the room with the assembly as usual, Dahui asked him, "Who is it that does not consort with the myriad dharmas?
The Master replied, "He cannot be supported. Dahui said, "Who is it that cannot be supported? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
As the Master was about to respond, Dahui struck him with his bamboo staff. The Master—
Suddenly he attained awakening. Dahui spoke a verse to seal his realization, saying: "A single blow shatters the cave of birth and death;
at that moment, both ordinary and sage leave no trace of their path. One might laugh instead at Zhaozhou for never resting his mind, still wandering from west to east even in old age."
Master Wuyan Xin of Luyuan in Western Xiangxi was already renowned for his poetry within the monastic community.
Xu Gong Shichuan and Hong Gong Yupu ranked his poetic style as being high and archaic, placing him a head above the likes of Shouquan and Laie.
Later, when Dahui was at Xiaxi in Quannan, he was accompanied by two practitioners from Kang and Nan who were providing vegetarian offerings for the assembly.
While they were tilling the ground with a hoe, Nan said, "Hoetou (The Hoe-head), bring me a phrase! Kang took a clod of earth and threw it onto the handle of the hoe.
At that moment, the Master suddenly attained realization. He once wrote a poem that says: "A new hermitage atop a small stream; The eminent and talented are quite numerous. From... [text continues]
Let him be a Buddha or a Patriarch; let him understand Chan and the Way as he pleases. I take up my hoe and head toward the eastern garden, vowing to spend my old age tending the vegetables.
I begin carrying the water jar at moonrise; I break the midday heat precisely to kill the weeds. The mustard greens are eaten by insects; the autumn eggplants are withered by drought.
From now on, the alms bowl shall depart; I only wish for the turnip to grow well. When gentlemen and scholars visit Xiaoxi, those who are fond of composing poetry— [The text ends here.]
Huìbiàn remarked, "There is a garden master here who is capable of composing poetry. He then accompanied [the Master] to Mount Jing and passed through Hengyang, wandering freely at Mount Heng.
He resided for the longest time at Daowu, where he carved wood to shield himself from wind and rain;

on the western side of the monastery, he hung a signboard for his "Board Hut" (Bàn-ān) and cultivated himself in the leisurely silence of Chan. When Layman Zhang Shitán of Yúhú heard of his lofty character, he sought him out.
The wind exerts its power; he emerges from the world at the Deer Park. He presents him with a poem, saying: "A scroll of poetry has accompanied me for forty years;
In weariness, I have mastered the 'Bamboo Rake' Chan. Now, in my final years, I cast it aside to go to Xiangxi; Lying down, I watch the waters of the Xiang River lap against the sky.
If one has the "eye" within these lines, one will know awakening only upon awakening. One must still strike with a sharp awl; there is not a single body or mind.
Two Uses. When Niaoke picked up a tuft of cloth and blew on it, the Master [Zhaozhou] composed a verse: "The story of the bamboo stick was selected from years past;
Directly, there is no self-interest—this is not Chan. Yuan encountered the Champion Graduate, a true eye; He dares to pick up the agalloch incense before the assembly of humans and devas."

The Master of Zhufeng Hermitage in Quanzhou was named Qinglao; his courtesy name was Guiyan. At the summit of Beishan in Quanzhou, there was a horizontal rock shaped like a boat, which people of the world called "Zhufeng" (Boat Peak).
Since the Master had built a thatched hut at the foot of the mountain, he was subsequently known as the Master of Zhufeng Hermitage.
From an early age, he was admired by both the monastic and lay communities of Southern Quanzhou for his virtue, learning, and literary talent. [He was patronized by] Chancellor Li Hanlao.
Once, when he visited [Dahui] and did not find him, there was a poem that ran roughly as follows: "Huiyuan crossed the stream and should have seen off Lu;

Yu Chuan entered the temple but did not meet Xie. At that time, Dahui’s hut was situated above a small stream, where those in the hundred-seam robe (the monastic community) resided; the Master was also among them.
Yin said to Huì, "The Master’s story of the bamboo stick is like a commoner being harassed by tax collectors:

their property has already been confiscated, yet they still demand payment. Huì replied, "You have only grasped half of it. If there were no one to pay, why not throw yourself into a river or hang yourself?
You should cast off your body and surrender your life! From that time on, the Master’s realization of the Way reached its deepest depths daily. Huì then moved [to another location].
Jingshan subsequently traveled with him and served as his secretary (ji-shi). His compositions were elegant and abundant, greatly enhancing the splendor of the monastic community.
He once inscribed his own portrait, saying: "Examining my eyebrows, they are remarkably lifelike; the hidden horn protruding from my brow reveals my spirit."
Frost-tipped whiskers gradually sprout—what harm is there in growing old? Wearing tattered robes constantly, I endure poverty. All my life, I have been solely wary of my own shadow;

from now on, I am weary of manifesting my body throughout the ten directions. Look at those who chase after clods of earth, countless and chaotic—who among them compares to the solitary rhinoceros of Qingyuan?
Written in the first month of autumn, the Guihai year of the Xiangxing era, as I yield to the natural course of things.
When the Senior Seat Huaiyu first heard Master Wenxiang’s informal sermon at Huangbo in Jinyang, he was struck by the words:
"A single leaf drifts through the void; the great earth is autumn. The Dharma-body must penetrate the clamor. Suddenly, he attained realization.
He subsequently traveled to Mount Jing, where some remarked to Dahui, "Xuan from Mingzhou has come to inquire about our school's fundamental tenets. Dahui replied, "My Chan is like..."
"When the shells of oysters and clams open, their five internal organs are all exposed; what need is there to probe for them? Upon hearing this, the Master was struck with awe and wonder.

Later, while traveling in attendance upon him through Hengyang, he served him diligently for a long time until he attained realization. He once composed a verse on the "Bamboo Ruler" dialogue, saying: "To turn one's back or to touch—both are greatly discordant."
The eyes of those who practice meditation with delusion are like those of sheep; for the sake of another's single grain of rice, they lose their provisions for half a year.
When Xuefeng Huiru heard that Master Wen had received the jade tablet of Huaiyu, he commissioned the Master to travel with him, and together they established a monastic community.

Later, when Wang Shengxi served as a Vice Prefect in Yichun, he presented an official letter and ceremonial gifts to invite the Master to reside at Nanyuan. The Master said, "I have long been a monk who merely prepares porridge and rice; I vow never to..."
"I wish for him to emerge from the world of men. Wang Sheren Pan climbed the mountain to pay his respects and presented him with a poem, which said:
"A master who wears his robe while serving steaming congee; No one has ever seen him descend the mountain. When meeting others, he says only that he has no skill;
Yet he is willing to compose regulated verses for the Red Tower."
○ Nánmín Xiūyǎng, a *shuji* (secretary), served as the head of the record office at Lètán during the Shòngxīng era.

He went to consult Dàhuì at Hénghuáng and attained realization of the essential meaning beneath a single word. Not long after, he followed his master to Méiyāng. The Prefectural Governor, Xiè Cháoyì, said to his subordinates:
"The so-called 'Elder' whom the Imperial Court has exiled is but a single monk. [His quarters shall be] to the east of the Military Command."
He took up residence in a cleared plot of land near his dwelling. Soon, monks arrived daily in numbers reaching several hundred.
They were provided with spades and mattocks to level the foundations, and bamboo and timber were transported to construct huts. As they responded to his commands, none dared to be negligent.
Although the Governor had heard that they were so diligent in their service, he did not yet know who they truly were; he therefore invited one or two of them for an audience to observe them.

The Master was able to comply. Having received the command, he engaged in relaxed conversation for several days; his discourse was brilliant and inspired, as he evaluated the past and deliberated on the present, finding the source of all things at hand.
When Shou Fu and his peers asked, "Are there others who possess extraordinary talents?
the Master replied that there were those who bore the great sutras and śāstras, those whose knowledge of books and history was exhaustive, and those whose poetry and prose were sublime and exquisite.

There are such individuals. There are those whose calligraphy is elegant and unrestrained. Yet, the reason they have not yet attained clear and thorough realization lies solely in the great matter of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
For this reason, he did not shrink from hardships as he came to attend upon me; that he may rely on my benevolent governance is a fortune beyond measure.
I was both startled and filled with wonder, knowing that his disciples were all men who had forgotten their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma. From that time on...
Dahui’s respect for him increased day by day, and he dispatched his son, Chui, to seek a shortcut to the Way. Dahui showed him eight pieces of Dharma discourse.
The Master was rich in learning and gifted with talent; his entry into the Way was steady and authentic. Consequently, he contracted malarial poison and passed away at Chaoyang Guangxiao Temple.
Nun Zhēnrú of Guān-xī was selected for entry into the palace at an early age. On account of her talent, she became an inner lady (*neì fūrén*) and was assigned to the quarters of Consort Qiáo.
Lady Qiáo revered the Buddha and permitted her to shave her hair and travel to various regions to study the Way. She entered Fú-mén and joined the Dharma assembly of Dàhuì at Xiǎoxī.
One day she composed a verse, saying: "Stumbling unexpectedly upon level ground, When one falls, there is nothing at all to be said."
If someone were to ask further how it is so, one would smile and point to the clear wind and bright moon. Hui gave a small lecture (xiaocan) and spoke a verse, saying:
"Today he is like a nun; in former times he was a patriarch-king. Dwelling amidst silks and brocades, he wears only coarse hempen cloth.

Opening his mouth, he speaks with lofty discourse; he detests being a Buddha and refuses to act as one. Leaping out of the pit of right and wrong, he cuts off the path of birth and death. [He] entered...
In the tiger’s den and the demon’s palace, there is no fear in his heart. He has fabricated the *Eight Yang Sūtra* (Bāyáng jīng) himself in three thousand volumes.
He loves to chant rhymed verses, yet refuses to fix their character count. He has wandered the world on foot, but has attained nothing through his Zen practice.
Lately he arrived at Yunmen, and all at once everything was exposed. Mistaking the tip of the pestle for something else, he calls it a winter melon or a gourd. It is like this...
"This is the nun; she advises you to eat less vinegar. There is yet another point that is perverse—tell me, which one is it?
The Great Statue of Jiazhou eats roasted flour; the Iron Ox of Shanfu rips its belly open. From this, the Master’s realization can be seen in general.
The one known as Zu Lin Dao was formerly an upper-tier scholar at the Imperial Academy, named Yang Lin.

In the summer of the Dingchou year of the Shaoxing era, he went to Yuwang Temple, where he donned his official robes and cap to pay homage to Dahui in the Wuyi Hall. Weeping profusely, he said, "I wish to leave the household life under you, Master.
Having finished speaking, he cast down his headwear; then, drawing a pair of scissors from his sleeve, he cut off his own hair himself. Dahui hurriedly called out to him.
Those around him asked for the reason, and he answered them with the facts; they then took him under their care. On the following day, Huìzhào ascended the hall to address the assembly, saying:
"The stall has already been prepared; let us follow the error with the error. Mounting the Holy Monk, one is not without joy. The treading of dragons and elephants is not the work of a donkey.
It is laughable that those in various quarters vainly produce such forced interpretations. Stop this forcing! A rare qilin possesses only—"
A unicorn appeared with a single horn. It prostrated itself and said, "I thank the Master for bestowing a name upon me. He was thus named Zu-lin (Ancestral Unicorn).

Hui further used the words spoken by the Sixth Patriarch to Shiming Upasaka—beginning with "Do not think of good or evil" and ending with "The secret intent lies within you"—to cause him to maintain mindfulness during his daily activities.
From then on, except when Hui himself asked questions, he would respond; both the lay practitioners and the monastic disciples [regarded him as such].
He would not exchange a single word with him. Huiqian was at Ling Shan, and Lin also attended upon him. Having attained thorough realization in the Way, Lin suddenly fell ill.
Huiqian sent his attendant Liaode to inquire after him. Lin wrote a verse on a slip of paper, saying:
"Robes and cap are no longer worn; my hair reaches my eyebrows. In this solitary room, all is tranquil and I am unaware of myself. My physical form is indifferent; I merely manifest this illness."
He aroused many doubts in other bodhisattvas. He then went to the market, purchased three pieces of incense, and as he burned them, he made a vow, saying:
"In a future life, may I be born as a male and encounter an enlightened master; may I enter the Way in my youth. Once the incense had been burned, he passed away peacefully.
The Lin family was of Jianyang origin and were descendants of Wen Gong.
The Wayman Wujì was the daughter of Minister Zhāng Yuándào.
During her time as a laywoman, a physiognomist passed by her and said, "This is one who shall sit upon a precious throne to preach the Dharma. Later, she indeed became a nun named Huìzhào.
She succeeded her tonsure master, Master Shòu Wúzhù, in his seat. She once praised Chan Master Yuánwù with a *Yújiā'áo* verse, which says: [Verse omitted per instructions]

Seven times he sat at the site of enlightenment, three times he received imperial summons. When will the flowers in space and the moon in water ever end? Within the sound of the young jade bell, he once awakened to the Way.
Truly it is laughable how, from the beginning, he has deceived his descendants with such fine sophistry. The sound of the ocean tide rolls on vast and great;
as clear as the bright moon shining in the sky, he returns westward with his flying staff as the clouds vanish into the distance. The gibbons of Ba cry out; let everyone join in the song and return.

Local Customs: After his passing while seated in meditation and following his tonsure, countless śarīra relics were found. Although it was the height of the sweltering summer, his countenance remained solemn and intact for several days.
○ The Daoist Chaozong was the mother of Liu Jigao’s younger son; she was a fellow practitioner with the Daoist Wujì.
Regarding those who received their predictions together at the gate of Mahamati: Wujie once visited Jingshan to sweep the pagoda, where he composed this verse:
"The robes are damp with the tears of Vulture Peak; The incense burns in the cauldron of Shaoshi. Clouds and mountains fill the eyes with emptiness;
I do not see the King of the Dharma. At that time, Zong had not yet arrived. Wujie sent someone to urge him on, to which Zong replied with a verse: "The pagoda is originally free of dust."
What is the use of going to sweep? Sweeping only causes dust to arise; that is why he did not arrive.
[This concludes the section on] Chan Master Xiatang Yuan, Dharma heir of Lingyin.
○ Lake-yin Jidian’s Daytime Record contains a verse on the story of Bodhidharma meeting Emperor Wu of Liang, which says: “He did not accord with the Emperor of Liang.”
Crossing the river in secret: with no place to hide one’s shame and fear. What was accomplished by facing the wall for nine years?

It only deceived ordinary people and sent them into the cauldron of boiling oil. The Verse on the Life and Origins of the Fifth Patriarch: Originally a monk from the old days of Huangmei, serving his master until old age, his vigor only increased.
Turning his body, he cast down the mattock for planting pine trees; taking a step, he came to divide the lamp that illuminates the world. His leather bag—
I entrusted her to a maiden by the stream; her robes and bowl were given to Neng of Lingnan. Her excellent reputation shall endure for a long time;
after the rain has passed, the mountains of Huai stand tier upon tier in emerald green.
The Dharma Successor of Chan Master Cizhao Chun:
Zen Master Donglin Bao of Zhengzhou. A monk asked, "When humans and devas meet and ordinary beings and sages arrive together, what should be discussed when teacher and disciple see one another?
The Master said, "At the place where Kāśyapa smiled, the time for Mahādeva’s teaching is now. The monk said:
When the sandalwood tree produces a sandalwood branch, people know it exists. "The blue surpasses the indigo"—I beg the Master to speak quickly.
The Master said, "Crows do not cry out in confusion; magpies do not chatter in disorder. The monk said, "If that is so, then the lineage is divided at Linji and the lamp is transmitted to Cizhao."
The Master said, "Since arriving at the peak of the solitary mountain, the majesty of the surrounding peaks has naturally become high.
The monk said, "It can truly be said that though the myriad flowers differ, the power of spring is fundamentally impartial. The Master said, "What was the phrase you spoke just now?

The monk said, "A brand-new sun and moon; a particularly striking splendor. The Master said, "Where else could it be anything but clear? Ascending the hall, he said: "A man of spirit should act for himself..."
Powerful! First he seizes the six bandit kings, overturns the black mountain cave, and raises high the banner of radiant light.

Entering into phenomena, he perceives the human mind; entering into principle, he awakens to the non-constant. But tell me, when awakening to the non-constant, what is it like? The cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of burning coals are the ground of True Suchness (Tathatā);
the sword-trees and knife-mountains are the ancient site of enlightenment. [The Master] rests his staff horizontally upon his knee, makes the gesture of drawing a sword, and then descends.

Taking his seat, he ascended the hall and said: "The Great Function manifests before us; it is fundamentally not a matter of intellectual understanding. Revealing its entire reality, it is perfectly true, responding to conditions with sovereign ease.
It stands solitary and prominent, towering and majestic; encompassing all of space, it is neither internal nor external. It harmonizes the myriad phenomena without a thread’s breadth of separation;

it shines universally throughout the ten directions, pervading the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātu*. It may be called that which is free from names and forms, transcending even the slightest hair’s breadth or speck of dust—wondrous indeed."
The light of the subtle mind of renunciation shines brilliantly. Not dwelling in what is heard or seen, one dwells in leisure everywhere.

Such discourse has already entered the realm of idle words; as soon as there is form or sound, it becomes a sentence or meaning. Since names do not intersect [with reality], how can they be raised or chanted? With his whisk, he drew a perfect circle and said:
"The primordial radiance and auspicious signs of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are like this. He then descended from his seat.
*Supplement to the Five Lamps Compendium* (End).
Succession unknown; appended here.
Chan Master Foguang Daowu was a native of Lanzhou in Shaan-you. His surname was Guàn. He was born with teeth. At the age of... [text fragment ends]
At sixteen, he shaved his head. Two years later, while traveling, he returned from Lintao and stayed overnight at Wanzi Dian.
There, a monk in monastic robes called out to him in a dream; upon waking, he happened to hear a horse neighing, whereupon he attained sudden enlightenment.
He sang to himself: "Good indeed, Luo! Good indeed, Luo! Throughout the entire realm of empty space, there is but one. He told his mother, "Last night I picked up something. His mother—
He asked, "What have you found? He replied, "It is that which has been lost since beginningless time.
One day, wishing to visit a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), a villager sought a verse from the Master. The Master’s verse contained the lines: "When water flows, it must reach the sea;
when a crane emerges, it rises above the white clouds. Upon reaching Xiongeri, he visited Master Baoyun Hai and their minds were in accord. Previously, there had been a question [posed to him].
The Duke asked, "Why do you not select a dharma heir? Haichang did not answer. He spoke slowly, saying, "A fragrant orchid has blossomed, uniquely emerging from Western Qin.
When the Master arrived, the Duke heard a voice in the air saying, "Tomorrow, receive Guest Minister Guo.

This was because the temple where Haichang resided had been built by Guo Ziyi, and the Master was his later incarnation. After Master Haichang passed away, the Master entered the world and resided at Zheng.
He succeeded to the Dharma at Puzhao Temple in the prefecture. Subsequently, he retired to Zhuge Hermitage and lived amidst the common folk along the Luo River, such that no one could fathom him.
He once said to people: "If you say I am an ordinary person, I shall go toward the rank of a sage; if you say I am a sage..."
I am going into the realm of the ordinary. I say that I am neither saint nor ordinary person; I go into your eyes and nostrils, tumbling and rolling about.
On the thirteenth day of the fifth month in the fifth year of the Taihe era, he passed away without illness.
At his dwelling, there were five-colored clouds above the roof like a canopy; within them was a red light, circular like the sun, appearing three times.
His lifespan was fifty-five years.
Master Xuanming Yi, the first patriarch and founder of Qingshou Monastery, ascended the hall for discourse. He first illuminates and then employs [his means] to examine [the student].
After striking, first apply it and then reflect upon it to examine the matter. If reflection and application are simultaneous, there is no need for even a single squeeze.
If reflection and application are not simultaneous, everyone stands while the old monk sits. But what about when neither of these is the case? How then?
He gave a shout and said: "In this vast expanse of red dust, how many people have a forehead? He ascended the hall and said:
"Nowadays, among the monks who practice Zen, those who wish to become Buddhas or Patriarchs are as numerous as hemp or millet.

But those who would rather be donkeys or horses—though one might search the entire Great Jin Empire with a torch, not a single one could be found. Fortunately, there are none; such is the case under the gate of Qingshou."
How could there be so much idle grass and idle fodder to feed and discard? Take care. Descend from the seat. Ascending the hall:
This play on the crossroads street, the monkey climbing the flagpole—though it be but an idle feat, do not regard it as trivial. To cite Yunmen:
"Within the realm of heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure, hidden within the mountain of form. [He] picks up the lamp.
He carried the lantern toward the Buddha Hall and placed the mountain gate atop it. He spoke this verse: A thousand-foot surge of whitecaps on level ground;
Two or three peals of thunder in a cloudless sky. Pitiful is the traveler who waits by the stump under the moon; The cool rabbit never encounters the spring grasses growing.
Chan Master Lingyun Sheng’an Si of Wenzhou was a native of Ninghai, Tiantai. His family name is unknown.

Of four brothers, he was the eldest. At one time, they all resolved together to leave the household life and distributed their ancestral inheritance entirely among their kinsmen, retaining only the house where they lived.
When the clan members continued to dispute over it without ceasing, the Master and his younger brothers...

Each took a torch, set it ablaze, and departed. Later, the Master went on pilgrimage and attained the higher realization and insight. He appeared in the world at Lingyun Temple. During the summer retreat, he ascended the hall and said:
"The Great Perfect Enlightenment, the horns of an ox, and the horns of a horse—these shall serve as my monastery’s melon basket, vegetable basket, and greens basket.
Ascending the hall again, he cited the koan of Zhaozhou’s "The dog has no Buddha-nature" and composed a verse, saying: "The dog has no Buddha-nature."
"The dog has Buddha-nature. The monkey frets, searching its head; the dog runs, shaking its mouth. Later, he retired to a thatched hut before Lingyun Temple.
In the year Jia-shen of the Zhi Zheng era, when Yuan Zhongshu and Ming Xingyuan went to pay their respects, the Master was over ninety years old.
With bushy eyebrows and white hair, tall and dignified, he came out trailing his sandals. Moreover—
As he was walking by, [the Master] asked, "Where have you come from? Shuzhong replied, "From Jiangxin. [The Master] asked, "How many fathoms deep is it there?
Shuzhong said, "You cannot deceive the Old Monk. The Master bowed and said, "Sit and drink tea. The Master’s character was upright and austere. His poetry was much like that of Hanshanzi.
He inscribed a poem titled "Abusive Verses on Monks" upon a wall, which read: "The Five Pestilence Spirits do not strike; One shaves one's own head. A yellow cloth encircles the body, and then..."
This monk knows neither the Buddha-dharma nor the worldly dharma; he is simply quite capable of feeding on pigs and dogs. I beg you to spare me and allow me to pass by;

I dare not again challenge his sharp edge. That evening, he stayed at Lingyun, where he heard the old master recount several instances of the Master’s words and deeds, all of which were worthy of transmission.

Chan Master Juezhao Hui of Shouchang in Wenzhou sat in summer retreat at Jingci Monastery. Within the plastered wall of his eastern purification quarters hung a water-ink painting of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Every night the Master would prostrate before it with the utmost sincerity and earnestness.

Suddenly, he saw the water from the pure vase surge forth from the wall; his entire body was filled with joy. From that time on, his spiritual realization deepened further and his wisdom and discernment became increasingly clear. Once...
A verse says: "Before one's efforts have reached the ground of perfection, How many times have I leaned on the railing, grieving alone?
Today is the third, tomorrow the fourth; The snow and frost easily take their toll upon the human head."
Chan Master Sian Rui of Yuan Tong at Mount Lu in Jiangzhou possessed unimpeded eloquence.

Whenever a practitioner sought a verse from him, the Master would say, "Speak a phrase. One day, a monk intentionally sought to challenge the Master, saying, "The Western Mountain enters Tengwang Pavilion.
The Master then wrote a continuation of it, saying: "All the people of the great earth search for it in vain, yet suddenly—"
Yet it protrudes from the tip of the staff; its peak towers over the Five Marchmounts, its eyes are triangular. This has been widely acclaimed throughout the seas.
○ Lord Wang Wenxian was a patriarch of the Confucian school for his generation, yet his realization of Buddhist principles was profound.
Although his writings were not intended for such purposes, they harmonize perfectly with the proclamations of the ancient worthies. He inscribed this for a monk: "Orchids on a Precipice."
It is said: "The spring breeze blows equally upon all, yet what can one do when perched so high? Let them harbor their own inverted thoughts;
they must see the moment of letting go from the precipice. On the Portrait of Dongpo: "The Fifth Patriarch was a man beyond the world;
long ago in this Sahā world he severed the cause of birth. Who would use a hand that paints empty space to seek his body in years to come?"
Regarding the outer body, I inscribed this upon a portrait of Master Shan谷 (Shangu): "It would have made the old Huìtáng laugh to death, When we met, he insisted that the osmanthus was fragrant.
Beholding the portrait, his features remain exactly as they were; How could there ever have been any difference in the length of his nostrils?"
Lady Ding, whose courtesy name was Juozhen and style name Zhuxin, was a native of Haotou in Huangyan. Initially, she attained a realization while attending Tian Juegeng at Weiyushan;
she subsequently abandoned her family to dwell alone in a thatched hut. Later, she visited Gu Yu at Yongquan.
Yunyu said, "Why is it that a woman of good family is running here and there? Ding replied, "I have come specifically to see the Master.
Yunyu said, "I have no room for you here. Ding clapped his hands once and said, "That which you used for thirty years has been caught out today.
Yunyu then desisted. Later, Ding went to see Wuji at Chūn-yu Hermitage on Eagle Mountain. Upon entering the gate, he called out, "Chūn-yu! (Spring Rain).
It was like a traveler with grease on his hands who detested the mud; when he reached the gate, Yun said, "Not it! Not it! As he prepared to offer a word, he was shouted out.
In his later years, he established a reception hall before Mingyin Temple. A monk carrying a bundle entered straight into his quarters, and he asked, "What kind of monk are you?
The monk replied, "A wandering monk. He asked again, "Why is the string on the straw sandals at your feet broken?"
[The monk] did not know. The monk remained silent. Ding then threw the bundle out and said, "There is no place here for you to set foot.
Furthermore, as soon as another monk entered the gate, Ding said, "Master Bodhidharma has arrived! The monk said, "I am not he. Ding said, "He certainly is;
it is just that our nostrils are different. One day, he met the nun Mingyin and the Elder Kui, and asked:
Yunwen asked, "Elder, did you give birth to a son last night? The Master replied, "Tell me, is it a boy or a girl?
Ding said, "A rooster runs off with a lamp; a turtle bites a fishing rod."
